TIADOWB7. How we love the lingering lights As the eveiiing shadows fall. When the wings of hovering night Spread in darkness over all. How we p 1 z 8 departing day, Hoping for return of morn, When the sun's last, farewell ray, Blushing from our gaze is borne " How we miss the happy hours When they mingle with the past, When unsweet affliction lowers, And our pathway, cvercast, Pains us with the somb:e stain That disfign es ali we see; E'en we sigh. prrelranc,s In vain, Gazing backssards longingly ! How we shudder in the storms When the d-eper shadows glide, When entombed beim, dl torms, Coldest clays lie side by side. ,4h! the dimming mist of grief Chills us with i's utter dearth; Even hope gives no relief With such shsd ,ws o'er the earth t' Yet the sl.adows should not awe, Though predominant i heir sway; Who in darkness sver saw Night prevent the dawn of day? Should we crush the na•cent life, Hope all trembling in the bud, Just as though the present strife • Robbed us of the future good? Shnuld we yield to each dark care, Cautioned by the bassing gale, That the load. perhw_is, we bear Will eternally prevail? It is foolish to repine, -- It is wise to hope and w‘it, Letting raiih our heats entwine, 'Though the shadows seem so great; Let them fall. Is ea, frowning hide The noontldb do d of lle.t Clouds that now before u.s glide, To-morrvv; quit our sight. A "still. small voice" its unction gives. Soothing ele-h aching !yeast. It /Nnetrates the heart, it lives! Setting all fears .a.t re t Warrington, Sept. 25, 1882.
BENJAMIN SIWDON.
MAN% MORTALITY.

[The original of the following beautiful poem is found in an Irish MS. in Trinity College, Dablin. There is reason to thiini that it was written by one of the primitive Christian barns in the reign of King Diarrnid, about the year 554, and was sung or chanted at the last grand wsembly of kings, chieftains, and bards ever held in the famous halls of Tara. The translation I, by Dr. O'Donovan.] Like a damask rose you see, Or a blossom on a tree, Or like the dainty flowers In May, Or like the morning to the day. Or like the sun, or like the sh,cle, Or like the gourd which Jonah had. Even such a man, whose thread is spun, Drawn out and out, and so is done. /benne withers, the blossom blasteth. Tio; fou-wer the raOroing hasteth, The sun sets, the shadow The gourd consumes, the man—he died. Like the grass that's newly sprung, , Or like the tale that's new begun, Or like the bird that's here to-day. Or like the pearled dew in May, Or like the singing of the swan— Even such Is man, who lives by breath, Is here, now there in life and death. The grass withers, the tale is ended, - , The bird is flown, the dew's ascended, The hour Is short, the span not long. The swan's near death, man's life is done. Like the bul,ble in the brook, Or like a glass, or like a look, Or like the shuttle in a weaver's hand, Or like the writing on the sand, Or like a thought, or like a dream, Or like the gliding of the stream, Even such is man, who lives by breath. Is here, now there, in life or death. The bubble's out, the look's forgot. The shuttle's flung, the writing's blot, Te thought is past, the dream is gone, The wales glide, man's life is done. Like to an arrow from the bow, Or like the swift course from water flow. Or like that time 'twist flood or ebb, Or like the spider's tender web, Or like a race, or like a goal, Or like the dealing of a dole. Even such is man, whose brittle state Is always subject unto fate. The arrow shot, the flood soon spent, The time no time, the web soon rent, The race is run, the goal soon won, The dole soon dealt, man's life is done. Like to the lightning in the sky, Or like a post that quick doth hie, Or like a quaver in a song, Or like a journey three days long, Or like a snow when summer's gone, Or like a pear, or like a plum, Even such is man, who heaps up sorrow, Lives but this day, and dies to-morrow. The lightning's past, the post must go, The song is short, the journey so, The pear dn.h rot, the plum cloth fall. The snow dissolves, and so must all.

If the thought of dying were oftener before us, sfrfal things would lose their deceitful inflaence.—Rorcland Hill. He is truly great that is little in himself, and that maketh no account of any heieit n 1 honours. Begin with modesty if you wouldend with honour. Let your religion be seen. Lamps do not talk, but they do shine. A. lighthouse sounds no drum, it beats no gong; yet far over the waters it." friendly light is seen by the mariner.

Jost in proporti xi as you gain a victory over the evil which you have become a,,are of in yourself, will your spiritual eyes be purged for a bright perception of the Holy One.—,Ohanning. 'Homes are like harps, of which one Is finely carved, and bright with gilding, but ill•tuned, and jarring the air with Its discords; while another is old and plain and worn, but from its chords float strains that are a feast of range. It is a very indiscreet and troublesome ambition which cares so much about fame; about what the world says of us; to be always looking in the faces of others for approval; to be always anxious about the effect of what we do or say; to be always shouting, to hear the echoes of our own voices. Neither rich furniture, nor abundance of gold, nor :a descent from an illustrious family, nor greatness of autho- rity, nor eloquence and all the charms of speaking, can pro- cure so grett a serenity of life as a mind free from guilt, kept untainted, not only from actions, but purposes, that are wicked.—Platarck.

Two soldiers were bivouacking in the neighbourhood of Alexandria; lying beneath their blankets, they were look. tag up at the stare. 841 d Jack, "What made you go into tie army, Tom 2" "Well," replied Tom, "I had no wife, and loved war. What made you go fighting, Jack ?" "Well," said Jack, "I had a wife and loved peace; so I went 1"

Never talk about a child's peculiarities before it. The great charm of childhood is its forgetfulness of itself, its utter ignorance of the state of its own attire and its own mind, its e.apability of forgetting whether it is ill or well clad. Do not tell it that it is studious, or playful, or proud, lest you make it affected; and do not let it hear its beauty or its ugliness alluded to. There are some dispensations of nature which are not easily comprehended by the casual inquirer, and do not be- come very much plainer when carefully examined. One of them was remarked upon the other day by a young lady. "It is very curious," she observed, "altogether unacconnt- able, indeed, that the tortoise, from whom we get all our tortoise-shell combs, has himself no hair whatever." The Washington Critic tells an odd story of Oscar Wilde. A Baltimore lady asked him when he was going South ; to which he responded, " South ? South? What do you mean by South ?" The lady had to explain that he was only on the border of the Southern States, and asked him if he had never studied geography. "Oh, no," WO his reply, "I could not, for the colours on the maps are so discordant, and they distress me so, I could never brirg myself to look at them."

THE MYER. Clear and cool, clear and cool, By laughing shallow, and dreaming pool; Cool and clear, cool and clear, By shining shingle and foaming weir; Under the crag where the ouzel sings, And the ivied wall where the church bell rings, Undefiled, for the undefiled; Play by me, bathe in me, mother and child. —Kingsley. A widow called at the sculptor's study to see the clay model of the bust of her husband. "I can change it in any particular that you may desire, madam," said the artist. The woman regarded it with tearful eyes. "The nose is large." A large nose is an indication of goodness," re- sponded the artist. The widow wiped away her tears and sobbed, "Well, then, make the nose larger." LIEN IN TE.NNESSIEIL—There is, perhaps, no part of the United States where life goes on more calmly than in the region of the Cumberland Mountains, Tennessee. This beautiful wilderness is thinly peopled by a race of et natives "—that is, white settlers and squatters, who are as unaffected by the fierce activities of their fellow-citizens in the Eastern and Western States as if they were inhabitants of another continent, or men of another age. Their home- - steads are remote from highways; and these highways are so little frequented, that weeks may pass without a stra-ger appearing. Havirg very imperfect means of transport 11,r corn or cattle to paying markets, they grow just sufficient for their own use; and simple wants are easily satisfied in a sub-tropical climate. Maize is the staple food, wheitel, bread being rarely eaten. Swine-flesh, of the toughen an least nutritious sort, farnisheo much of the "heel fe°4' Milk is little used. Intoxicating drinks are rarely partaken of, though a good deal of peach brandy and corn whisker are said to be made illicitly. Bat these are sold to saloon- keepers in bye-places, and the money expended in powder, hot, and the few articles required for a primitive house- hold. Tea and coffee are the favourite stimulants of Ten. nessee natives, particularly the later. WLea whisky is not made, game is sold at the nearest town ta obtain what is needed; and often the hunter will go ten miles with a pair of deer hams, half a dozen turkeys, rabbit, or other spoils of the chase; and glad is he to to-rine; b.mk a few pounds of ;;;Tea eidarz3—Citalti!,frs' Jc,uena'.

RICHARD WAGNER AND VEGETARIANIsSI.—It has been frequently raid that Wagner is a vegetarian. This is a mistake, whose origin is best explained in the following passege from a letter written by a well-known German vegetarian and author :—" Richard Wagner's publications on historical, literary, and philosophical subjects fill many volumes, and are not so well known as they deserve to be. Last year be published a pamphlet on 'Religion and Are,' which was full of the deepest thoughts, and be showed in it that vegetarianism is one of the most powerful of the agents for the regeneration of mankind. The newspaper correspondents came to the conclusloa that the daeulty of , providing food for all the visitors to the Nieelungen in 1676 at Bayreuth had forced Wagner in 1882 to become a vege- tarian by preouoopi The feet is, that 'Richard Wagner considers himself too old to change Hs accustomed mode of life, and therefore his eiteocacy of vegetarianism is theoreti- cal only. His words, however, have Influenced Some of his friends and admirers to be practical vegetarians. In July and August, at the performancee of . Pereira' ' in Beyreuth, care was taken to provide for the vegetarians, who had a separate dining-room in the rooms of the club 'Frohsinn.' The vegetarians were about forty in number, and the society downstairs became curious to taste the Venetian soup, which was found to be good, and so the soup and the vegetables were cooked for all without flesh•meat. Consequently the separation ceased. 'Clean' soap and vegetables were given to every visitor, and after that the vegetarians ordered their fruit and the fleeh•eaters their roast beef in close proximity. But it was very agreeable for a vegetarian to feel himself nearest to the heart of the 'Master of Bayreuth,' and to be a folly acknowledged guest not liable to the sneers of publi- cans. The days of ' Patellae' will be a pleasant memory of every vegetarian who witnessed the performance." SMOKY CIIIMNEYS.—The attention of the Mathematical and Physical Section of the British Association was, on \August 30, called by their president, Lord Rayleigh, to the i very hutelle practical inquiry as to the effect of wind on the draught of chimneys. As a prime feature in the arch'- : tectare of dwelling-house, the chimney demands a chapter to itself. And it is well that the basis of this chapter rhould i he mathematical. With regard to draught, we have more i than once had occasion to remark that it is a function of the , height of chimney tubes. We do not, of coarse, apply the 1 remark without modification to the details of ill-constructed ' chimneys. Many chimneys smoke from positive illmon- , etruction, having a narrow part, an ugly band, or a down- Iward portion, in-their conduit, which the normal draught is not strong enough to overcome. Others smoke because they form the shorteet channel by which air can enter the house to supply the draught of the loftier chimneys. Where there are two chimneys in one room, and the doors and win- dows are closed, lighting a fire in one chimney will ordi- narily cities, down draught in the other, as the readiest mode of maintaining the atmospheric equilibrium. In most cases, however, the addition of a yard or so to the height of the chimney-stack, supposing that to be already above the • highest part of the interior of the house which it ventilates, will prove more useful than the addition of any of those curiously contorted and wholly non-pneumatie contrivances ' the endless variety of which tortures the eye of the n2echani- cally-minded man as be whhets along the suburb on railways. We think it cannot be too strongly insisted on that when, , first, the subject of up-draueht, and, secondly, that of wind- , protection—or, rather, wind-induced draught—are seen to be thoroughly within the control of science, it will be felt to j be unpardonable to be condemned to the great nuisance of a ! smoky chimney. 1 'The NECESSITY TOR HOLIDAYS.—If it were strictly , true, as Dr. Fothergill assumes in a paper in the current , number of Good Words, that "some little time ago, not more than a generation, holidays were associated with school children; and rarely d:d any one of adult years talk of a holiday," that would go far to prove that the "necessity for hoddays" was a demand created by supply. Such, how- ever, is not quite the fact. It is undoubtedly true that holidays are more cammon than they used to be and that : they are now enjoyed by classes of the people to whom they were until recently unparticipated luxuries; but for all 1 time it has been the practice of brain workers to rest from their labours for a short time periodically. Those who did not do this, except in rare instances of particalarly wisely ordered work or of extraordinary vigour, wore compelled by an oft-recurring threat of breakdown to take the rest they would otherwise have refused. In short, holidays are a ne- cessity, growing out of the physiological need for periods of store replenishing, when the reserves of strength can be made. up. It is impossible to lay too great stress on the fact that the economising of the buoyancy and vigeeir of life i very much depends on the integrity of those reserves of ! mental and nervous force which it is the main purpose of 1 the holiday to replenish. Mere "rest" will not accomplish this result. Every part of the organism, the brain and ner- vous system included, feeds as it works. There must be exercise, or there will not be appetite; and without appetite an abundant supply of food is of little avail.—Leecet. THE INFLUENCE OF rOI2ISTS ON CLISIATE.—Dr. Sehom• , burgh., the Director of the Botanical Gardens at Adelaide, I has added to his recently issued report an appendix on the subject of the influence of forests on climate. The object of this Paper is to prove that the destruction of forests usually has the effect of reducing the rainfall, while, on the contrary, the planting of trees broadcast over a country is one of the Is ‘t methods which can be adopted for ameliorat- ing its climate and increasing the anneal fall of rain. It cannot, indeed, be proved that the climate of South Aus- tralia is altering for the worse in this respect. In fact, a comparison of the meteonslogical records will chow that the annual average rainfall for the colony during the past ten years has been 21.1 in., as compared with 20.1 in. for the pre- vious ten years. The fact is that in the agricultural dis- tricts of the colony, and especially in those which were not originally timbered, the bringing of the land into cultivation has had the effect of slightly favouring the fall of rain. Plonehed land attracts moisture to a much greater degree than the unbroken soil. In considering the effect which the removal of forests per se has in altering the climate in South Australia, the only direct test that could be taken from the records issued by the Government astronomer is the experience of the neighbourhood of Adelaide. If the time is divided which has elapsed since 1839, the year in which observations were commenced, into two periods, there is found for the first an average rainfall of 22.81 n.. and for the second one of 21-7 in. It will thus be seen thet, on the whole, the rainfall at Adelaide is diminishing, though very slightly, and perhaps the diminution in the amount of tim- ber may have something to do with the change. Dr. &item- hurgke in searching for illustrations of the effect of trees on climate, goes farther afield, and brings forward some strik- Leg instances, in which it is evident that leas of forests means loss of rainfall, and vice versa.

FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE.
The Czar's visit to Moscow has been crowned with com- plete success. He has been enthusiastically received every- where, and has ridden about in an open carriage in perfect safety.
A. "constantinople correspondent telegraphs that the Greek question is arranged, the Porte having cons.mted to waive its claims on all the four points of the frontier which were at issue.

The sugar refinery of Messrs. Harrison, Havemeyer, and Co., of Philadelphia, was totally destroyed by fire on Mon- day. The loss is 1,000,000 dols. This was the largest sugar refinery in the country. The rebels at Atcheen, in the Dutch East Indies, have sustained a crushing defeat. The combined Dutch land and naval forces attacked the enemy and drove him with great loss from all the positions he held. Nya Hassan, the chief of the rebellion, was seriously woanded. The destruction caused by the floods in the Tyrol is so I extensive that the railways in several parts will not be in a condition to be worked for at least a month. tome villages have been almost entirely destroyed, and there is great distress.

A train carrying Sell's circus and menagerie has been wrecked on an American railway. Men and animals were crushed together, and a tiger escaped from its confinement, but, apparently not liking the "situation," the animal voluntarily returned to the cage, and was secured. It is re- ported that three men were killed and eleven injured. The suggestion to construct a second canal through the Isthmus of Suez has called forth a communication from M. F. de Lesseps, who states that the concession of the Sipz Canal Company declares that the company possesses for 99 years the exclusive privilege of a maritime communication between the Gulf of Peluse and the Gulf of Suez.

ZPLITLAND.—According to the most recent news from Natal, apprehension as to the result of the restoration of Cetywayo is dying away, and fear of any real opposition is no longer entertained. The secret of this change of senti- ment is to be found in the announcement that General Smith, Commander-in-Chief of the British forces in South Africa, is to accompany Cetywayo with a force ef cavalry and artillery.' The Military Governor of Taieff has deposed Ablul Moutahif, the Grand Shereef of Mecca, and imprisoned him, appointing in his stead Alalullah Ahuoun, brother to the Shereef, who was murdered some time age. This action gave rise to considerable agitation both at Mecca and Taieff, but order has been restored for a time. The Porte has des- patched troops to Jeddah. Congratulations are offered by4aerman newspapers of all shades of opinion to Prince Bismarck on the twentieth an- niversary of his admission to the Prussian Ministry; hut many Liberal papers, 'while admitting the krince's high statesmanship, take exception to his reactionary financial policy, and the list of Ministers who have resigned one after another—Dr. Delbrueck, Herr Von Camphausen, Dr. Falk, Dr. Frfedenthal, Dr. Achenbacb, and the two Counts Eulen- burg—is produced to show how dangerous a thing indepen- dence is when it runs counter to Prince Bismarck's will. , A FATAL EXCHANGE Op SALT-MS.—The French frigate M:nerve, with Admiral Grevy on board, 'arrived in New York harbour on Sunday. Arrangements were made for ex- -changing salutes on Monday with the garrisost of the Governor's Island. After ten rounds had been fired from Castle William, on the island, two guns prematurely ex- ploded, and two men were killed and four badly wounded. The sparks that were blown back by the strong wind into the embrasures, it is believed, caused the explosions. Stanley, the finder of Liv;- intone and the hero of gle "Dark, continent." ein ban ord- • en sy_ reappeared in Europe, having arrived at tal.'s)aon on Wednesday from Loada, at which place hu Mitered gYeatly from malaria and fever. After a month' a busing he recovered sufficiently to Cotttinue the journey, He gives a glowing account of the success of hi a most recent undertaking, having opened up 300 miles of country, established fifteen trading stations and so conciliated the natives that his men do not need any defensive weapons, except walking-sticks. This introduc- tion of trade into the valley of the Congo may be the founda- tion of a great African trade By way of this river immense fertile regions can be reached, and by forming locks at the rapids it is believed that it can be made navigtble to a point more than half way to Zanzibar. Our Inaian Empire had no more encouraging a commencement. TERRIBLIA RAILWAY ACCIDBNTS.—A terrible accident happened on Saturday to a train which was crossing a wooden bridge over the Drava at Eszsg, a short distance from the junction of that river with the Danube. A por- tion of the bridge fell, and the vine and trucks following it were precipitated into the river' dragging with them a number of carriages containing hussars on furlough. Fifteen soldiers are missing, and thirty are injured. Fortu- nately the latter portion of the train, which contained the general passengers, escaped injury through a coupling chain bre tking. The exceptionally high water in the river, caused by the recent heavy rains, was, it is alleged, the primary cause of the disaster.—Twelve passengers have been killed and forty seriously injured by a collision in the tunnel of the railway past outside the Grand Central DepOt in New York.

I RAPE NOTES, A large contingent of Hull joiners arrived in Glasgow, on Tuesday, to fill the places of the Clyde shipjoiners who have been on strike for some time, seeking an advance of a halfpenny per hour on their wages. The Barrow Hematite Iron and Steel Company have re- ceived an order from Australia for 10,000 tens of steel rails. It has been incorrectly reported that the whole of the 30,000 tons required were ordered from Belgium. It will be seen that a third part has been given to Barrow. BILLS OF SALE AND Fstmenns. In the week ending September 23, 1882, there were 711 bills of sale in England and Wales, .a decrease of 289 over those of the correspond- ing period last year; and the failures gazetted numbered 159, a decrease of 15. The totals for portion of year to September 23, 1882, are bills of sale registered for England and Wales, 34,744, a decrease of 1,996; the failures gaz Ated numb-r 7,774, a decreaee of 753.—Stubb's .3fercantile Gazette. A conference of delegates, representing all the mining die. trims of Scotland, was held on Wednesday at Glasgow, and it was unanimously agreed to demand an increase of wages to the extent of 15 per cent. over the present scale. The employers' replies will be received a week hence, and should they prove unfavourable a general strike is anticipated. In North Wales the leading proprietors, in response to the de- mand for an advance, have issued a notice increasing the price of coal, aid state that this proceeding is instituted so that they may be able to meet the men's Wishes. THE WEATHER AND THE CORN TRADE.—The Mark Lane Express says :—" The rainfall has not yet been more than sufficient to make ploughing of dry land easy and agreeable. As a rule land hi eaks very well, and present in- dications are in favour of good seed beds for the autumn sown wheat. The results of the wheat crop up to the pre- sent have ben found to be very variable, both in respect of quality and quantity, the yield in most cases being less than growers expected. The condition of native offerings does not improve, and values continue to droop. Provincial markets have generally shown about a shilling decline during the past week, whilst ia London on Friday values appeared to be 2s. lower than on Monday last. Low as values now are, a still lower basis seems likely to be reached. Country flour in London has also declined about Is. per sack since Monday, making 2s. during the week. Malting barleys of fine quality and good colour, and old oats, appear to be the only description of native produce which are now in favour of sellers. Trade for foreign wheat off stands in London gets trom bad to worse. Foreign flour for the moment is in smaller supply to London; but values on Fri- day were generally lower." The Farmer says—" Fair weather and fair supplies are against activity in the market', which remains dull. English wheat is offered at lsedecline, foreign sorts at 6d. to is. from last Monday, rates being really low. Flour neglected; is. cheaper forcountry made and 6d. for foreign. Barley in fair request at old prices. Oats steady at late reductions. Beans and peas unchanged. Maize irregularly cheaper. The position of the market re- mains discouraging to holders." THE SALVATION ARMY AT BOMBA.Y.—An account of the landing at Bombay of tke Indian contingent of the Salvation Army last week points to the probability of serious distur- bances. We are told that during the procession of war chariots and tambourinists through the streets one of the army, who persisted in blowing a trumpet in contravention of the police regulations, was arrested.. The natives seem to have takna the band for circus people, and it is even sug- gested that the procession was taken as a gratuitous display by the Government in commemoration of the victory inEgypt. The correspondent of the Times remarks :—" It is generally felt here by those most experienced in the special charac- teristics of native thought that the attempt, however honest in intention, to proselytise the natives of India by clothing the solemn tenets of Christianity in an unseemly surround- ing of vulgar buffoonery can but end in defeating its own object, as it will disgust the feeling of grave reverence almost universally experienced by the natives for all religious sub- jects, and will tend in their eyes to degrade the solemn cha- racter of Christianity, and so render the labours of missionaries still more difficult by making ridiculous the religious doctrines which they are en&avouring to induce the natives to accept." Upon the arrival of the Indian con- tingent of the Salvation Army at Calcutta they were all arrested except one, as_a riot was imminent.

A CORONATION IN WEST AFRICA. Duke Ephrim J. Orok was crowned King of Duke Town, at Old Cal tbar, on the Sth August, by Mr. Edward Hyde Hewitt, Her Majesty's Consul on the West African Coast. The ceremony took place at the Mission-house, and was attended by the traders, merchants, chiefs, and natives of the district. A throne was erected in the church at the left side of the communion rail. At the request of the Consul the big chiefs selected O. ok in the church as their ruler, the latter agreeing to the stipulations laid down by the chiefs as to his future conduct. After retiring to the vestry the king emerged robes in a huge coat of a semi-state and semi-mail description. The coat was of native manufacture, an was tied round the middle by a fancy clrd, The Rev. Messrs. Anderson and Edgerley officiated. The crown and sceptre were placed before Consul Hewitt on a table. The throne itself had been tr..nt out from England, and bore the English Royal Coat of Arms, being upholstered in crimson brocaded satin. The existing treaties with the English Government were read over to the King-elect, who took the usual oath binding himself to uphold them. He further promised to govern his people to the best of his ability, and to enc3urage and develop the trade of the place. Consul Hewitt then placed the crown on Orok's head, invested him with the symbols of authority, and proclaimed him King Duke IX. Tne cere- mony was most impressive throughout, and was engaged in by the natives in the most earnest manner.

div.head: SOCIAL SCIENCE CONGRESS.
div.p: THE SOCIAL SCIENCE CONGRESS.

The Social Science Congress at Nottingham met again on Saturday, but only part of the day was devoted to depart- mental business. Most of the members took part in the organised excursions to the Dukeries, Wollaton, and to Sonthwell. Sir Rutherford Alcock, president to the Health section, delivered the address to the Congress in the Mechanics' Institute. In the Economic Section Professor Leone Levi discoursed upon Free Trade, and in the dis- cussion which followed not a word is said to have been uttered io favour of a return to Protection. The audience in the Educational Department consisted mostly of ladies, who attended to hear a paper read by Miss A. Beale, of Leicester, on the phonic system of teaching children to read. Criminal reform and vagrancy engaged the attention of the Jurisprudence Dep lament. In the International and Municipal Section, Miss Helen Blackburn, :Bristol, read a paper on the legal status of women. . . _

- At the Congress, on Monday, an address was delivered by Professor Bonamy Price, the president of the department of 'Dade and Economics. The learned Professor confined his remarks to a review of two great struggles which have this year lyten carried on within the domain of political economy, one having reference to the war which has raged with so much heat in England with regard to Free Trade, and the other to the assault made by the Bi-metallists on the character of the money with which the important o peration of buying and selling is carried on. Is the sections the attendance, with the exception of the Health Deprrtment, has not been so large as on previous days, nor have the pipers read possessed the same amount of interest. In the Education Department, the Rev. Joseph Wood read a paper on "How far can workhouses and industrial schools be asso- ciated with the existing system of public elementary schools?" A resolution was !mood recommending unifor- mity of control and inspection in the case of industrial schools and workhouses, As well as 04 other elementary seiools of the country. The business of the Congress was practically concluded on Tuesday. An address on art was given at the caamence- inent of the day's proceedinus by Mr. G. Aitchison, A.R A. In the Health Section Mr. George Smith, of Cealville, con- tributed a paper on the condition of the large number of people who live and work on our canals. He also called attention to the gipsy population. The gipsy of romance, he said, wast dead long ago. "The gipsy of reality MIS a lying, plundering, dirty, cheating, crafty vagabond, a dis- grace even to civilisation." Of the 30,000 gipsv children growing up amongst Ili not 2 per cent. could read or write. Mr. Smith made various suggestions for improving the con- dition of these children, especially in rec,':!rd t &Inc:Acton, ['he English Bankruptcy Law occupied the attention of the Jurisprudence Department. The Social Sciente Congress at Nottienani, its sittings on Wednesday. Speakine. a i;neral of the members, the president I-Listings, M.P.) pointed out the co:;. directions in. „fah, in •• Er light of the discussions it 'see'rneal to him they should press for legislation. These included an alteration in the devolu- tion of real p?operty in cases of intestacy, the raising of the edocational efficiency of workhonse and industrial schools, e..nd compulsory notification of infectious diseases. The feeling of the Congress also appeared, he said, to be in favour of the Berkshire poor-law system and popular eonlrol of licenses.

The factory of Messrs. Smyth and Co.. Balbriggan, and the machinery and stock which it contained, have been destroyed by fire. Over 303 workpeople are thrown out of employment. ALLEGED REDISCOVERY OF A LOST ART.—A. West of Enkland correspondent writes—Some interest will be felt in a claim just put forward on behalf of the Marland Pottery Works, situate near Great Torrington, Devonshire. For a long period the art of making what is known as Egyptian black pottery has been lost to the world. This black is of a peculiarly beautiful brilliant appearance, and can hardly fail in a display of art pottery to arrest attention. It is now asserted that the works named have rediscovered the art, and at a Inner recently held in the county they exhibited a vase ornamented with groups of flowers of a bright blue hue, but with a body made of the brilliant blach material. It was much admired, and it is said that the body of the vase Is the only example in the world at the present day corres- ponding to the ancient Egyptian black.

CANNIBiLISM.—The gat:queens or Palliser, or Pearl Islanders, were known to be cannibals, and among other horrible tales of this practice it is related that a captive child, famished with hunger, on begging some food from the savage conquerors of her native isle, received a piece of her father's own flesh! The Hervey Islanders also ate their enemies, in order that they might imbibe pert of their courage. And it is probable that some such stimulus as this hid led to the practise of man-eating, rather thin simply a desire to feest on human flesh; though a tribe of Papuans, who have been only recently discovered, ia the vicinity of Sumatra, absolutely fatten up the captives they have taken in piracy for this purpose—no religious rite being apparently connected with it. It WWI even looked upon as an honour to be eaten. "Kill and eat !" the chief cried to his men in battle; and the warriors hurled the threat of "Kill and be eaten" at the enemy. When they were preparing for battle the cry always was, "Clear away well, that we may kill and eat, and have a good feast to- day." In the Island of Rarotonga they cut off the heads of the slain, piled them in the temple, and finished by eating the bodies. At other times they would be forced to resort to cannibelismte satisfy hunger. It is known that persons have ben stolen at midnight from their homes and killed and eaten before morning. Indeed, in some of the islands , In times of Etcarcity, we are told by Mr. Bourne, who vi.ited Mints and neighbouring isles in 1825, that members of the sums family are scarcely safe from their famished relatives. la3tances of depraved appetite are 039 not uncommon; but both this and the prevlons Cause of cannibalism are not without counterparts in civilised society. Tradition—lying, let us hope, in this case—relates that in former times if a corpulent man went to the island of Tepuaemann, or WAS seen on the lowland on the reef, he was seldom or rater seen again. The inference is patent. The Sand 'Rich islanders never seena to have been particularly addicted te whit is politely known as "long pig," while the Tongane and Savage Islanders (Nuiane) are reported never to have in- dulged in it. In the course of the whitewashing prouae a case of non-cannibalistic propensities has been attempted to be made oat for the Ithrquesan3 also, but only at the ex- pense of fasts. As these respectable islanders have lately awoke to the error of their ways, and discovered that a coat of tattoo and a cotton umbrella is scarcely wardrobe snfli• dent to satisfy the wants of Trans-Patific civilisetion (es- pecially on Sundays), we have no desire to rake no old fail- ings. Still there is no getting out of the nelz-s of the fact repeatedly vouched for by natives of other islands, mis- sionaries who have resided amongst them, and voyagers of undoubted veracity—such as the Russian Admiral Krusen- stern—who have visited theme who state that in times of famine the menThutcher their wives, chilJten, and aged parents, stew their flesh, and devour it with "the greatot satisfaction." Even the females will, if permittel, join in his horrid repast.—From " The Peoyes of the World."

div.head: RAMI3LE ROTTND NEWTON.
div.p: A RAMI3LE ROTTND NEWTON.

A walk along our c,;,intry roads "at the fall of the leaf" is full of i t n- P.....cet and instruction, and the almost general h, ihniday of the week affords time to those so disposed to enjoy the fresh air and rural scenery of our neighbourhood. Having to make a passing call on a few friends in the ad- joining town,thips, we took the field path nearest to our home in the direction of Winwick. The weathercock on the church steeple pointed to the north-west, and there was a tendency to rain. The farmers along the way were sus- picious of the gray day, and were busy beyond the first plantation gathering in the rich after-ma of the previous good hay crop, while the sheaves of corn in the opposite fields showed that the harvest was not "home" vet. Further on were fields of red clover waiting for the scythe or the reaping in ichine. The site of the projected cemetery from this point of view is much more romantic than when seen from Park-road, or perhaps it was that a sentiment had just then arisen in our mind along with the upspringing of a "pee weep" or lapwing, apostrophised by Burns in "Afton water "

Thou green-created lapwing, thy screaming farbear ; I charge you disturb not my slumbering fair " which the vicinity of a tributary of the Sankey made us think somewhat apposite. Here and in several other places we met boys and girls gathering blackberries, although they were as yet hardly ripe, and many of the gleaners were so young as hardly to be able to know the poisonous nature of the bright red berries of the deadly nightshade, which also grow plentifully along the same hedgerow. Turning to observe the flight of small birds, we get a good view of WarrinJeton and part of Wiowick. Resuming ourovalk, we notice that there is still some corn to cut, and that the small birds are taking toll or tithe while some' are keeping watch on the branches of the stunted trees by the way side, and a few steps further on we meet the object of their fear in the person of a fowler with double-barrelled gun. On the one hand is a wire-rope fencing, to which we have become accustomed in these parts, and on the other is an open ditch or waterway, which some day may, perhaps, be converted into a main sewer for Wargrave and led into the aforesaid confluent of "the Saukey, which slowly but surely is losing its character for purity and clarity. The grounds of the Newton Gun Club are on the south-east eide of the pro- posed cemetery, and separated from it by the Sankey Brook, which is the overflow of Newton Mere' Dean Dam, and Lady Hill Dam, and by no means a pellucid stream, as it passes Red Bank Mill, now the out premises of the Liver- pool Reformatory School, where the results of spade hus- bandry may he seep in tloO aoUndande of its kitchell gardene, Both are by the highway side, the latter near to the "BlOoly- stone ". (an ironstone boulder) marking (afresh) the spot mentioned in the note e to "the betrothed" where the pro- genitor of the Earls of Belcarres slew the Welsh Te;night on his return from the crusades. Passing 11.:etier the railway, recently constructed to facUitate the passage of the mail to and from the north, and, past New Hey, we cross the brook and find ourselves at Gallows Croft, a trim-infer piece of ground by the hiseirway side, and forming the comer of what may be called, lieviton Paw, For here many of the gab lant CAO;aiiere lost their in their encounter with the gOldiera of the CoMrnoowealth, and many a good man and true was ntadO to rue the day. This is the boundary of the teWnship of Newton-le-Willows, and with exception of the plantations at "The Willows" and brook-side, the only place which still keeps up its osier beds. But here they are in abundance as we pass the boundary-stone and Dr nd- rick's Traveller's Rest with scriptural inscription (peace be with his ashes), and so on towards Hermitage Green. Time has wrought great changes in the very configuration of the ground, and roads have ben made where no roads used to be, the road from this point on to Winwick being quite modern. Copholthill, the site of the Royalist camp, is there to be sure with its farm-house, and beyond it is the battlefield, but the original road must have gone by this willow ground at that time a very "slough of des- pond" where both friend and foe lost their lives, according to Carlyle, who made a study of this very spat when writ- ing his life of Cromwell. We have just passed Red Bank Mill where the Royalists made the cernbin their treasury, and which a late local celebrity wished to transport to War- rington Museum, but it was tr o big and balky and rather like a white elephant. This same willow is an excellent febrifuge. We ought, if possible, to have more of it planted in marshy ground, and we would suggest that it would be both useful and ornamental if it could be wrought in with any plan of landscape gardening for the cemetery, in place of the reeds and rushes by the waterside at the foot of the chosen site. To be sure, it is rather remote from the pre- sent habitations, but still whether or not, its presence in the cemetery would serve to correct the air there, and set at rest the minds of those who look upon such places as plague spots. We are by no means disposed to be wrong- headed over this matter, although we could quote pre- cedent for our suggestion, and this leads us to say that we wait with some degree of cariosity to see what sort of trees they are to be, that our unknown benefactor will give us for the High-street. We shall almost feel as if we were in the village of Waterloo, of world-wide fame, the only street we ever thought anything like the High-street in Newton, plus the trees. Beech or birch or larch or whatever will form an arch, and make us think we are walking on a Boulevard. But pray don't give us anything that is likely to be stunted or unsightly, which would be a dear gift, and would make us abhor the very sight of them. Something that will not suffer by an infusion of gas-tar at times but that will agree with a sandy soil of which the High-street consists. had the gift only come a year ago, the sewers might have been turned on to their roots now and then with the invocation, " Let Newton flourish," and a practical experiment in sewage farming made. As it .is an oecasiunal drenching by the water cart or hydrants will suffice, and an occasional ablaqueation can always be pro- vided for them by rooting up a few boulders. The taste for carving may be tempered for a while by planting a few thorns along with the saplings. But this is a digression end so we return to " Ganders Croft " now an enclosure like the piece of land on the (apposite side of the road, cribbed from the highway. Even the Railway Company is prac- tising small economies for they have a hay-rick at the arch we passed, to feed the herd of cows, which we hear they have recently bought to supply their refreshment rooms with " sweet " milk. As we turned down the lane there was a pleasure party passing to Winwick in an open waggoaette, evidently bent on making the best of the day, and bowling along the macadamised road at a pace that would have been impossible a very few years ago when the road was bouldered. With a few reflections as to how Newton, once "a hundred" in Lancashire, and mentioned in " Domesday Book," came to have le Willows tacked to it,' which le we suspect was originally leserlez in Norman French times, otherwise it would have little if any meaning; but a good deal with it, for drainage and cultivation have dons a good deal for Newton within our time, and willows were more plentiful in it some forty years ago than they are now, and hedges and ditches have been cleared off and levelled up since then, and this bit of osior-ground only serves to remind the present generathin of by-gone days, and utilizes an otherwise useless bit of low lying land. A very civil Irishman is clearing up the hedgerow on the up- land to the right where the Aelds are in a high state of cultivation, thanks to a neighbouring capitalist. Here the earliest spring .flowers are seen, and ferns in autumn, with nettle enough to supply the whole parish with that healthy edible. Birds may be seen and heard here both late and early in the year. There is a marl pit or quarry, too, with a legend of the pig's performance that finally allowed Winwick Church to be built where it is, but it is a lame one, for the mason monks who built churches knew better than Ito build even a pig-stve irm such a place. A little further j on, and to the left of the road, in the ravine, is the Hermit's Well, a shallow basin of water oosing out of the reddish- yellow sandstone rock, which crops up here, and although there are two pails full of water just drawn—the well is beyond the reach of our faithful dog who is panting for a drink. Whoever the Hermit might be, we hope be did not die of the ague or cold fever, indeed we think that im- passible, owing to the presence of the willows, but he might easily have had chronic rheumatism, if such a name was known in those days, the malady itself is quite as old as the time of the patriarch, Jacob, who complained of the frosty foe. This is supposing that there ever was such a local genius, which, in this sceptical age, we may be allowed to doubt. There is Hermitage Green a little further on, anti not many years ago, there was what might be supposed to be a true representation of him over the door of the public- house there, but all that is now left is the name. It is much mere likely to have been the name adopted for the neigh- bouring mansion once occupied by Bishop Claughton, when a boy, and still by members of his family. And from whence we assisted in bringing the flags of the Wigan Militia Volunteers to Newton Church, where in passing we bear there is to be a week's thanksgiving services, "far the abundant harvest" "and to the God of Battles for our glorious success in Egypt," the former of which, this year, we are happy to say, is a fact, and not a polite fiction, as the well-filled barns and yards just passed, testify where the thatcher is displaying his artistic taste in numerous well- built stacks Of wheat and oats, while the hedger and ditcher is busy at work, no half holiday for him, for the rank vege- tation has been making haste to outgrow his trim hedges. The cottager's child may reasonably this winter expect to be well fed if prices are not run up artificially, and it will promote many marriages, of which we have not a few, for there is corn to the right, corn to the left, corn all round about, with potatoes now and again, all the way we go. Here is a monstrous big boulder, which, for a wonder, has no legend attached to it, although as old as the glacial period. But a few minutes walk further on is St. Osvrald's Well, which has, and no doubt was, the resort of many a pilgrim to obtain a drink of its healing waters. It is almost certain that there were waters in this corner of the county that were accounted " miraculous," both in Pagan times and in times not so remote, for, if we are not mistaken, the "Sankey " obtained its name from some such quality supposed to be inherent in its waters in early British times, whoa it received its name; and we know by practical experience that of the 22 wells of water in Sewton none were so sweet or palatable to the invalid as the waters of the Tea Well, a natural spring which trickled into the " Sankey " near the old bridge and blacksmith's shop at " Willow Bank." Where the road croeeed the stream, eoreow, ing'a we reach the crest of the hill marked by mound and flagstaff, and after 1001-ing down at the site of demolished cottages of yore, cannot but admire the bountiful harvest being brought home to each and all of the well-kept farm-houses just here. The village maidens are returning from a visit to the corn fields, where the youths are "leading" home the harvest along the well macada- mised roads. Passing the old and new stone delphs and fine fields of grain, which our friend the retain is eying atten- tively, we are made aware of the presence of the volunteers at I-Fglifiald-mces by the report of their rifles, so, as travel- lers always do in novels, "we wend our way" in that direction. Leaving the rosy cheeked apples and sweet smelling clover, we pass on to the derelict goods and passenger

Late on Monday night, the headless body of Mr. Graham the foreman of the Mitcham Leather Works, was found be- tween the Mitcham and Hackbridge Stations of the Brighton Railway. His head was discovered near the London-bridge station. _ _ _

._______. Cosr op WAR TELEGRAMS.—Taking the best available route the London dailies have to pay 7s. 21. a word for their telegrams from Egypt. A column of leaded messages in a daily paper averages from £2OO to £250. The lowest average of the daily papers in London is £l,OOO a week. SiIoCKING OVERWINDING ACCIDENT.—A shocking over- winding accident occurred at Earl Granville's Spendcroft Pit, Handley, on Tuesday. Ad two sinkers were being drawn up the shaft, the engineman lost control of the engine, and the cage was drawn over thd head gear. One of the men, named Goldstraer, was thrown out, and, falling down the *heft, was knocked to pieces, death being of course instan- taneous. Tile ether saved himself by springing upon one of the conducting rods. The ens-inemen, named Pemberton, has been arrested. Father Hyacinth, in a funetai eerttori Ofl Dr. Pusey, de- scribed him as one of the precureare of fhe grand religious unity of the future, and he read eiftacts from a Latin letter addressed to himself on September 26, 1869, immedi- ately after his rupture with the Roman Church. In this letter Dr. Pusey expressed admiration of his powerful pro- test, and his conviction that, like the old doctrine of the great Bossuet, this almost annihilated Gallicanism, was the sole hope of union among the Churches. THE THEFT OF £15,000 Woerrit OF BONDS : Aer ARREsT.—The Hamburg police:have, says the Globe, suc- ceeded in capturing John Novitsky, a Russian, for whose apprehension, on a charge of stealing £15,000 worth of Russian and Italian bonds from a fellow-countryman in London, a few weeks ago, a large reward has been offered. The prisoner, who is about 45 years of age, is said to have formerly been a Russian officer and subsequently a corres- pondent of the Moscow Gazette. After preliminary pro- ceedings at Hamburg, he will probably be brought to England under the Extradition Treaty. 7 A SINGULAR Accinaerr.— A singular accident is re- ported from Bolton. A labourer, named Robert Hutchinson, of Eagley Bridge, while searching for a stray ferret ncar t) the Cox Green Quarries. Turtme commenced prob:ng in a culvert with a rod, when a load explosion occurred, and he was so seriously injured on both arms sod in the face as to necessitate his removal to the Infirmary. It was afterwards discovered that a dynamite cartridge had exploded, which it was supposed had been abstracted by a rat or a rabbit from a box at the quarries. Another man who was standing by was also in jured. An impudent attempt to intimidate a firm of tankmakers in the East End of London into making concessions to their workmen is exposed in the Times. Messrs Laecaster and Hawn being in dispute with their .men, "A member of the Tankmekers' Unity" wrote to a shipping firm in Leaden- hall-street, who bad business relations with them "advising them in their own interest to carefully inspect any work they might receive from them." The mercantile house in question brought the fact to the knowledge of Messrs. Lancaster, awl Hawn, who publish the letter to " show how workmen would injure their employers." Mr. FAWCETT AND HIS CONSTITDENTS.—Mr. Fawcett and Mr. J. Holms addressed their constituents at Hackney on Tuesday evening. The Postmaster General said he did apt think there would be any chance that the parcsl pest would be in operation until some months after Christmas. Speak- ing of affairs in Egypt, the right hon. gentleman said the future settlement of the question involved so many points of the utmoet delicacy and difficulty that he would not re- mark upon them, but they might at least feel confident that in Mr. Gladstone's hands it would be proved that English- men had no selfish object to serve. Mr. Fawcett also referred to Ireland, and deprecated any extended application of the principle of facilitating the purchase of land by means of State money.

OIL INA MOUBLED WiTIMS.---The Earl of Aberdeen, General Gordon, M.P., Professor Siemens, and other dis- tinguished parties, witnessed, on Titosd fy, the operation of laying down the pipes and tanks at the harbour entrance of Aberdeen for the purpose of putting into permanent use the practice of pouring oil on the water to cairn it in stormy weather, and thus facilitate the entrance of vessels. The bar at Aberdeen is exceedingly dangerous in rough weather, and the sandy bottom of the channel is peculiarly fitted fco: puttin, to the test the efficacy of the plan proposed by Mr. Shield's. It will be sometime before all the pipes are laid and arrangements completed, but the work is being carefully done, as Mr. Shields is confident of its success. The matcril.l uscd is colutuoli ash oil, übtalllable,at a very cheap rate.

MUTINY ON A REFORMATORY SRIP.-At the Liverpool Police Court, on Wednesday, six boys, belonging to the re- formatory ship Clarence, were charged with having refused to obey the orders of Captain Hudson, on tha 19th instant, and also with wilful damage. Captain Hudson stated that be had issued an order prohibiting the boys from using tobacco or bringing it on board. Great dissatisfaction was thereby caused, and a number of the boys made a distur- bance on the day mentioned, and broke several panes of glass on board the ship. The prisoners, who were petty officers, were the ringleaders of the disturbance, and when Captain Hudson spoke to them they tore off their badges and threw them at his feet. Three of the lads were sent to prison for three months with hard labour, and the others for six weeks with hard labour.

SHOCKING DISCOVERY NEAR PRESTON.— I Shocking dis- covery was made at Walton, near Preston, late on Monday night. The body of a man, apparently about 30 years of age, and a factory operative, NSW found lying on the outskirts of d wood at the top of the tram road. In the abdomen there was a large wound, from which the bowels protruded, and this was, no doubt, the cause of death. A weapon has been found, and there is every reason for assuming that the man has been brutally murdered. The body was discovered by a boy, who gave informatiorno the police. There is no evidenca of a struggle having taken place near the spot. The police are making investigations, but nothing has yet been ascertained to clear up the mystery. The inquest was held on Tuesday afternoon. The body remained unidenti- fied. The medical evidence showed that death resulted from a wound in the abdomen inflicted apparently by a knife found near. Verdict," Found dead." THE CURSE WHICH HANGS OVER ENGLAND.—Not drunkenness but licentiousness is, in Biehop Fraser's opinion, the most deadly curse which hangs over England at the present time. "That licentiousness which they see rampant through the streets of Manchester every evening" is, the Bishop believes, eating oat the moral life of the nation. There are, he believes, two things in danger; first, the faith of the nation, and closely connected with it the moral life and well-being of the people. How it happens , that the national faith is shaken the Bishop does not say, r but he is, at least, convinced that it is useless to build and restore churches, enlarge schools, and opee mission-rooms, unless the clergy can influence the people spiritually, morally, and socially. It is because the clergy have ceased to exercise such, influence that the national faith is in danger; they cannot regain it until they become the leaders instead of the followers of the advanced thought of the time. Salvationists and revivalists may fill churches, but they do not, any more than clergymen who are out of harmony with the spirit of the times, give a faith to an intellectual people. THE TRADES UNION CONGRESS.—The Trades Union Con- dreas concluded its 15th annual meeting on Saturday. Mr. M'Crae, a London delegate, submitted a resolution in favour ' of the opening on Sundays of all places of rational recrea- tion and instruction, such as the National Gallery, the British Museum, and the South Kensington'Museum ; but it was ruled that as the Standing Orders Committee had not thought fit to include the resolution in the business brought before the Congress it could not be entertained. A letter was read from Mr. Burt, M.P., explaining the circum- stances under which Mr. Sexton had blocked at an early period of the session the Employers' Liability Amendment Bill. Mr. Sexton explained in a telegram to the Congress that in consequence of the extraordinary unfairness of the Government in objecting to his motion for leave to intro- duce a bill repealing the Coercion Act and afterwards blocking his motion, he felt called upon to emphasise that unfairness by objecting to the introduction of bills moved for by them or their supporters, but immediately after an explanation from Mr. Broadhurst ho at once withdrew his objection. The hon. member also explained th it he had been one of the steadiest supporters of the Employers' Liability Bill and every measure of benefit for English workmen. - -

ANEW ARMY.—" The Church Army" is the title of an organisation brought into existence by the action of the Salvation Army, and in a circular calling attention to !tie new " army" we are told that the need of some organisa- tion has long been felt, to develop within the lines of the Church of England the work that has been regarded as the chief feature of the Salvation Army. After careful con- sideration in the different parishes, a movement of this character has already been set on foot at Bristol, Oxford, Tunbridge, Richmond, and elsewhere. The services, which are usually preceded by processions and short open-air meetings, are of a bright and lively character, consisting of stirring hymns, many of them set to secular tunes, personal testimonies, and brief appeals to the irreligious to turn from the paths of sin to holiness. Those who are responsible for the initiation of the latest evangelisation movement are not. it would appear, prepared to go the eccentric lengths tc; which the Salvation Army go. We hear nothing of generals and majors and other military titles in connection with the army such as are so prominent a feature of the older organ- isation, nor, so far, do the promoters seem to call in brass hands as an aid to the reformation of sinners. They work in a much quieter, though it may be quite as effective, manner. A little work, entitled " Church Army Songs," has just been published, and the some words and music have also been issued under the title of " Church Militant Hymns," to suit the•needs of some, while thanks are tendered to the leaders of the " Salvation Army" and others for their courtesy in permitting the use of many of the new pieces.
