The Bank of Bengal has reduced its minimum rate of interest and discount from 5 to 4 per cent. Preparations are b-;ing made At Windsor Castle for illu- minating a portion of the interior of the palace with the electric light. Miss Emily Faithfull, who sails for America next week, intends to deliver throughout the States her lecture on " M dern Extravagance." According to the Prohibitionists, alcohol in the last ten years in the United States has sent 100,000 orphans to asylums, caused 10,000 suicides, and has made 200,000 widows.

OCCUPATION OF DANHETTA. As was stated in our list issue, on Friday General Sir E. Wood, with a considerable force, proceeded to Damietta, and the following day he occupied the stronghold without resistance. The occupation is thus described by a corres- pondent telegraphing from Cairo on Sunday evening : " Damietta, the last rebel stronghold, was occupied vester- ' (1.17 without resistance. We halted for the night at Chebin, and while the soldiers were getting such rest as the mos- quitoes and sandflies permitted, Sir E. Wood prepared the final arrangements for attack at daybreak. In the, middle of the right ft trail came down from the direction of Damietta. It stopped some yards outside the station, and after a quarter pf an hour's pause retired. This incident, together with the reoorfs received by tne, FhediYes fi.le-cle-c imp, who acc.:mf- panied General Wood, that the line of railway had been mind, confirmed the hopes of the troops that the enemy meant fighting. At two a.m. the reveille sounded, and Captain Slade having reconnoitred with the line our train proceeded elqwly towards Damietta. Through the semi- darkness of an Egyptian summer night all eyes were strained eagerly from the window hoping to catch a glimpse of the enemy, but as daylight broke we steamed past earthworks commanding the -line, with guns and horses abandoned, rifle pits empty, and deserted trenches, and the troops felt with deep disappointment that there would be no fighting, and that the success was, from the soldier's point of view, won by a mere walk over. White flags were hoisted in the villages we passed, and at Kafr Dottich, the last station from Damietta, Abdel-Al himself was waiting with three officers. He advanced, saluted the General,and surrendered his sword, and thus the last of the original trio of mutinous officers was our prisoner." Another correspondent says that General Wood, on taking possession, found that the 800 black warriors, who on Friday were all that remained of the original garrison of 7,000 men, had taken to Melt after committing all the plunder they c mld. They sacked the Governor's treasury, the barracks, and several private houses, and carried off large quantities of ammunition. THE KHEDIVE'S DEPARTURE FROM ALEXANDRIA.

The sale of invisible photographs, which become visible when plunged in water, has been interdicted in France, the salt of mercury used in their manufacture being injuriou,) to health. Seine idea may be gained of the number of ingli'ats ill New York from the fact that a fortnight since 100 were held in a single day. Two coroners and two juries disposed of the lot.
Heavy Norman liorae3 are now being imported into New York for breeding purposes, to supply brewers and parcel delivery companies with larger horses than the American breed.

, A clever swindler is going about Kent victimising hotel prop' ietors and other persons in a wholesale manner, un- der the pretence that he is en the staff of a London news- paper. James Crowther, aged 60, a retired coachman, residing at Moortown, Leeds, has died from voluntary starvation. He was in good circumstances, but too miserly to allow himself the necessaries of life.

The freedom of the city of Glasgow will probably be con- ferred on Sir Stafford Northcote next Wednesday, and on the evening of that day he will address the Conservatives of that city in St. Andrew's Hall. The Astronomer-Royal has received a telegram from the Paris Observatory, stating that a superb comer was observed at four o'clock, on Wednesday morning, at 10 degrees alti- tude, hearing north 60 degrees east. The death Is Announced at Newcastle of Mr. Peter Burt, father of Mr. Burt, M,P. The deceased; Who was seventy- two years of age, was a working miner; and only forsook his calling when incapacitated by failing health. The City Press understands tbat the Prince of Wales has consented to own the new City of London School on the Thames Embankment. The date is-not ya definitely fixe..4, but it will be some time early in December. Admiralty instructions were received at Chatham Dock- yard, on Wednesday evening, to provide immediately the guns and equipment which will be required for eight ves- sels of the mercantile marine which are ordered to be armed as mercantile auxiliaries.

The Khedive left Alexandria for Cairo, on Monday. Re- ferring to his d,parture 3 correspondent says :—At 9-45 a.m., a salute of artillery proclaimed that the Khedive had left Ras-el-Tin Palace on his way to his capital. The streets alon2, wbichie would proceed to the railway station were at 8 am. lined with British troops, and in the station yard the Derbyshire Regiment was stationed. In the carriage with the Khedive was Sir E. Malet, the British Consul-General. The carriage was escorted by a squadron of the 13th Bengal Lancers, and followed by the Mounted Infantry. The crowd along the line of route was by no means large, and was com- posed of natives and Europeans, who, -at some points, cheered the Khedive as he passed, but upon the whole preserved a cold silence. The procession was not imposing as the Khedive's carriage and escort were followed by the Ministers, who were for the most part conveyed in cabs. The station was decorated with flags, flowers, and plants, and carpets were laid. The train started at a few minutes after ten. The English in the station chrered as it went out, but it cannot be said that the foreigners or natives joined with any heartiness in the farewell greeting. No one could have wit- nessed the bearing of the Egyptian crowd upon this occa- sion without feeling that England has upon her hands another Dost Mohammed Khan or Wali of Candahar. These indeed had a party among their people; but the Khedive has not, outside his own entourage, a single loyal follower.

, There are no less than 88 applications for the Borough turveyorship of Burnley, rendered vacant by the resignation of Mr. Walsh. The salary is £250, and the appointment , will in all probability be made at a special meeting of the Council, to be held next month. At the consecration of a new Mission Church at Eastville, Bristol, by the bishop of the diocese, on Wednesday, the Free Methodists placed their schoolroom at the disposal of the church committee, and the public luncheon in connection with the ceremony took plase there. Two privates of the 2nd South Lancashire Regiment were sentenced by court mlrtial, at Devenport, on Thursday, to terms of imprisonment, one for assaulting a constable, and the other for attempting to rescue him. One was a ring- leader in the recent fracas at Stonehouse between military and police. At Oldham, on Thursday, Frank Brett was committed for three months for an assault on his wife. On Saturday night the prisoner came home drunk, and began kicking his wife in a shameful manner until, as she said, the blood came through her stockings. Her legs were all black. Prisoner's defence was that his wife had "humbugged him for being drunk."

ARRIVAL OF THE KHEDIVE AT CAIRO. The Khedive returned to the capital from Alexandria on Monday, and his arrival is described by a correspondent of the Daily News as follows :—" The Khedive arrived here at ten minutes past three this afternoon from Alexandria. As he greeted the multitude which welcomed him on the platform he looked nervous and excited, but quickly re- covered his self-possession. A few minutes after the stop- page of the train a royal salute of 21 guns was fired. In about ten minutes the Duke of Connaught arrived, and greeted the Khedive in a frank and generous manner. Next came Sir John Adye and Sir Garnet Wolseley, with whom the Khedive spoke for several minutes. Last of all the Shiek-nl-Islam appeared, and pronounced a brief religious ceremony, during which the Khedive appeared to be much affected. The great platform literally swarmed with crowds of native officers of all ranks, and wearing gorgeous uni- forms. The scene was a veritable Field of the Cloth of Gold, pins jewels innumerable; yet the fellah is not happy. The wealth lavished on acres of gorgeous cloth would go a long way towards paying the debt. The guard of honour was furnished by a hundred men of the Brigade of Guil:ds, who were also in attendance at the railway station, which was tastefully decorated. Long rows of pillars stood on the platform adorned with branches of date palms and pen- nons bearing the national symbol of the Crescent and Star. The doors and windows of the station offices, which were surmounted by round arches, were ornamented in a similar manner. The passage through which the Khedive went to his carriage was still more prettily adorned with palm branches and varieties of flowering plants, and all the way from the station to the Ismailieh Palace the Khedive's progress resembled a triumphal procession. There were abundant evidences of pleasure and delight among the population. The scene presented by the great multitudes who had been waiting patiently and .sitting in the side streets for hours by thousands, by gaily coloured flags and miles literally of ornamental colonnede., was extremely effective, while, to add to the pleasant condition of holiday makers, the sun was not oppressive, and cool breezes were blowing. There must have been at least 150,000 people in the streets. With his escort of the Household Cavalry the Khedive drove in a magnificent carriage towards the bridge over the canal road. It was lined on both sides by cavalry. The bridge over which His Highness next passed was lined by 200 men from each battalion of the Guards, who also occupied the route to Kantarat-street. Counting 200 men from each cavalry regiment and 400 from each infantry regi- ment, the road, which is about three miles long, by which His Highness advanced, must have been lined by about 5,000 men. Riding in the procession towards the Abdeen Palace,l noticed that. M. Da Lesseps's house did not show a rag of bunting. Nebar Pacha's house was decorated in a style worthy of the occasion, while in a manner worthy of them- selves, Messrs. Thomas Cook and Sons displayed a profusion of flags crossing the street high overhead, and covered their walls with lamps, red cloth, and tinsel. Shepherd's Hotel, close by, was much less gorgeous but more tasteful. The railings of the beautiful Eshekies Gardens were adorned throughout the entire circuit. The houses of Selim Pacha, Righeb Pacha, and others, presented an appearance similar to that already described, but the finest display of all was at the Abdeen Palace, Sir Garnet Wolseley's bead-quarters. The entrance to the great square lay through the Roman triumphal arch, and round the vast enclosure ran a line of round arches ornamented with small flags of various colours. This spot will offer one of the most effective scenes in the coming illuminations. The route from here on the road to the Ismailieh Palace is not nearly so gay in appearance as that already described. On the arrival Oi the Khedive at the Ismailieh Palace a royal salute was fired from the Kasr-el-Nil Barracks, between which and the palace men of the Royal Horse Artillery end of the field artillery were posted. ,Some minutes after the Khedive entered the palace gate a third and last selute boomed fcrth from the citadel at the other end of Cairo. :RECEPTION BY THE KHEDIVE. On Tuesday the Khedive held a grand reception at the Ohezireh Palace, which was attended by more natives than even on the occasion of the accession of His Highness, no fewer than 992 representatives of different villages in Upper and Lower Egypt being present. The Khodive , refused to receive many Pashas and Heys who, although they werg concerned in the rebellion, came to profess their loyalty to their Sovereign, while on the the other hand many other personages of lower degree were admitted to kiss his hands. On receiving the Ulemas, the Khedive, address- ing them, said ; "You are men of letters and not politicians. The first who is again guilty of interfering with politics will be severely punished." They replied by unanimously declaring their unswerving loyalty to the Khedive. His Highness adopted a similar tone in receiving the Pashas and Beys. At ten o'clock the British Generals, his Royal Highness the Duke of Connaught, Sir John Adye, General Willie, Sir E. Hamley, Sir H. Macpherson, and General Graham, with the officers of the respective staffs, arrived at the palace and were presented to the Khedive- -102 officers in all. Sir Garnet Wolseley was unwell, and unable to .ttend. The reception of the diplomatic body followed at eleven o'clock. : MISCELLANEOUS ITEMS. ' The Khedive has bestowed upon General Wolseley the decoration of the Grand Cordon of the Osmanli. •

Major Marindin on Thursday made the offiial Board of Trade inspection of the new Bury and ToWngton Railway, which has been constructed, by the Lancashire and York- shire Company. The line is about 31 miles in length, and has occupied five years in completion. It will probably be opened for traffic on Monday. - The Democratic Federation discussed, on Wednesday night, the question of the importation of Chinese labour. An Italian member pointed out that the Federation, which proclaimed absolute equality among men, was run- ing its head against a fundamental portion of its creed. It was resolved to "inform" the working classes of the coun- try on this subject. Lieutenant-Colonel Gt. B. Wolseieh York and L3ncasiei' Regiment, a brother of Sir G. Wolssley, has received a five years staff appointment as Assistant Adjutant-General of a division of the Bengal Army. Another brother, Brigade Surgeon R. Wolseley, M.D., has been appointed secretary to Surgeon-General Sir A D. Home, V.C., K.C.8., principal medical officer in India.

At the Oswestry Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Lord Trevor, of Biynkinalt, was fined £lO and costs for contra- vening the Mines Regulation Act, by not providing the attendance of an engine-man on the surface at his Lord- ship's Ifton Colliery whilst men were at work below. In June last a collier was killed by a fall of roof in a pit, but his only companion was unable for same time to communicate with the surface, the engine-man being gone away without orders. The prosecution was ordered by the Home Secretary. On Thursday morning a youth, natMed Walls, had a narrow escape at Accrington railway station. He was in the e:nploy of Mr. Ashton Taylor, newsagent, and when the Manchester train arrived he was so eager to get his news parcel that he fell between the train and platform. Three carriages passed by him before the train was brought to a standstill. The lad was then picked up only slightly injured, having escaped the wheels. Although activity is still general throughout the engineer- ing shops of this district, there is a decrease of employment in the moulding shops, which is an indication of a falling off in the quantity of new work in preparation to follow up the orders on which engineers are at present engaged. Dur- ing the last week or two the applications for work by moulders out of employment have been more numerous than for a considerable time past, and the last issued returns of the Moulders' Society report trade to be gon4 in only two important Lancashire centres Salford and Bolton. Man- chester, Liverpool, Warrington, Rochdale, Hyde, Bury, and Widnes are returned as moderate. At Birkenhead hands were being discharged; in Oldham and Blackburn trade was declining or bad; and at Bury, Burnley, Stalybridge, Wigan and Darwen, bad. The Central News New Rosscorrespomlent telegraphs that a man named James Hickey, of Gurteen Maher, near Templeinere, county Tipperary, only son of an aged widow, was brutally murdered on Wednesday night near his own house. Two brothers, named Carrolls, whose lands adjoin the farm of the deceased, have been arrested on suspicion. The Carrolls were lately evicted for non-payment of rent, and were both in gaol recently for a murderous assault on the deceased, whose arm they cut open with a scythe. The- property defence men are at present in possession of the Carrolls' borne, and it is alleged that the prisoners were ex- asperated against Hickey for lending the property defence men tools and utensils. Mrs. Mary Hill, of New Ross, county Wexford, is landlady of the farm, and Mr. Boyd, of New Ross, is the agent. All the tenants on Mrs. Hill's estate paid their rents on being visited by the sheriffs except the Carrot Is, who were the ringleaders in resisting payment. Many of the tenants paid privately all the year. .

Mr. H. M. Stanley, the great African traveller, has arrivcd in Paris, having accomplished his mission of establishing stations for trade and exploration on the Congo. He says it is abundantly evident that this river with its 4,000 miles of navigable way must exceed in present and future importance all the other known modes of communication with the interior of the Continent. England at present has no settle- , ment there, but France has some stations. The society for which Mr. Stan!ey has been working, though under the pre- sidency of the King of the Belgians, is international in con- stitution, and its aim is to obtain information about the Congo for the benefit of all the world. Taking advantage of this, M. de Brazzl, the French traveller' obtained a view of Mr. Stauley's plans deposited at Mussels, and hast med to Africa in the hope of anticipating some of his most important operations for the sole benefit of France. He reached the Congo in a pitiable plight owing to insufficient preparation, and was glad to accept assistance from his rival Mr. Stanley is now 150 miles ahead of him with his station on the great river. TERRIBLIZ FAMILY HISTORY: SUICIDE OF A FATIIER AND' DAUGHTER-Mr. W. J. Payne, the Southwark coroner, held an inquest on Wednesday at the Vestry-hall,.Fair- streq, Horselydown, on the body of Daniel Carter, aged 50, presiding at 16, Peabody Buildings, Great Wild-street, Drury. lane, who was found in the Thames on Saturday last. The evidence of Emma Carter, the wife of the deceased,dieclosed a very sad family history. She stated that a few months hack one of her daughters, aged 17, committed suicide, and shortly before that her son was found dead in bed. The trouble caused by these occurrences had affected the mind of the deceased, who was very fond of his children, and lat- terly he had acted very strangely. A fortnight ago yester- day, instead of going home from his business as a bookbinder, he wandered about the streets all night, and next day, Friday, witness received a telegram to say that he was in the Tottenham Hospital. Upou going to him she found he could give no account of himself or how he had got there. She took him home and they went to bed, but when she woke on Saturday morning, about six o'clock, she found he had got up and dressed himself and was gone. The jury returned a verdict of " Suicide while mentally deranged."
A somewhat sensational case is now under investigation

in London. Last November a master maker in St. Luke's, named Stanger, disappeared, and to this day nothing has been heard of him. The day after he was last seen a man named Stamm, who had been in Stanger's company over- night, was at Stanger's house, and ten days after he took up his abode there, Mrs. Stanger also livipg on the premises. In July of this year the missing man's executors proved his will, although Stumm had told one of them at different times that Stanger was in Germany or America. Previous to this there had been dealings with Stanger's property, and auaongst other things his account with the London and County Bank had been et-awn on as though he was alive. One of the cheques—for £76—is the subject of a criminal accusation, Stumm being charged at the Worship-street Police-court, on Wednesday, with having forged it and with having cons.pired with Mrs. Stanger to defraud the execu- tors. It was stated that Mr. Chabot, an "expert" in hand- writing, would show that no part of the cheque was n the handwriting of Stanger, but that the body of it was written by the prisoner and that the signatvre was a counterfeit. The executor above referred to denied in cross-examination haying circulated a report that the prisoner had made away with Stanger, but said that such a report was current. In remanding the prisoner Mr. Barstow• said the case as now presented had a far wider bearing than that of the forgery charged in the warrant. The police arrested Mrs. Stanger on Thursday.

1 The Admiralty bat% Ordered the dispers.ii e the Cam 1 blued fleets recently engaged on war service in kgyptidni Ivraters. A Genera correspondent telegraphs that the firat batch of recruits for the Egyptian gendarmerie who have been raised in Switzerland !tare for Alexandria on Friday. • It is considered certain in, Berlin, a correspondent there states, that the attitude of Germany in regard to the expected actio.n of England in Egypt win be very favourable. It is semi-officially announced in Berlin that a com- munication from the British Government is expected by the Powers within the next few days, soliciting an ,ax- ' pression of their views upon the state of affairs in Egypt. A special correspondent at Cairo describes the illumina- tions on Monday night as magnificent. The house of M. de Lesseps was the only one where darkness reigned. The Kh,dive admits it WAS true an order had been given to burn Cairo; saying only a few of the Pashas' houses. There have been great rejoicings at Gibraltar over the English victories in Egypt. Business was suspended, and the houses were profus?ly decorated during the day, and at night there were illuminations and fireworks. Sir Edward Malet 'ming formally conveyed to the Khe- dive the congratulations of her Majetity's Government on his return to Cairo his Highness on Wednesday visited the Consul-General to express his thanks for the message. The Khedive has also paid visits to the Duke :of Connaught and Sir Garnet Wolseley. In a Cairo telegram it is stated that Sir Garnet Wolseley and Sir Edward. Malet concur in thinking that 10,000 men will suffice to maintain order in Egypt until the re-establish- ment of a normal state of affairs. Part of the Indian con- tingent has alieidy been ordered to prepare for re-embarka- tion. The Duke of Connaught is expected to leave with his brigade for England next week. A motion will be brought before the Corporation of the city of London to present an address in a gold box and a sword to Sir G. Wolseley, who has already received the freedom of the city, and the freedom with a sword, to Sir B. Seymour. It is also propGsed that the Corporation should entertain the distinguished officers upon their return to this c)untry.

From statistics furnished by the Army Medical Depart- ment it appears that the hundt,sr of sick admitted t 9 the base hospital did not amount to one per cent. of the forces in the field. These figures, however' only relate to the period from August 24 to the first week in September. A special correspondent at Cairo states that a good deal of sick- ness prevails and that the hospital is full. Sir G. Wolseley, in his despatch to the War Office announcing the arrival of the Khedive at Cairo, states that His Highness expressed to him in most gracious terms, and begged him to convey it to Her Maj-sty's Geyernment, "the deep gratitude he feels towards Her Majesty, and to the English nation and army, for all that has been done for him."

One cannot but be struck, a correspondent says, by the virulence of language in which the Continental European residents and officers in the service of the Khedive denounce Arabi. Hanging, they say, is almost too good for him, and shooting certainly. The natural consequence is that the Egyptian population adopt such sentiments as expressing the real opinion of the majority of Englishmen. The belief in diplomatic circles at Constantinople is, according to a Correspondent, that a conference to decide on the settlement of Egypt is unnecessary. Negotiations are constantly going on between Lord Dufferin and the Porte, with the object, according to general belief, of making a new Convention for the Government of Egypt with the consent of the Powers.

_ . Official announcement is made of the deposition and im- prisonment of the Grand Shereef of Mecca. The matter gave rise to considerable excitement at Taif, but order is said to be restored now. Abdullah Doun Pasha has been appointed Grand Shereef. The ostensible cause of the deposition is that the late Shereef was engaged in treasonable correspon- dence with Arabi.

The Khedive has issued a proclamation, in which he states that England has been compelled to interfere to pre• tect her great interests, but has no intention of annexing the country. His Highness states that he has authorised the leader of the British army to represent him in restoring order and in punishing the rebels, and dec3ares that anyone refusing to render assistance will be treated as a rebel.

Out of Egypt the tremendous effect of the British suc- cesses is beginning to be manifest. Great delight is felt in India at the praise which Sir Garnet Wolseley has bestowed upon the Indian contingent, and throughout Syria, as well as at Constantinople, bPeris, Vienna, and other European clpitals, the result of the victory is marked. Existing feeling only shows what terrible results would have followed a British reverse. Lord Dufferin has communicated to Earl Granville a note from the Porte, thanking the British Government for the re-establishment of order in Ezypt, and expressing a hope that the bonds of friendship at present existing between the two countries may be drawn still closer. Earl Granville has instructed his Excellency to convey to the Porte the satisfaction of the BritDh Government at the friendly assurances contained in its note. A report has reached Cairo that 18 Mussulmans have been arrested for an attack made some days ago upon some Christians at a place called Awseen, in the province of Glaizeh. It is stated that the outrage took place in the Coptic church, in which the Christians had taken refuge upon the town crier making a public announcement that Arabi had driven the English from Egypt and had ordered a general massacre of Christians. On Wednesday the Council of Ministers met at Cairo and agreed upon the wording of three decrees, which will be signed by the Khedive. The first institutes a special Commission to be held at Cairo for the prosecution of all acts of rebellion committed by the military 'br by civilians. The second orders a court-martial to be held at Cairo to give judgment according to the Military Code, without appeal, in all cases submitted to it by the Commission. The third institutes another court-martial, to be held at Alexandria, for the trial of all cases submitted to it by the Commissioners appointed there and: at Tanfah. Ths inhabitants of Cairo were startled on Thursday afternoon by a tremendous explosion—se startling indeed it was that both Europeans and Arabs took to flight, and it was some time before confidence was rgstored. It was found that a train containing shells Aid ammunition which was standing at the railway station had caught fire. The first great explosion was followed by minor detona- tions at intervals of about half a minute, and in the course of twenty minutes there was another alarming explosion followed by the discovery that the station was in flames. The day had been intensely hot, and it is believed that the heat of the sun actin.. upon the iron roof of the station was the cause of the disaster. We regret to learn that thirty persons were killed, and probably a large num- ber have been injured.
THANKSGIVING SERVICES AT ST. PETER'S CHURCH, NEWTON.

Special services of thanksgiving for the harvest, and for the success of our armies in the East were held in St. Peter's Church, Newton, on Sunday last. The interior of the sacred edifice had undergone elaborate decoration at the hande of a number of ladies in the congregation. Beneath the stained glass window at the back of the altar-table was a deep fringe of ferns, flowers, fruit, atc., along the bottom running a border of corn and wheat, with well sized toma- toes interspersed. Immediately over the altar was the text, "The harvest of the earth is ripe," formed with gilt letters on a red ground, while on each side of the altar were arranged a numher of valuable plants in pots, kindly lent for the occasion by Mrs. Birley, of the Brookside." The top of the pulpit was encircled with a border of fine red and white dahlias. irnrtiediately beneath which were rows of barley, oats, Lic. Several bunches of luscious grapes were suspended at intervals, while in front of all was a most attractive floral cross—the "arms" being formed of red dahlias, while the centre flower at the point of junction was a massive white dahlia. The choir stalls were artistically decorated with wheat, corn, and barley, and the reading desks were none the less attractive in their covering of flowers, fern, ke. From the lectern was suspended a large bunch of delicious-looking grapes, immediately beneath which was a floral decoration in the shape of a cross, while at the b)ttom were two miniature baskets of flowers. An in- numerable quantity of flowers, apples, and other fruits were arranged and artistically interspersed with the other decora- tions. At the opposite end of the edifice thelkent had been literally covered and well laden with ferns, mosses, flowers, grapes, apples, melons, corn, wheat, &c., the whole having been most attractively and splendidly arranged. Among those who took a share in the work of providing forth the fruit, flowers, &ea were Mrs. and Miss Binley, Miss Pearson, Miss Pennington, and Miss Jones and many other willing helpers gave their services. The services of the day commenced with the celebration of the Holy Communion at eight o'clock, at 10-30 matins, sermon and second celebra- tion, 3-3 C the Litany, and at 0-30 evensong, sermon, and choral. In the forenoon the preacher was the vicar, the Rev. H. Monk, M.,A., whose remarks were appropriate to the occasion, and they were lisitened to with the greatest of interest. The choir impressively rendered the anthem, "0 Lord, how manifold are thy worke" (Hamby). In the even- ing the pulpit was occupied by the Rev. Canon Dodd, M.A., vicar of Stretton, who, after pointing out that the Lord had. given us a law which should not be broken by which we were enabled to make due provision for our wants and necessities and have a regular succession of seedtime and harvest, summer and winter, observed that for those bless- ings and mercies they were met to thank Him. But, he said, it was also his duty to remind them that they had to thank God for the victory, swift and entire, that had attended our arms. We had to thank Him for the sagacity of our generals, for the courage and hardi- hood displayed by oar soldiers and sailors, through which great results had been obtained with a small loss—possibly an immense evil had been averted and future prosperity secured. They believed it was God who had determined those things, and that with him rested the issue. The choir very tastefully rendered the anthem "Ye shall dwell in the land" (Dr. Stainer), while the hymns for the whole day were specially selected in keeping with the services. An earnest appeal was made for liberality, so as to enable the work of restoring the west end of the church, according to the plans adopted to be carried out, and the collections were as follows: Morning, £2 Is. 5d.: forenoon, £2O is. .*l.; evening, £9 4s. 9d.; total, £3l 7s. 7d.

It is understood that when Sir G. Wolseley returns home, Sir A. Alison will take the chief comtnand of the army of occupation. With the approval of the British Government, Baker Pasha has been reque,sted by the Khedive to undertake the reorganisation of the Egyptian army. Samples of the new Egyptian cotton crop have been ex- hibited at Alexandria, and the quality is sahlato be good. Tile crop, however, is failing for want of irrigation. It is announced that peerages have been conferred by the Queen on Sir Garnet Wolseley and Sir Beauchamp Seymour, in recognition of their distinguished services in Egypt. Accounts of the British victories in Egypt have reached Syria, and have hada tranquilising effect there. Business begins to show signs of improvement, and refugees who had fled to Beyrouth from Egypt are returning thither. Aftet making the best estimates from all sources, a correspondent at Cairo calculates that the native losses during the campaign have been nearly 5,000 from and including the day of the bombardment of Alexandria, and that the English losses from all causes were less than 300. It has been determined, it is said, as soon as the authority of the Khedive has been re-established, to grant a plenary amnesty to all who have not taken an active part in the rebellion. The prominent leaders are to be tried by a special Commission, and it is expected that severe punishment will be inflicted upon the ringleaders. Taking advantage of the pacification effected by the Eng- lish troops in Egypt, the French Government has ordered to be sent back to their country the Egyptian refugees who have been staying at Marseilles for three months. Six hun- dred and ten embarked on Monday. The remainder will be embarked on Saturday. div.head: VIE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. SPEECH fiY MR. ALDERMAN DAVIES, OF WARRINGTON.
div.p: VIE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. SPEECH fiY MR. ALDERMAN DAVIES, OF WARRINGTON.

What Liverpool terms "Manchester's ambition to bec )me a seaport" has develop2d into the virtual adoption of e ' scheme which, if not the favourite one of a tidal canal, , seems far more practicable, and bids fair, Parliament con- senting, to be carried out with all the enterprise Manchester can display. In June, a Provisional Committee was ap- pointed to further the project of a ship canal, and oil Tees- day presented a report at a meeting of subscribers to tee guarantee fund. Separate reports were read of the engineers employed to make surveys of the Mersey and 'retell— namely, Mr. E. Leader Williams and Mr. Hamilton 11. Fal- ton, with the observations thereon, of Mr. Abernethy, CE., of London, the advising engineer, who had carefully weighed the evidence adduced by Mr. Willimns and Mr. Futon. As a preface to his own statement, Mr. tWilliams described the I original proposal to widen and deepen the whole channel, to cut off bends in order to shorten the distance from Manches- to Runcorn, to build retaining wells and dredge the tidal _estuary from Runcorn to the sea, and to bring up the tide to Manchester through a deep cutting. He then condemned it. Such a result might be achieved by excavating a deep channel, but it would have to be a channel gradually in- creasing in size the whole length of the cutting, and not ant" of uniform width. To such a scheme many objections may ; be made, but Mr. Williams presented one which was deemed to be fatal—namely, its demonstrable insufficiency. This was the scheme which Mr. Fulton essayed to work out. He would make a navigable channel for large vessels from Liverpool to Manchester, a distance of 42 miles. To this end he would improve the navigation by construe ing train- ing walls between Otterspool and Runcorn, so as to ensure a minimum depth of 22 feet at low water of spring tides, ; and would excavate a channel with a bottom width of 80 feet, with passing places to Manchester where the canal would expand, and end in a tidal basin of 128 acres of sur- face. Upon this scheme Mr. Abernethy advised the cam- mittee adversely. He did not believe that by the formation of a channel of such length with parallel sides the result anticipated by Mr, Felten would follow, nor did he find in Mr. Fulten's report the data by which lie satisfied himself • that the tidal range will be secured. What be did find was a scheme which would cost over .£5 I ,000,000 based on ' general and limited information, and not so well calculated to serve the purpose in view as the scheme of Mr. Williams, the salient features of which be approves. These were the straightening, widening, and deepening of the tidal portion ; of the river Mersey, and the construction of a canal for the other portion of the distance. Mr. Williams would continue the tidal river from Garston to Latchford, above Warrington, and above that point to Manchester, a distance of 15 miles, and construct a ship canal, with locks to raise the water level to nearly its present height at the proposed site of the docks at Manchester. At Latchford he would have a group of three locks of different sizes placed side by side, *lose to and parallel with each other, for the passage of vessels of various kinds without waste of water. This idea is harrowed from Holland. Through a similar group of locks on the Amsterdam ship canal nearly 700 vessels of different tonnage have been passed in one day. The width of this canal would be 100 feet at the battom between Manchester and Warrington, wider than the Am- sterdam Canal by 13 feet, and than the Suez Canal by 22 feet. In the Suez Canal large steamers can only pass at certain places, whereas Mr. Williams intends that in the Manchester Ship Canal all sizes of vessels shall pass at any point. From Warrington to Runcorn the bottom of the canal will gradually widen until it reaches 300 feet, where it meets with and ends in the great tidal stream of the Mersey. Mr. Williams had carefully considered the-subject of floods, and is prepared to prevent them once for all by , permanently lowering the water level between Throstle Nest, Manchester, and Latchford an average of 10 feet, with a much wider and deeper channel for the passage of the flood waters at the lowered level. Below Warrington the low water level will be reduced on an average 15 feet, and the deeper and straighter course of the river will assist in decreasing the height of the floods. The gigantic character of the whole work may be indicated by the size of the great dock at Manchester,' which is designed to be 70 acres in extent, with gates 80 feet wide. The dock will gradually widen until it has a surface of three-quarters of a mile, when four branch docks will issue from it with wide quays between them, on which sheds will be erected. One curious and highly important feat of engineering skill may be re- ferred to. At Barton the river is crossed by the aqueduct of the Barton canal, principally used at this point for coal traffic. "1 propose to construct here," says Mr. Williams, "a new aqueduct, the centre portion of which will be a wrought-iron caisson, kept fell of water, which will swing on a central pier in a similar way to a railway swing bridge, leaving a wide opening for the passage of vessels on either side." Even if a boat is on the aqueduct and passing through the caisson it need not delay the opening of the aqueduct; it will remain floating in its basin while the caisson is swinging. Mr. Williams offers to complete the work for £5,400,000, a sum which Mr. Abernethy con- sidered reasonable and sufficient.

At the meeting on Tuesday, Mr. Peacock presided, in the absence of Mr. D. Adamson, the chairman of the Provisional Committee (who is attending the meeting of the Iron and Steel Institute at Vienna) and narrated the steps which the Committee have taken since their appointment last June. He also foreshadowed the course to be pursued in order to get the necessary Parliamentary sanction for the prosecution of the scheme, observing that, as it was a scheme largely for the public benefit, substantial support was expected from the public. On the motion of the Chairman, the report of the Provisional Committee was unanimously approved, the scheme of Mr. Leader Williams being thereby fully accepted; and it was resolved, "That steps be forthwith taken by the Provisional Committee to raise a fund and apply for Parlia- mentary powers to carry out the scheme as recommended by the report." The Clammily proposed "That as soon as, in the opinion of the Provisional Committee, an adequate fund has been raised.a further meeting be ?onvened to appoint a permanent committee to carry out the undertaking." In answer to a question as to the continuance of the present guarantors, the Cbairman said that a certain number of gentlemen had given their names to the extent of some £1.2.000. That enaran- tee had been given with a view of making preliminary in- quiries, and to prepare everything to bring before them that day. To that extent only it was intended that these gentle- men should guarantee their money. Many. of them, he thought, would now became shareholders, but that was not a question he need trouble them with that day, inasmuch as the intention of the committee was provided the scheme went on and money was raised to justify them in goitg be- fore Parliament—that £lOO,OOO be raised. So far as the-.ex- penses were concerned they simply allowed the present guarantors to contribute their quota of expense up to that day, Anti all after expenses were to be paid out of the further guarantee fund raised. Mr. Alderman DAVIES (Warringtoraseconded the motion. He said he was pleased to have the opportunity of seconding it, because it enabled him to say that the meeting should allow a little latitude in the matter of expense before going to Parliament, and some further expense might be unavoid- able. He thought they ought not to draw the line of ex- penses too tight, and say that they were ts be confined to a certain amount. It might be desirable not to restrict the expenses too far, because the duties of tbe Provisional Com- mittee were not yet qaite eaded, and they would have to go on with their labours in carrying out the three resolutions. He thought it desirable that they should consider the best way in which the Provisional Committee might promote the general acceptation of the scheme and place it before the public, and if the public were favourable and would take up shares at the same time that the promoters were raising £lOO,OOO he thought considerable impetus would be given to the people who would contribute that amount. The Pro- visional Committee shouli be instructed to esp cially invite the co-operation of the Corporations of Manchester, Salford, and Warrington, who, he thought, might leeally contribute to the support of the scheme. He had great pleasure in seconding the resolution. The motion was carried, and so also was another, thanking the chairm an for presiding.

Hon. 1876), for five years Head Master's As- sistant at Leamington College. Boarders are received in the Head Master's house, which has recently been fitted for the purpo,-e, and their comfort and well-being secured under the care of the Head Master and his wife. The climate is identical with that of Buxton •, education sound and thorough in preparation, either for the Universities. the various Local and Prelimivary Examinations, or for Mer- cantile life.
