div.head: TURD-Y, SEPTEMBER 30, 1882.
div.p: TURD-Y, SEPTEMBER 30, 1882.

- - THE extraordinary silence of the Irish members of Parliament was broken on Sunday by Mr. Healy, who was the principil speaker at a meeting held at Mihewn Malbay, County Clare, described as a "charming kipot on the edge of the Atlantic." The meeting was convened in support of the new pro- gramme of the extreme section of the Irish party, who, since the passing cr the Land Act, have found their field of agitation limited. From time to time hints have been thrown out es to the nature of the new crueade, but it was reserved for the Stoiday .Yatits of New York to publish the tex4; of the programme, which has been compiled by Mr. Michael Davitt, and is to be submitted to a convention of the Irish mem- bers, or rather of the Parnellite party, to be held in Dublin on an early date. How far the programme may be accepted is as yet doubtful, and without saying more of its objects and aims at this stage than that they are of a very sweeping and somewhat revolutionary character, it may bo open to us to doubt whether even their attainment, if practicable, will produce the results which Mr. Davitt and, we may say, everybody else se much desires. It is some satis- faction to know that legal and eonetitutioaal

div.head: EX/M[l'4TR, SATUR DA Y, SEPTEMBER 30, 1882.
div.p: THE EX/M[l'4TR, SATUR DA Y, SEPTEMBER 30, 1882.

th resources only are to be employed in furtering reforms whieh are now formulated—aid we do not believe that Mr. Devitt would airail himself of any other, for no man during the earlier stages of the land agitation was more careful than he to resort to other than constitutional means to fight the battle of the Land Lertgue—but we could have wished that the present agitation had been delayed. The major portion of the time of the pre,sent Parliament so far has undoubtedly been absorbed with Irish affairs, to the exclusion of almost everything English, Scotch, or Welsh, and though much yet remains for Parliament to do before Ireland may be said to have had only justice conceded to her, Irish members should not forget that it is sometimes necessary to rest (for a time at least) and be thankful until other matters of equally pressing importance have been attended to. The new combination is to be known, it seems, ad "The National Land and Industrial Union of Ireland," and a few facts taken from its programme may be profitably cited. Its object is to improve the condition of the Irish people, and the reforms the Union contemplates are classed as social, industrial, educational, and political. S)eially the Union aims at the complete abolition of the landlord system, bu• which, by the passing of the L snd Act nod the kindred measure dealing with arrears, he been practically aceemplished ; it further aims at the amelioration of the condition of the agricultural labourer, whose circumetances at best are wretched and demand relief; and it aims also at the ereetion of better dwellings for the people, a matter in which there is room for very great improvement. In- dustrially the aims of the Union are such that we can accord to them a hearty support. No one can cavil at the proposed revival of manufacturing indus- tries, which we fear were only destroyed through capitalists being driven from the couutry. The development of Irish fisheries, another object aimed at industrially, would, we believe, be productive of much good ; whatever can be done towards an " im- provement in methods of land cultivation" must be attended with profit, alike to the cultivator, producer, and the consumer; and in the "establishment of co- operative loan societies for the advance of money with which to work unoccupied or waste lend," we recognise a &ma .ficie effort on the part of the people to help themselves instead of depending on the State. The educational reforms of the Union are stated to be (1) to improve the scientific and practical education of the artisan and labouriug classes by the establish- ment of mechanics' (evening) institutes throughout the country; and (2), encouragement of national literature and cultivation of the Irish language. Here, too, there is nothing with Which fault can be found ; and it may be well to remember, as Mr. Fawcett pointed out only on Tuesday evening in ad- dressing his constituents at Hackney, that the principle of elementary education applied to England and Scotland has not yet been applied to Ireland. If, as the Postmaster General asks, education is so essential to England and Scotland as to indace the State to step in between parent and child, is it less important to Ireland? and if English and Scotch children need all the aivantageS that education Ering them, is the additional moral strength secured by education less important to the Irish child? Surely not. Educational reform, then, is another legitimate field in which Irish wiln ixiiy work and Parliament I will riot have discharged its duty to the Bmerala Isle until it has conferred the same advantages in this respect upon Ireland that it has upon England and i Scotland. The political reforms contemplated by the Union do not all of them come within the range of practical politics. It is absurd, for instance, to sup- pose that tke "repeal of the Act of Union and obtainment of Irish self-government" is ever likely to be realised. The most 'advanced member of the Cabinet, Mr. Chamberlain—and probably ho will go as far towards making concession to Ireland as any member of Parliament—has declared that the repeal of the Act of Union is impossible; and in this he accurately interprets the feelings of those who may follow his lead. The tie is indissoluble; the prosperity of both England and Ireland is besund up in its maintenan* ; and its severance, if ever that should occur, is sure to militate more itifuriously to Ireland than ever it can to do to this country. It is useless agitating for something which is impracticable, and therefore the suggested reform would, in our opinion, be much better expunged from the list. " The abolition of the grand jury system of county government," another of the political reforms, is something more reasonable, and in "the improvement of representation of local boards," all sections of the community may join with reasonable hope of success. The organisation of the Union is to be sufficiently comprehensive to include parish branches, electoral district branches, county central branches, provincial executive branches, and central executive councils, each having its duties assigned, and sending representatives to the parent Union. If deemed practicable, an operative land and labour association for the working of unoccupied and waste land, with a capital of £1,000,0e0 in shares of Li each, will be established in connection with the Union; and the laudable object of this association will be to provide profitable occupation for labqurers arid evicted tenants, so as, if possible, to stay emigration and increase the general prosperity of the country. Pending the repeal of the Act of Union, it is proposed to establish "a more national party representation," though how that is to be accomplished is not indi- cated ; certainly it will never be secured by "the pay- ment of national representatives," which is advocated, for it will be a.serryAay for Ireland when she cannot find any of the gifted sons of her soil to represent her without fee or reward. "The extension of the fran chise," forms also one of the planks of this new plat- form, which is to be the panacea for all the ills to which Ireland is heir. As regards the franchise Ireland is unquestionably less favoured than England, but this is a reform which has been delayed only in vonsequence of the land question pressing for selu- don, and it may be fairly expected to claim the atten- tion of Parliament very soon. Such are the salient points in the new land league programme; and even though Mr. Parnell should be of opinion that such an organisation is impossible under the existing Coercion Act and the arbitrary powers of jurisdiction which it confers upon local magistrates, that is scarcely sufficient to deter some of the more ardent of the Irish members from launching it upon the coun- try. Once fairly launched, there is no telling where or when its course may be stopped. With many of the reforms, as we .have seid, we heartily agree, and long to see them accomplished. Others, again, we be— lieve to be impracticable if not suicidal to Ireland her- self ; but we very much doubt whether the present time is opportune for pressing any of them upon the attention of Parliament. We have had Irish affairs tor nauseam, and we incline to the opinion that Irish members will best consult Ireland's own interests if for a time they content themselves with the advan- tages they have already gained and allow other parts of the Kingdom to have some attention paid to them. Unless the Irish members are willing to do this, they may find that their persistent advocacy of Irish affairs, to the exclusion of everything else, will do Ireland a great deal more harm than good.
THE BOUNDARIES OF RUNCORN. IN ERESTING PARTICUL3RS.

We have had brought under our notice an Act of Parlia- ment which has become law during the past s?ssijA, which is of some interest locally, as it considerably afLets the' townships of Runcorn, Halton, Prodsloam, and Frodsharn Lordship. Some few mouths ago a local Government in- quiry was held at Frodsham by R. J. D orsey, Eq., under the Divided Parishes Act of 1870 and 1879, for the .p7.17-p-Ose of hearing evidence for or ag tint altering the boundaries of the above-mentioned townships, And we remernbee looking with some degree of curiosity at the coloured maps pro- duced. That of Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship was very like a paint-bospattorad roll of pper. So intermixed

was one township with the other that the only possible course seemed to be either the union of bath or the absorp- tion of one into the other, and we should not be surprised to hear that the ultimate result of that inquiry will be an order of the Local Government Board to carry it into effect. The difficulties of the sewerage question of the present, and the water scheme of the very near future, seem to render such a course more and more imperative. he map of Run- corn and Halton, though not of so chaotic a character, revealed such a mixing as called for remedy. In connection with this state of things we h eve gathered a few particulars. Very many years ago the village or hamlet of Runcorn lay on the west side of the Sprinch Brook, the site of the , Town Hall, and all above being agricultural land; some few fields of which bionged in some way to th 3 township of Halton while one belonging to the township of Runcorn, going her the n ImS of the Poor's-field, lay embesomed in the Halton fields, near to Halton Brook. When the Bridge- inter Canal was constructed one of these fields belonging to Halton was cut through, and as a consequence of the growth of Runcorn the rest of the fill became building ground, and a portion of Bridge-street occupies the outer edge, so it happens that the property comprised within the four boun- daries of the Bridgwater Canal, GAS street, Bridge-street, and Stone-street, including a poi tion of the gas wo, ks, is a part of the township of Halton, thouah in fact in the busi- ness centre of Ruccarn. A litt'e higher up an the left hand side of Bridge-street there was another field or fields, and from the fact that one of the houses now standing on a pcetioe is of ceprhold tenure, subject to a ground rent of ad a year, we think must have been either crown or common lands. A road, c,lled was cut through this plot, as, we think, for commenication between the Old Quay Canal and Docks and the Bridgewater Canal, which.at this point are very contiguous, and so it again happens that the left bail side of the top of lr lge-str-t,t, ton Mrs Lr-oc-rs' shon to Me7eey 11 ,u Irwell-lane, and we blirt ilr Tortler'a shop ant i f -Nc I 011S!S t n other side of Irwell-lane are Also a at or the township n If tlton. ! A rah eeta elne inciden- a, st out ot theees c to lieations at ar c •tit School Board election. A ratep tyer oce..pying the larg,st block of prop,rty pri,scfuted herself At Pie ballot box, eel oo b ing told her n tine was not on the register AS a voter for Runcorn was great:y attonished. She protested that she had vo,ed in the Ccemnissioners' elections, an admitted fact, as she paid Ruecorn cts!rict ratee for the same property, but all in vain; the presidingofficer wasinexorable, and she returned to her residence in the township of Halton situate in the heart of Runcorn, "a wiser if not a sadder " educationalist. In the part of Runcorn known as Millbrow there were also fields belonging to the township of Halton which have long since been built upon ; on one side of the road the overseers of Halton collect the poor's rates, while on the other the Runcorn overseers exercise The same duty. A lithe further on the long row of houses known as Union- street are very capriciiusly divided between the two town- ships, some little way up the street being in Halton, while above and below their neighbours reside in Runcorn, while at the extreme edge of the boundaries at the Stonehills and the Duke's Meadow tho two townships are interlocked or dovetailed in such a singular manner as to suggest the idea of keeping Runcorn fast to her moorings lest she should drift away with the ebb tide of the river Meraey. We should not forget to mention that the whole of these singular Hal- ton colouies are within the limit of theßuncorn Improvement kct, and pay the district rates of that town, while the Hal- ton overseers are practically compelled to keep two sets of accounts; one for the township of Halton proper, the other for Halton-within Runcorn. For several rears after the passing of the Education Acts these detached places were beyond reach of the School Board and its beneficent work, and they remained until the act of 1878 called into existence school attendance officers, having jurisdiction in all places where there had not been previ- ously a school board termed. But to return to the point from whence we started. The Act of Parliament in ques- tion absorbs all detached portions of a township with the township by which it is surrounded from attd after the 25th of March next, so that Halton will have added the piece of land behind Wood's-row, near Halton brook; and Runcorn will become, possessed of Halton-within-Runcorn. Fried- sham and Frodsharn Lordship will have to agree on the "give and take" principle; and thus we shall have reason te remember that in a session of Parliament which seems to have been given up to Irish affairs a piece of very useful legislation has been accomplished, which we !live no doubt will benefit the country in general and our immediate neigh- bourhood in particular.

Israel has published a letter identifying Mr. Gladstone with the Beast in the prophetic vision whose number was 668. The letter is so remarkable that I make no apology for publishing it here. The writer says :—" For more than two years past I have felt confident ia my own mind that Mr. Gladstone, our Prime Minister, was the great deceiver who is to deceive all those carnal professors whose names are not in the Book of Life. Here is his word and the number. In the Greek language every letter stands for a number. G stands for 3, L for 30, A for 1. D for 4, S for 200, T for 300, 0 (short) 70, N 50, E (long) 8-663." Politicil feeling may have something to do with this effu- sion, which, however, is nething if it is not ingenious.

The Postmaster-General has this week been addressing his constituents at Hackney. He is not a member of the Cabinet, and cannoi, therefore, be expected to give utter- ance to Cabinet secrets, consequently his remarks on the Egyptian question, for instance, are scarcely so important as they would be were he a Minister of Cabinet rank; vet gr. Fawcett is one of the most respected and at the same time independent members of, Her Majesty's Government. In the administration of the Post Office he has shown remark- able ability, and whatever be says on this point is deserving of attention. From him then we learn, and I confess with some degree of regret, that the Parcel Post is not likely to come into operation until after Christmas. This is the more to be regretted from the fact that the chief railway com- panies have already lowered their rates for the carriage of parcels. These rates came into operation on . the ticst of this month, and it will be a pity if they should in any degree militate against the Parcel Post, which is, as Mr. Fawcett says, the greatest development of the postal system since the intro- duction of the penny post. Considering, however, the evra work which the parcel post will entail, and the care that should be taken lest it should interfere with the letter service, it is better that the scheme should b 3 thoroughly perfected before it is tried so as to render it a success. Not less important than the pa& post is the project which has been sanctioned for enabling annuities and policies of life assurance to be more easily obtained throu!4h the Post Office, and the working class.es will learn with satisfactioa that not only is the scheme being rapidly matured, but that when completed it will be of such a nature that it will be possible to devote as small a sum- as a penny a week to make some provision for old age, or to provide for a policy of life assurance. I could have wished that Mr. Favece.tt had given some information as to the contemplated change in the working of the Post Office Savings Bank. It is well known that considerable inconvenience aris to depositors because they cannot draw anything on demand; while on the other hand the fact that every deposit has to be registered at the head office points to the expenditure of unnecessary labour in the Post Office itself. It is said that the system is about to be very touch simplifled, and so that cammunie ttion with the head office wi:l be unnecessary. The alteration is one which will be heartily avelcoated by depositors, and for my part I believe the Treasury may well be trusted to work out its accom- plishment. FLACCUS.

WIDNES PALISH CHIJILCII MISSION ROOMS.—About a fortnight ago a mission room was established in Alforde- street, Widnes, as a kind of auxiliary to the Parish Church The room is capable of holding about 140 people, and the services so far have b3en attended with gratifying success. On week days the room is used for holding temperance gatherings. SUDDEN DEATHS AT WIDNES.—The police report the sudden death of Margaret Ann Heyes, a new barn babe, whose parents live in Tithebarn-street, Appleton. The infant was born about half-past seven on Tuesday morning. It appeared to lel small-sized and weakly, and it was at once taken to St. Bede's Catholic Chura, Where it was baptised by the Rev. Father .Finegan. Afterwards it was taken to ' the surgery of Dr. McDonnell. It died abeut • half-past twelve.—On Wednesday nnrning, Elizebeth Arnold, a widow reeidiag at 52, Catherine-street, Widnes, died sud- denly about noon. Oa rising that morning the woman appeared to be in good health, but at eight o'clock she became ill. Dr. McDonald's assistant attended her, but she died as stated. The Coroner has referred the death to the registrar. THE FUNERAL OF TA LAtE Ma. JNO. PARTLY, OF Rreereoner.-The remains of Mr. John Parry, who di. d on Thursday, were interred at the Runcorn Cemetery, on Saturday afternoon. The deceased, who was 42 years of age, was for several years inspector of nuisances to the Run- earn Board of Commissioners, and he was also the deputy superintendent of the Runcorn Volunteer Fire Brieade. The members of the brigade honoured the memory of their late chief by attending the funeral. The corpse was borne to the graven the Prince of Wales engine, which was preceded by Messrs. Brookes, Barker, C. Dutton, and A. Hough ; while following were a nunaber of tradesmen and relatives of the deceased. The Rev. J. J. Bryant officiated at the grave, TRESPASSING ON Tlll3 RAILWAY : A CURIOUS POINT. —Peter Tarry and John Tuley were summoned, More the magistrates at the Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, for trespassing on the joint lines of the Midland and Manches- ter, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railways at Widnes.—Tarry did not wean—Mr. Wm. Bartley, detective sergeant, stated that on the let inst he was on the line near to the Tan House Crossing, which was between the road and Messrs. Sullivan's works, when the defendant opened the gate and walked down the lino in the direction of Messrs. Sullivan's works. The company. had received so many complaints of trespassing in this manner, that they were determined to put a stop to it.—The Clerk asked if the defendant. had been warned not to trespass.—Witness replied in the negative, adding that the Act did not require the company to do so.— The Bench said the company were bound to warn people before they could take proceedings, and they consequently dismissed the case.

DID E[ll CONSENT? ALLEGED RODBEaY LT WE.STONT. William Galloway, a youth, was brought up on remand before Ctptain Hazlehurst, at Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, to answer a chary of having, on Frid t.T, stolen a pair of boots of the value of 103., the prop?rtv of Richard Worthington. Worthington, tt seemed, is a horse driver on the banks of the river Weaver. On Friday. he and the pri- soner were together in the drivers' kitchen, Weston Point. After dinner Worthington fell asleep, and when he awoke he discovered that his hoots had been stolen. Suspecting the prisoner, who had left the kitchen, he went in search of him. Prisoner, however, Was captured by a dock police- man and given in charge of P.C. Wallace, of the Roncorn force. He was then wearing the prosecutor's boots, but when charged denied having stolen them. He alleged that while Worthington was asleep he went to him, shook him, and asked him if he might wear the boots. The reply, he stated, WAS an assenting grunt, accompanied with the words "Go on." Mr. Superintendent Williamson said the prisoner had been twice previously convicted. The magistrates, refusing to believe Galloway's plausible story, committed him to the sessions for trial.

HARVEST THANKSGIVING SERVICE AT BETHESDA CHAPEL, RUSCORN.-1 thanksgiving service for the in- gathering of the harvest was held in liethesia Congrega- tional Chapel, on Sunday evening, when there was a large eongregation. The floral decorations were of a pretty but modest description. The pulpit was adorned with a fringe .of oats. On the Communion table were arranged several bouquets of brightly blooming flowers, miniature sheaves of the " waving golden grain," and some dishes of choice fruit; while on the gallery front, behind the pulpit, were displayed in artistically cut capitals on a blue figured ground, the words" He crowns the year with his goodneSs." The service was commenced by the choir singing Curwen's anthem "Sanctus." In the course of the evaning the choir also sang the anthem 'Gloria" (Hadyn's 12th Miss.) The singing in both instances was of an enjoyable character. Mr. F. Fair- hurst was the conductor. Tne Rev. J D. Thomas preached an appropriate sermon from the 13th Matthew, 18'h to the 23rd verses. At the conclusion of the service the Iltllcltijsli Chorus was played on the organ by Mr. John Ravenscroft ; and collections were made in aid of the chapel fund.

ALLEGED ROPE ROBBERY AT RuNconx.—At Runcorn Police Court on Thursday, before Mr. John Brundrit, James Williams, a nun( boatman, formerly of Raucorn, was charged with stealing 51Ibs. of rope, value 255, the prepertY of the Bridgewater Navigation Company. It, was als ) charged with receiving the ropes keowing them to have been soolen.--Mr. Lake appeared to defend the prisoner.— Mr. W. H. Cnadwick, manager of the-ropery belonging. to the Bridgewater Navigation Company at Top Locks, said he I had examined the ropes (produced), which bieloneed to the company, and had been made at the company's works. He identified them by a thread of a particular Colour which ran through one of the strands, and also by the way in which , the material was made up.—ln reply to Mr. Brundrit, the witness said the rope WAS not made to be sold, and the pri- soner Could not buy it from any one belonging to the corn- pany.—By Mr: Johnson (assistant mtgistrates' clerk): The ropes were supplied exclusively for the company's own use. —By Mr. Lake: He did not allege that the rope had been stolen from the works. It WAS likely that they hod been stolen from one of the flate.—James Weedall, cousLah:e, employed by the Navagation Company, stated that a little before seven o'clock on Tuesday night. he saw Pr-" Ion market boat alongside the prisoner's boat, and the way in which they were tied together aroused his susftioas. He, however, did not 4se anything take place, and I a went to the pier head. After he had done his otlice work he again went to the boat, which was then up the locks, and ab nit 11 o'clock the prisoner yymt aboard the worse for drink. Between one and two o'clock on the Wedneslay morning he (witness) and P.S. Whalley searched the prisoner's boat, and,l,tied in a s.ack, which was concealedat the forecastle end of the boat, they .found the ropes produced.—P.S. Whalley deposed as to the recovery of the ropes, and said lie appre- hended the prisoner. whom he took to the pclice.station. He charged him with the robbery, and he repliel "I Ito Owl nothing about them.—Mr. Superintendent Williamson ap- plied for the prisoner to be remanded until Monday, remarking that it was necessary on behalf of the prisoner and the public that the (lice Should be thoroughly investi- gated.—The prisoner was remanded, and Ir. Lake asked that he mioht be almitted to bail.—Mr. Superintendent Williamson objected, re irking on the diffic& my in provin:Y these'cases. The police had difficulties to contend with when the prisoner was in gaol, bat they wonid besgreatly increased were the prisoner set at liberty.—Mr. Brundrit re- t fused 1,0 grant bail.

THANKSGIVING SERVICE AT THE PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, RUNCORN. To-morrow (Sunday) a harvest thanksgiving service will be held in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Greenwav-road. Special music will be rendered, and the edifice will be decorated with flowers and fruit, dona- tions of which are asked for.

WIDNES LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.—On Monday evening next a soiree, to be followed by a public meeting, will ba held in the Volunteer Hall, in connection with the Widnes Liberal Association. Mr. E. K. Muqpratt will preside, and the principal speaker will be the Res. Charles Beard, of Liverpool. Mr.. Holbrook Gaskell and others will also deliver addresses.

RUNCORN COUNTY COT/RT.—At this court, on Tues- day, before the judge, Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes, and Mr. E. J. Nicholson, registrar, there were 160 plaints and 2) julg- ment summonses for hearing. Alllthe cases, however, were of a trivial nature, and of no public interest. THE SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK AT WIDNES.—Mr. Danby, clerk to the Widnes School Board, appeared at Widnes Petty Sessions on Wednesday to prosecute the following persons for neglecting to send their children regularly to school :—Michael Monaghan, Peter Riley, James Cppock, John Keating, and Stephen White. The usual fine of ss. was inflicted in each case. TARPORLEY AGRICULTURAL Snow.—There is every pros- pect of the Tarporley Agricultural Society's show, which will be held in a field in Greenway-road, Runcorn, on Thursday next, being a great success. Upwards of £2OO will be offered in prizes, and the entries, we understand, are very numerous. The programme for the day contains several events of great interest. Tne leaping of horses over hurdles and water, will no doubt be a rather exciting sight, and the parade of horses and prize cattle will lo& viewed with pleasure. A public luncheon is to be held at half past one.

A WIDNES RS.GDEALER'S RUSE. —At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, before Messrs. Holbro—ok Gaskell, junr., and H. S. Hall, Henry Steward, a rag and salt dealer, was charged with stealing 3d. by fraud from Maria Oxley, wife of James Oxley, pointsman, Halewood. From the state- ment of Mr. Superintendent Barker, it appeared that on Tues- day the prisoner was selling salt at Halewood, and Mrs. Oxley asked him the price. He replied "3d. a lump," and Mrs -Oxley purchased one, giving the prisoner a 2s. piece. Not until a few minutes after the prisoner had departed did she discover that he had only returned her Is.. 3d. change' and she then informed her husband, who went in pursuit of the prisoner. Mr. Oxley tracked the prisoner fer a mile and half, when overtaking him he asked for the 6d. Ibe prisoner - declined, and descending from his cart, he struck Mr. Oxley a blow on the band with a saw. The prisoner, who was very boisterous, stated he had returned the correct change, but the Bench took a different view of the case, and sent him to gaol for 14 days. 1 RUNCORN YOUNG MEN'S CHRISTIAN ASSOCIATION CRICKET CLuß.—The annual meeting of the Runcorn Young Men's Christian Association Cricket Club was held at Mr. Arthur Riley's Coffee and Cocoa Rooms, Bridge-street, on Thurs- day evening, when over 20 members sat down to an ex- cellent tea, which did great credit to the caterer. Subse- quently an adjournment was made to a large room upstairs. Mr. F. J. Adams occupied the chair. Mr. John Saunders (the secretary) read the report, which was adopted. The club, it appeared, was only formed late in June, but, despite this drawback, and the want of a suitable field, the matches being played on Runcorn Heath, the members had a fairly successful season. Out of the five matches played three were won; one lost, and ene drawn, the howling of the team haying been above the average. Mr. Saunders.also read a financial statement, which showed there was a small balance in hand. Encotraged by their favourable start, the mem- bers are emboldened to aspire to a position in the cricketing world, and as there is no representa- tive, Runcorn team, will, with judicious management and 3 good captain, no doubt accomplish their object. A field is an indispensable factor, and every effort is being made to obtain one. The meeting decided to request Mr. Robert Shaw to accept the presidency of the club, cud the following gentlemen were appointed vice-presidents, subject to their acceptance of the post :—Mr. Thomas Norman, Mr. J. R. Frith, Mr. S. C. Beckett, Mr. J. D. Jones, and Mr. C. Nickson. The following officere were also appointed : Messrs. John Birkett, captain; F. J. Adams, sub-erten-lin ; H. Wright, hon. treasurer; J. Saunders, bon.. secretary ; auditors, J. Langshaw and T. Millington ; committee, W. Williamson, R. Morton, P. C. Williams, J. Pickthorne, and J. Pownall. The officiel part of the meeting concluded with a vote of thanks to the retiring officers, and the rest of the evening was spent in a convivial manner. Messrs. J. Bir- -1 kett, W. Millings, H. Wright, and Johnson favoured the I comptny with songs, whilst Messrs. E. Sherratt arid H. Grice each performed a pianoforte solo. Messrs J. D. ! Jones, C. Nickson, and T. C. Williams gave readings and recitstiOnl. JUTENILE TEMPLAR.? IN RUNCORF.—A public in-,:ti,g and entertain.nent to celebrate the re-establishment oi Juvenile Templary in Runcorn; and the opening of a temple, was held in the Bethesda schoe.- -osin, on Monday evening. Several years ago a juvenile temple existed I amongst the many temperance organisations of Runcorn, but from some cause it was allowed to die out. Ab iut two months ago, Mr. Kirkham Evans, a native of Runcorn, returned from South Australia, where he had siij Jorned for a few years, and becoming aware of the extinction of the temple, he set to work to form another in its piece. Havieg been the Grand Superintendent for the Temple in tl e tem coloniee of South end West Australia, he was well acqu drated with their organisation, and his efforte were rewasded with 1 suceees. The " Pdth of Safety" Temple was established, i the opening meet.dig, as previously stated, being held on i Monday evening. Already there is a membership of about 150 children, a facr which cannot fail to gratify those persons who are interested in the cause of temperance. The I pledge which the Juvenile Templar is required to sign is ' four-fold, lie (or she) promises to abstain from intoxicating • liquor, .smoking, gambling, and swearing. The les- Es Williams presided over the meeting, which was well attended. Appropriate addresses , were delivered by the chairmen, Bro. Bebbington, D.C.T., I of Aighurth,Sieter A. M. Green, R.W.S.J.T., of West Derby, I and the Rev. G. Heck, of Runcorn. The music 'l part of the programme was a successful and enjoyable feature in the evening's proceedings, the various pieces being rendered in good style. Miss Aslin, Miss. Hortoo, and Miss Lead- better, each give their services, which were much appre- cieted. An interesting incident occurred during the evening. While one of the speakers wae addressing the audience, a drunkard, evidently much impressed by what he had heard, walked up to the platform, and desired to take the pledge. His request, of course, was gladly complied with, and his good eximp!e was followed by about a dozen other persons. We ought to state that Mr. K. Evans is the superintendent of the newly-constituted lodge. TICK ALLII.3I) ROBBBR? OF A 120 NOTE AT WISXBS.— Henri, Wileon and Thomas Henry Ridgway, youths from Warrington, were brought up on remand at Widnes , Petty Sessions on Wednesday, before Mr. Holbrook Gasket), junr., and Mr. H. S. Hall, to answer a charge of having on the 15th inst., stolen a .i',2o bank of Eaglarad note, the property of Thomas Roatrou, stone mason, living at 18, Shaw-street, Rarecorn. Prosecutor repeated the evidence already pub- lished. He related how be received £33 Ils, from a beer- seller named Thomas Heys, of Liverpool-road, &Ilford, on Friday morning, and returning to Runcorn, broke his journey at Warrington, where he inet with the two prisoners, , who aided him out of a difficulty, and he in return treated' them to drink. Afterwards the three entered a third-class carriage to go to Runcorn. Rostron laid down on the seat, when Wilson put his hand into the pocket where the money was. He missed the £2O note when the train arrived at Widnes. A window of the carriage was broken, he believed by one of the prisoners kicking it with his foot. Rostron :omitted that he had had a" good soup" of liquor.—Crosee examined by Mr. Davies, (who appeared for the prisoners): lie went to Manctieeter on Tuesday, aud then to 13Iackpool. He received the £2O note from Heys on Friday morning. He did not know the name of the beerhouse. The money was for horse racing. After having some rum at a number of pnblichouses, he asked the prisoners to go to the station , with hint. He purchased tickets for himself and the prisoners. In the train when Wilson put his hand in his pocket he told him he should give him in charge at Widnes. He meant he would give him in charge for putting his band in his pocket. He did not know whether he was carried from the carriage into the waiting-room at Widnes or not. ' He believed he asked the prisoners at Warrineton to go with him to Et33C3r3.—P.C. Thompson said on Friday afternoon, the • 15th instant, he accompanied the list witness to Warrington, and about 10 p.m. he met the prisoners, who, in answer to his qesstione, seid they hid seen Rostron in the morning and taken him to 11/41 les. Re then apprehended them and bon:gilt them to Widnes, where he charged them with the robbery. They replied "We have no note." He (witness) hid searched for the note, but had been unable to find it.— Me. Joseph Smith said be was the stationmaster of the London aud North-Western Railway station at IVidnes. On the arrival of the train from Warrington at 12 o'clock, his a!tenzion was called to a broken carriage window. He went to the carriage, and in it he found the complainant Rostron, who seemed stup'clly drunk. He ti ail him removed to the wa•ting-room, and then went to his dinner, from which he returned about three o'clock. A few minutes after Elea 'mu he was informs(' that Rostron hail been rebbed of a £2O note. When the train arrived, lie saw Wilson running quickly down the stepe.—Cross-exainined by Mr. Davies : The prisoner was asleep in the waiting-room for two hours and a half.—Mr. Davies addressed the Bench for the defence, pointing out various discrepancies in the prose- cutor's evidence. His clients had acted the pert of friends to Rostron who was so drunk on the day in question that he had only a vague idea of what he was doing. Seeing . that the prisoner on at least two occasions dropped gold from his pocket, was he a fit person to be in possession of a £2O note, if it were true that be had one e lt was quite possible for him to have lost the note from his pocket. If it was not roved to the satisfaction of the Bench that time prosecutor had a £2O note, lie cliinaed on n,eliiilf of the prisoners, the benefit of that doubt. Tim p,ironere were youths who had very respectable psreuts in Warrington, and had not been in a court of justice before.—The Bench retired, and en returnieg into court, Mr. Gasket' said the magistrates considered tl ere Was a prima facie case for .trial, and committed the prisoners to the teeeeitgeee

The following officers were elected :—President, Mr. E. Gandy; vice- president, Mr. F. A. Clatke ; secretary, Mr. John dolford ; treasurer, Mr. 11. Niel ; committee, Messrs. Scragg, White, and Rev. UNITED CHRISTIAN BLUE RIBBON A.II.IIV.—OH Monday evening a contingent of the above army conducted a short ; open-air service in the Market-Place, Runcorn. Meetings have been held every evening in St. Luke's Chapel, Mason- street, with pretty fair success considering other attractioms in the town. Many have been induced to sign the pledge and don the blue ribbon. The above movement is a special one ef the general Blue Ribbon Army, conducted on ,s 4 I similar lines to the Salvation Army. SUPPORT OF A SON AT WIDNES.-At Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, Win. Mort was summoned to answer a charge of neglecting to contribute towards the support of his son James, who is in Bangor Industrial School.--Mr. Superintendent Baker said the defendant was 7s. in arrears of payment. On the 11th May the Bench made an order upon Mort to contribute is. per weok towards the sup- port of his son, but since that day he had paid very irregu- larly, the total amount of his payments being £1 us. He could prove that the d,,fendant was in a position to pay, and he asked for an immediate order for the money due. The Sergeant informed him that the defendant had that morning paid L 1 into court.—P.S. Clarkson deposed that the defendant was receiving LI 10a pr week, and the Bench made the order asked fur. FUNERAL OF A SUNDAY SCW,OL TLACRER AT RUNCORN! —On Thursday afternoon the remains of Mary Ellen daughter of Mr Wm. Handley, of Greenway-road, • were nterred at the Runcorn Cemetery. by the Rev. G. Hack. The young lady, who was 20 years of age, had been a mem- ber of the Wesleyan Society, and a teacher in connection with Cambden Sunday school for a number of years. On Sunday last after suffering patiently from a protracted and painful affliction, she passed "through death triumphant home." As an evidence of the esteem in which she was held, the thiee superintendents of the school Messrs. G. S. Hazlehurst, S. C. Beckett, and W. G. Shore, with a number of teachers and friends, preceeded the funeral Cortege. The coffin was carried by four teachers. At the close of the ceremony the friends and relatives sans " Safe in the arms of Jesus."

_ A VIOLENT WIDNES WOMAN.—Catherine Carey, a well known character, was charged at Widnes Police Court OD Wednesday, before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jour., and Mr. . H. S. Hall, with having on the 22nd inst. wilfully broken the window of a cell at the pelice station. She WAS also charged with threatening to take the life of Martha Holden, on the 21st inst. Evidence was given in support of these e charges, P.C. Bridges proving the damage to the window to the extent of Is. The prisoner was bound over to keep the peace for three months, himself in £lO and two sureties . of .£5, or in default a month's imprisonment. On the first charge she was fined ss. and costs, and ordered to pay the damage, with the alternative of a further 15 days' bard labour. THE THEFT OF A WATCH AND CHAIN: A WIDNES PAWN- EHobEn COMPLIMENTED.—Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun., and Mr. H. S. Hall, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Margaret Rooney, a middle-aged woman, was brought up on remand charged with having, ten the 19th Inst., stolen a silver watch and chain of the value of £3 Be., the property of John Holden, barman of the Albert Hotel, Widnes. The particulars of the robbery were reported in lest Saturday's Examiner. Mr. Bleasdale, assistant to Mr. Syred, pawnbroker, deposed that on the day in question the ! prisoner brought the watch and chain to the shop, and I asked for a loan of 10s. upon them. He questioned her as to who the articles belonged to, and having some doubt as to the truthfulness of her replies, he detained the watch and chain. He afterwards learned she had stolen them, and gave them to the police. P.C. Brown related how be captured the prisoner, sv ho, in answer to the charge, alleged that Holden had given her permission to pledge the articles. Informed that this statement was virtually a plea of not guilty, the prisoner pleaded guilty.—Saperintendent Barker then read a long black list against her.—The Bench, in committing the prisoner to gaol for two months, complimented Mr. 13:ease- dale upon his foresight; but in reply to a request for a re- ward, said they had no power to grant him one. It was stated, however, that the prosecutor intended to reward. him with half a guinea. TRH REVISION OF THS VOTERS' LIST IT RUNCORN, On Monday, in the Commissioners' Board-room, the revising barrister, Mr. L. Ffoulkes, commenced the revision of the Parliamentary voters' list for the Runcorn township. The Liberals were represented by Mr. Paterson (solicitor) and Mr Leake (agent) ; and Mr. Bentley (solicter) and Mr. Lightburn appeared on behalf of the Conservatives.—Mr. George Howard, 20, Trentham-street, claimed a vote for a share in leasehold shops in Church-street. Mr. Bentley : How long have you had the shops? Mr. Howard: Two years; and they were left me by my father's will. Mr. Paterson : Have you got a copy of the will under which-von claim this property? Mr. Howard : I can get one. *Mr. Paterson: Is it not a fact that the property was bequeathed to the trustees with directions to sell ? Mr. Howard : Yes. Mr. Paterson : Is it not also a fact that some of those who are beneficially entitled are your sisters? Mr. Howard : Yes. Mr. Paterson therefore submitted that Mr. Howard was not entitled to a vote for this property, and the claim was disallowed.—The Conservatives claimed a vote for Mr. George Jepson Knight for offices in High- street, Runcorn: Mr. Bentley: What is the rateable vale? Mr. Knight: .£l7. Mr. Bentley : how long have you had. them? Mr. Knight; I have paid rent for two years. Mr. Paterson: Have you any sub-tenant? Mr. Knight: I have allowed a gentleman to occupy the offices; but he has never paid me any rent, and I don't think le ever will. Mr. Pat- erson : Has he Ins name over the offices? Mr. Kniecht : Yes._ Mr. Paterson: How does he pay you for this occupation? Mr. Knight: He has never paid anything. Mr. Patteson : Do you mean to say that you allow this man to occupy these premises without any payment ? Mr. Knight: We- have no positive airane-ement ; but his clerk does some work for me. The vote was allowal. Mr. Knight asked.: for his expenses as lie had come from Manchester purposely that morning to claim his vote, and had pointed the facts of the case out to the Liberal agent several times. The Bar- rister could not hold that the objection was a frivolous one, and therefore ceuld not anew expenses. The court was then closed.

div.head: LOCAL AND GENERAL NOTES.
div.p: LOCAL AND GENERAL NOTES.

There was, no doubt, too good a foundation for the re- marks made by Mr. Carey at the last meeting of the Whines Local Board with regard to the spread of fever in the town, but it is extremely reassuring to know that the disease is abating. At present there are only about 20 cases, many of which are in the c mvalescent stage. No fresh cases have been reported for over a week, and for a longer period no deaths have resulted from the disease. Notwithstanding the astringent properties of the atmosphere of Whines, all danger can scarcely be considered as past, and Mr. Carey's observations with regard to the carelessness of parents, in permitting their children who had not wholly recovered from the fever to associate with others who are healthy. still hold good. Doctors are agreed that in scarlet fever especi- ally the convalescent stage is the most contagious, because the minute particles of the skin as they peel off fi eat in the air, and are respired into the lungs of other human beings ; and each of these particles is a seed of the disease. A medi- cal book directs that "when the skin begins to peel off it should be rubbed all over with carbolic oil, one part of carbolic acid to 40 parts of olive oil, and when the peening has ceased the oil should be washed off in a warm bath." "The reason for this is that small scales of skin carry infection, and the oil clogs the scales and pre- vents them from flying, whilst tthe carbolic acid destroys their infecting paver." This is a precaution which can easily be adopted by persons who have care of children suffering from the disease. Speaking of fever, I should like to ask if the statement made by Dr. Robinson at Runcorn Police Court on Monday —that the high rate of infant mortality in the town was caused by an epidemic of scarlet fever and measles—is true. The medical officer of health made the sweeping declaration that it was the direct result of the nuisance from the glycerine works, and mentioned not a word about either fever or measles. Now I have it on unquestionable authority that ther town is suffering seriously from measles, and also from scarlet fever—that in one street in Newtown one or more inmates of almost every house are stricken down with disease—that other parts of the town are suffering as much —and that about a week ago at one day school, where the 'average attendance is usually about 120, there only at- tended a sixth of that number, the other scholars tieing either themselves patients, or resided in houses where the disease was present. This is an alarming state of things, rendered the more so by the seeming fact that the sanitary authority would seem a to be ignorant of its presence, if their published proceedings are reliable. I always scan the re- port of the medical officer of health with interest, bit I do not remember to have read any reference to these serious epidemics; and it is to him the Commissioners have to look for direction in such a state of things. It is a curious fact that the fatal cases occur ie the outskirts of the town —Duke's Feld, Halton-road, and Newtown—there seldom being one in the centre of the town, where the vapours from the chemical works generally descend. If what I hear is correct, the trade of Whines is likely to be seriously affected by the pending strike of the colliers. It is rumoured that in the event of the strike taking nlace, the manufacturers Of Widnes will stop their establishments, their losses on the last occasion, when they continued work- ing, having been so great. In November, I hear, the musical quidnuncs ot Runcorn will have an opportunity of listening to a new and original oratorio. The choir of Bethesda Congregational Church, aided by members from the choirs of other churches, are rehearsing Farmer's oratoria " Christ and His soldiers,' which has not yet been performed in this district, although' I believe, it was given in Liverpool about two years ago, The magnificent music gives expression to a story of thril. ling interest, and with a full orchestral b in I and a chorus of 50 voices, a treat may be expected. Mr. Win. Handley undertakes the duties of conductor.
*Egypt, under the prot2etion of the Bitish expeditionary

force, is now beginning to assume its normal condition prior to the rebellion. The last stronghold, Dainietta, sur- rendered to Sir Evelyn Wood at the close of last week; and its Governor, Abdelal, the last of the trio of mutinous racers who instigated the rebellion, is now our prisoner. The Khedive, who only a few weeks ago left his cipital a fugitive, has returned to Cairo amid minifeetations of delight on every hand. Here and there may he found isolated instances where his Highness's authority is dis- puted, but as a rule there is obedience to his commands, and I think that in the course of a very short time his reign will again be firmly established under, I hope, the sole tutelage of England. The next impottant move will be to try the rebel pris mers, and for that pur- pose a Commission is in course of formation. Opinion is, of course, divided as to what shill be done with them, but whatever punishment is meted out it ought to be such as will have a (lete,rrent effect upon other dissatisfied pashas. To Baker Pasha, better known here as ex-Colonel Valentine B tker, has been entrusted the reorganisation of the Egyptian army. This course Is said to have the s traction of the Eaglieh Government, but whether that be so or not, the ex-colonel's dislin4uished services are a sufficient guarantee that the work devolving upon him will be efficiently performed. The Sultan is show- ing signs of impatience, and new that the rebellion has been quelled he is anxiout to know when the British troops are to leave; but just as the expeditionary force was sent to Ei4ypt without the consent of the Sultan, so will it remain until the Government chooses to withdraw it. Sir Garnet Wolseley and Sir G. Malet concur in the opinion that 10,000 men will suffice to maintain order for the present ; as to what may become of the remainder nothing seems as yet definitely decided. Nor is it known wip.t is to be the future policy adopted towards Egypt itself, but it is an- nounced from Berlin that a communication from the British Government is expected by the Powers within the next few days, soliciting an expression of their views upon the state of affairs in Egypt. Meanwhile we must await patiently the development of events. -

TETE LATE REV. W. C. COTTON.

Sir,—lt is now upwards of three years since the death of the late Rev. W. C. Cotton, who for 22 years had resided amongst us, and was esteemed by all as the Vicar of Frod- siza ; but so [ix no organised movement has been com- menced to perpetuate the memory of one who was so highly reenected and who did so much for the benefit of the parish. I tel sure that the inhabitants generally, whether belong- ing to Church or Dissent, would feel a melancholy pleasure in contributing, to a fund for a memorial which would re- mind as of our late vicar's sojourn with us; and as itimust be acknowledged that he commenced the movement for the restoration of the church by obtainin:;. plans for the same at his own expense it would be a graceful act on the part of the Restoration C mmittee i, now that the work of restora- tion is drawing to a succ!ssful issue, they would give their support to the movement advocated in this letter. The Rev. Canon Barclay., is a sermon which he preached refer- ring to the late Mr. Cotton, said—" The place which he so faithfully and affectionately occupied would know him no more. The surplice vies exchanged for the shroud, the pul- pit for the vault, and the only sermon he could preach was the epitaph upon his tombstone." As the body of our late respected vicar rests in the family vault at Leytonstone we are denied the privilege of having his grave in our parish churchyard, and I trust that a memorial to his memory may at once receive the earnest and serious consideration of the parishioners and publis generally. "IN MEMORIAM." Frodsham, 28th September, 1882.
ENGLAND AND EGYPT.-IL

Sir,—One, and a far from unimportant phase of the Egyp- tian question, has changed complexion since my last letter. We have thrashed Arabi Pasha. It was "a consummation devoutly to be desired" a few weeks ago, from the stand- point of those who had the gifted eyesight of the Man- chester Guardian. Such people saw in Arabi Pasha a 'sself- seeking scoundrel," who bad accomplished a menacing feat, and who must be crushed if that Peat was to be disarmed of its imposing influence over a country whose affairs Yee con- sidered it our:duty to control, and appropriate for European, not native purposes. Did it strike them that it requires something more fascinating than an incarnation of selfish- ness after the Arabi Pasha type to effect a revolution such as we have just witnessed in Egypt? I cannot believe it possible for one man to execute the brilliant manceuvre of Arabi Pasha without a strong under-current of popular sym- pathy lending its aid to the work. It is impossible for one mar, however subtle and clever he may be, to manipulate an army to the extent referred to without public assent. In other words, Arabi undertook to perform a task which the Egyptian people applauded; and although Arabi's part in that task is now nil, that which inspired him, namely, the desire cf Egypt to be delivered from the slavery of a foreign monopoly, survives the "shock of arms," survives the defeat of her army, survives the inglorious SUCCESS of • British generalship, and will likewise survive the mock-righteous rigour by which Sir Garnet and his helmeted cenfederates intend to restore Egypt to order and prosperity. Even the Manchester Guardian recognizes this fact. At least it gave the prominence of a leading article to the views of a special correspondent, who telegraphed from Cairo as follows :—"Since our arrival I have conversed with many of the better-educated Egyptians, and it is useless to dis- guise the fact that all their sympathies are with the idea for which Arabi has become a prisoner, and a better apprecia- tion of the forces opposed to him alone prevented them mak- ing common cause." The Guardian then adds, "There was and is such a thing as a national party in Egypt," complet- ing the sentence with a statement as specious in inference as it is undeniably true in one sense, to wit, " Tbat the fact (of the national party's existence) is not affected by the complete overthrow of the adventurer who caricatured and misrepresented it." This is the Guardian's --excuse for our dubious position in Egypt. It knows very well that we have not simply attacked and assaulted an "adventurer," styled such for attempting to carry his patriotism over a gulph which his party were not strong enough to bridge, but that we have drawn the sword upon the hopes of thousands who would rejoice over a home government in which the foreign and alien element was a minority as much as eldo ovei our own "temple of liberty." This is the damning feature of the campaign. There is an old proverb that when your case is bad abuse, your plaintiff's attorney, and this is the glaring inconsistency of our Egyptian policy. Arabi, net the section of society he leads, is the offender. He is an adventurer! Hew easy it Seems to find a snaps goat for an offence not unlike that of maiming the wings of a bird so that in may be unable to get beyond the reach of the poacher! Arabi is a villain—so we say, who look at him as &formidable menace to British interests in Egypt. What about those whose lives were absorbed in a question before whose vitality and sacredness. "British interests,' pale into insignificance, who, whether Arabi be sincere or not, were ready to die for the "idea " he symbolised? If he were not a Cromwell, or a G arib thli, they at least were patriots, cherishing that affection for their country which we pronounce a virtue in ourselves. It is against them we , have rushed, in the name of Eritith interests, and realising the infamy -attaching to the procedure, we exeu,e our- selves on the score that Arabi Pacha is a " self-seeking' scoundrel." As though the National Party could not have dealt with him the moment he provei the traitor or caricaturist, the Manchester Guar liarn so glibly styles him ! But we English people do so delight in meddling with other people's businese. How we in maga it, is a secret 6f diplomacy. We do manage it, and leave it with time for disposal among other curious legacies of ,hitory. We are not ungrateful. We have received from our forefathers many specimens of diplomatic intricacies that entitle,if they do not always em- power, us with "a voice" in the universal Parliament. We show our gratitude by contributing liberally to this museum of national devices. The gift will be enhanced in all its diplomatic relationships ere it reaches the hands of the next generation, and when we are dead our sons will rise up and -perhaps deem us the "perfidious Albion" onr meet recent exploit in diplomacy convicts us of being. We are in Egypt, it is certain. The why and wherefore are political mysteries which Sir Wilfred Lawson is not the only men to ascribe to selfish motives. It may be that we cannot bear to see our Egyptian bendholders sacrifice one iota of their interest in Zgyptian finances. Having invested, it seems the Govern- ment's pleasure that their investments shall be immured from the risk connected with the ordinary transactions of commercial life. It must be nice to be a bondholder. Think of the tenderness with which you are regarded as such, when even the naval and military forces of your country are at your command, free of expense, to protect your investment. rou shall have your pound of flesh, my friend; it is gueran- -by Government.; And after all this is enother anomaly to the many which make eccentric in our modes of Government. ay be the plea for our equivocal doings in thrashed Arabi Pacha. He is brushed like -e, and this is a fait accompli over which pious hilarity. We have chalked it so that all the world may read and " What a trophy ! Clergymen ' admirers of red coat theology "olseley and Sir Beauchamp ^ it, and the British tax- he pays for it. The -cover e is not

swallow the physic. We have got Arabi, and we want to know what we shall do with him, anyway. Will he—like the Suez Canal shares—prove a fair Government invest- ment? Has he such a thing as five per cent, interest about him? Has he sufficient to pay for Sir G. W.'s first banquet "in town?" Would he pass as a revivified Egyptian mummy? By the way, is there a spare tank in the West- minster Aquarium? And if so, would it pay us to put him in it, labelled " The only living specimen I of that recently discovered reptile, the Egyptian Napoleon, supposed to be a lineal descendant from, the only serpent that had the temerity to look Moses in the face when Aaron's rod became a counterfeit ?" Or, is there a site on the Thames embankment, say by Cleopatra's needle, saitable for a cage in which the thing could be placed? A cage with a big window, barred and locked, and a label : "Dangerous, from the east ; our latest catch." Or why not get up a caravan. Now here is the very plan. Carried about the country, "On view, one penny admission," the thing would "draw." If the ex-King of the Zulus had been regaled in this fashion, we should in a very briel space have raised enough to pay for the Zulu campaign. Let the Government do this with Arabi. It would "go down" with the public ; and it would be such a relief to the British tax- payer to know that he would have a providential escape from the " little bill." Failing these, Mr. Gladstone might take him in hand. Why not matte him a junior lord, or a private 'I ecretary, or, better still, a confidential servant? In the latter capacity we might glean how muck the Sultan of Turkey had to do with the rebellion of Egyptian fellaheen, which would, as a State secret, be worth the millions we are pitching into the Egyptian sink.—Yours truly, BENJN. SAWDON. Warrington, September 28th, 1882.

THE COLLAPSE OF THE ORCHESTRAL SOCIETY. Sir,—When reading the report of the Musical Society's meeting, held last Tuesday evening, I noticed that reference was made several times to the Orchestral Society—a few remarks in particular from Mr. Monks with reference to the winding in of the above society, appearing to show such misconception that I feel bound to endeavour ta make the actual facts more clearly understood. I much regret that an engagement prevented my being present at the meeting, as I could have entered more fully into particulars verbally than is possible in writing; but as it is I shall be greatly obliged if you will kindly insert the few remarks I have to make in your Saturday's issue. Mr. Monks seemed to infer that there was no necessity for winding up the Orchestral Society, and that all was not quite straightforward. In order to show that this was not so, I will give a short sketch of the operation of the society. The Orchestral Society was formed in 1817, with the object of supplying a band to the Musical Society, and developing a taste for instrumental music in the town. It started under favourable circum- stances, and with a small but hard-working band which gradually increased. In the following season it numbered 19 members, and there was an average attendance of 15 per practice. For the next tivo seasons the band remained tolerably efficient., and gave concerts which were, to say the least, highly creditable to the society. From this time, however, the band began to fall off, having lost the services of several of its best members; at the same time the attendance at re- hearsals became irregular, the average falling to ten, and to- wards the close of the seasoa it became ahnost nil. At the two last practices held the attendance was nil with the ex- ception of myself and brothers, and Mr. Pearson, who of all, least needed to come. the financial position of the society was not good, but there was nothing in it to cause the so- ciety to be wound up, for it had some good friends, and owing to the excellence of the concerts given, the committee had every reason to hope for an increased subscription list. It will be seen from the facts brought forwatd, that the failure of the society was brought about by the great lack of interest in it by the members and Warrington instrumen- talists generally : and this is proved by the fact that, besides the committee, Mr. Charles White and Mr. Monks, there were only two members present at the meeting called to consider the advis- ability of winding up the society. After the eomplete failure of the two last practices, I consulted the president of the society, James Marson, Esq., and then called the com- mittee together to consider what course should be taken under the circumstances. After careful con3ideration, a conclusion was come to that, there being no prospect of keeping the band together, there was no other alternative than that of winding up the society. Without an efficient amateur band it would have been absolutely necessary to hire a professional band to carry on the society, wkich could not have been done without reconstituting the society, and to do this would have been acting in direct antagonism to the Musical Society. In conclusion, I wish to say that my sole object in writing this letter is that the causes which led to the failure of the Orchestral Society should he thoroughly understood. I have certainly no wish to throw down the gauntlet to anyone. I am personally acquainted with Mr. Monks, and gladly take this opportunity of acknowledging the warm and practical interest he took in the Orchestral Society when it existed. Trusting that I have not trespassed too much on your valu- able spac3.—l remain, &c, JOHN P. REYNOLDS, Late Honorary Secretary of the Warrington Orchestral Society.

------ - PS: I should just like to mention one other fact, which powerfully corroborates my statement, as to the great lack of interest sl;ewn in the Society by Warrington instrumen- talist, and that is, that from the first more than one-third of the band was composed of gentlemen residing out of,War- rington, some at a considerable distance; had it not been so the Society could not have existed so long as it did.
Woodbine-terrace, Latehford,Warrington, September 22nd, 1882.

ALLEGED THEvr OF A PURSE.—At the Wigan County Police Court, on Monday last, before R. A. Ffarington. Esq., Jane Foster, wife of a collier, residing at Ashton, was charged with stealing a purse containing the sum of 103. She was remanded. SUDDEN DRATH.—Jphn Roby, an infant, son of James Roby, A collier, residing at 29 Rose Hill, died very suddenly on Saturday morning last. The child had not been very well since birth, and commenced to vomit about three o'clock on the morning named. The mother attended to her son, but the child died in her arms a few minutes later. An inquest on the body was held before Mr. C. E. Driffield, coroner, avt etrhdeictßorifta4 eiaathlnfnro, from n convulsions." novnudlazo,nasn,d, the jury re- FUNERAL OF A NONCONFORMIST AT ST. MMUS'S CHURCH YARD.—On Monday afternoon last, the remains of Mr. Robert Dixon, 20 years of age, formerly residing in War- rington-road, and a member of the congregation connected with the Congregational chapel, who died recently, were interred in the church yard of St. Thomas's parish. Several of the leading members of the congregation were present, and the funeral service was conducted by the Rev. H. Wil- sor, Congregational minister. TEACHERS TEA MENTING.—The first of a series of quir- telly tea meetings for the teachers was held in Eke Church Association rooms, Heath-road, on Saturday afternoon last. About 40 of the teachers connected therewith, with a few friends, sat down to an excellent tee, which was served in the bottom schoolroom, After which the company adjourned to the large room above, where a most interesting address was given by Mr. Barlow, of Wigan. A number of magic lantern views were exhibited by Mr. T. Rigby, one of the teachers, and the meeting throughout was a most successful , and enjoyable one, the proceedings terminating about ton o'clock. . _ .

FATAL COLLIERY ACCIDENT AT ASIITON.—An inquest was held at the Oddfellows' Arms, Ashton, on Friday last, before Mr. Barker, deputy coroner, on the body of Henry Atherton, 26 years of age, a collier residing in Long-lane, Ashton, who met with his death under the following circumstances: —About six o'clock on the morning of Tuesday, the 19:h inst., deceased went to his work in the four-foot mine of the Garswood Hall Collieries, belonging to Messrs. Smethurst, Hoyle, and Grime, and was proceeding along the drawing road, when a large stone fell from the roof and caught him on the left 'side. He was very badly crushed, and was removed to his home. Dr. Roscroft, of Wigan' attended him up to his death, which took place about 6 30 on the morning of the following day. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." ALTR(NCEIAM.

THE ALTAINCHAII JUSTI-CHS-AND OFF LICHNSES.—The Altrincham justices, at the adjourned licensing sessions on Monday morning, decided not to avail themselves of the discretion which might be afforded them under the new Act as to the renewal of off licenses, until the superior courts bad decided the point. A large number of off lic,.ensns had been objected to by the police, but the bench resolved only to hear such as referred to the personal character of he ap- plicants or the rateable value of the premises. LIR RATING OF GREI3IIIIOIISPIS —An important question as to the liability of greenhouses to be rated was brought before the Altrincham Board of Guardians on Wednesday morning. The case had arisen before the Assessment Com- mittee in which a person whose land was rated erected a greenhouse in which he grew cucumbers for sale. He objected to the greenhouse being rated, and the question consequently came before the magistrates, who affirmed the principle of rating such structures, where used beneficially. CLOSING A. LODGING-HOLISM—At Altrincbam Police Court on Wednesday, David Hefferan was committed to gaol for two months in default of paying a fine of 40s and costs, for taking lodgers in a house in Beggars Square, Altrincham, the licence of the same having been withdrawn by the authorities, Recently a man, whilst drunk in his house, fell down stairs and was killed, the coroner at the inquest severely commenting on the fact, and urging that the house should be clos6d. _ _

It is announced that the Queen has been graciously pleast.d to approve of the honour of knighthood being con- ferred on Mr. Joseph C. Lee, of Altrincham, in consideration of his valuable services in the commercial negotiations with France.

AGRICULTURAL SHOW.—The annual show of horses, sheep, pigs, poultry, dogs, machinery, implements, Arc., opened on Thursday morning, at Bowdon. The weather was fine. There was a considerable increase in the number of entries as compared with former years, on this occasion there being nearly two thousand. The show of horses and cattle was a particularly good one, the receipt for entrance fees being nearly £lOO in excess of last year. The large show of cattle is due to the freedom of the county from disease and the consequent absence of all restrictions. The first prize for a bull any age has been awarded to George Cooke. The first prize for a bull under two years to H. H. Grierson, of Warburton, and the second to J. A. Railton, Whalley R Inge ; the first prize for a pair of dairy cows to C. W. Brierley, 'tenbury : for a pair of draught horses to James Cronshaw, Gatley ; a single draught horse, first prize to C. W. Brierley, Tenbury, and the second to James Cronshaw, Gatley.

was taken on a quarterly tenancy originally. But two years ago defendant was required to pay his rent weekly. Defendant relied on the original terms of the tenancy, but the Bench ordered his ejectment. The wife gave notice of appeal. MURDFIROUS ASSAULT ON A CEIESITTRII HOTSL-KEEPER.— Richard Slater and James Greig, of Manchester,were charged at the Knutsford Sasions on Tuesday with assaulting William Power, landlord of the Kilton Inn, Hoo Green ; and Mr. Rushton was charged with assaulting the ostler at the hotel. The defendants, who pot up their horses and traps at the above hotel On the 10th inst., refused to pay the ostler's charges, and upon the landiord coming out to see the c tuse of the disturbance he was beaten about the head with a whipstock by Slater in a most brutal manner. He fainted from the loss of blood, and WO carried insensible into the hotel. The other defendants struck the ostler. The whip by which the blows were struck had a handle a yard long, and at the end there was a large brass ferrule. Stater was tincd £5, including costs; the other defendants 10s. and costs. LY XI NI.

HARVEST' FESTIVAL AT LYMNI.—LytTIM Church was OTV Sunday tastefully decorated in celebration of the harvest which has just been athered in, and the thy was also set apart for thanksgiving for the victories which our army and navy have achieved during the Egyptian campaign. This was the first occasion on which thanks were publicly offered in the church for thq harvest, and large congrega- tions attended all the services. In the morning, the Very Rev, the Dean of York preached from the 116th NAIIII, and in the course of his sermon referred to our victories in Egypt. He showed how the English people had been corn- parattvely free from the devastations of war for many cen- turies, and knew nothing of the calamities that had lately taken place in Egypt. Englishmen as a nation, as well as individually, ought to be grateful to God for the peaceful times which we haa, and now were enjoying, and for the success that had attended our army both in Egypt and in other parts of the world. This fact, coupled with the pros- perous harvest, w.is a c tuse for quiet rejoicing, and taught them that periods of adversity and prosperity ought to bring them nearer to God, and that while they quietly bore their losses in times of darkness, faithfully trusting in Provi- dence. they should not forget the Giver of all good in periods of pler.ty. The rev. Dean gave an address at the. children's service in the afternoon; and in the evening the rev, gentleman preached from the 19th chapter of St. Matthew, 22nd verse, "For he ban great possessions." The organist (Mr. G. F. E. Reynolds) performed voluntaries both morning and evening in splendid style, and the singing was exceptionally good. In the evening an anthem, "Fear not, 0 Land," was sung, and three solos by Mr. Charlesworth. In the mornitig the National Anthem was played before ser- vice. Collections were made to defray the expenses incurred
n the rebuilding of one of the pimcles and other repairs 111 the tower.

A LYIOI ASSBSSMENT APPEAL CASE.—At the Altrincham Petty Sessions. on Monday, before Messrs. H. H. Joynson and A. W. Mills, Joseph Lawrenson appealed against an assessment made by the Guardians of the Altrinchatn Union.—Mr. Husband, of St. Helens, appeared for the ap- pellant; and Mr. Cave for the Guardians.—Mr. Husband said sometime ago, his client, who was a horticulturist at Lymm, bought a field or two. Previous to that, it was rated at alx)nt £ll. His client built a house and some outbuild- ings and a greenhouse, and he was in respect of that assessed at £23 gross annual rental. Tile next assessment was £43 mentioned in the appeal, rateable value being .£39 2s. 61. He was instructed to say that the only improvement to the premises between the rating of £23 and the assessment of £43, was a small addition to a greenhouse of 25 yards, so that if he could prove this he should then ask them to re- duce the assessment. • He did not ask their Worships to quash the rate, as they had undoubtedly power to do, but all they asked that it should be reduced. He thought it was an unfair valuation, but that was for their Worships consideration.—After hearing the evidence on both sides, the magistrates reduced the assessment to £3B.

skilfully played. Readings by Rev. S. W. Nenis, Mr. J. Waring. Mr. Daggatt ; recitation by Mr. W. Shaw, and a stump oration by Mr. Bigwood completed the programme; and were evidently enjoyed by the large audience. W fIISTON.

MUSICAL EN'TERTAINMENT AT WHISTONT. On Friday evening last a well attended musical entertainment was given in the National schoolroom, Whiston, in rid of the Whiston Wesleyan Sunday School. Farmer's oratorioi "Christ and His Soldiers," was the music submitted, in the rendition of which the principal vocalists were Miss Parry, Miss Pickavance, Miss Hewitt, and Messrs. George Barton, Elliott, Brearley, Povey, and Councillor Belsher, who were supported by the choir of the Cottam-street, St. Helens, Wesleyan Chapel, under the conductorship of Mr. Rhodes.• The instrumentalists were the Atherton brothers, assisted by Mr. W. Rhodes at the piano. The opening chorus, "Suffer little children," was excellently rendered by the fall choir, which at the very outset gave evidence of a judicious arrangement of voices, and a careful preparatory training. The succeeding solo, "Hark the glad sound," was given by - Mr. Barton in his usual masterly style and evoked the warm C applause of the audience. The carol, "In the field with their flocks," was a beautifully suggestive performance by the choir, and the chorus, "0, come, all ye faithful," was also given with considerable effect. The next solo, "And did the Son of God appear," was by Mr. Povev, after which the choir gave the chorus, " Ride on ! Ride on in Majesty," with a force and effect which won a hearty round of applause. The solos "When I survey the wondrous cross " and "By Jesus' grave," were rendered respectively by Mr. Barton and Miss Parry, both of whom received their accustomed meed—a hearty ovation. Miss Pickavance, was also deservedly well received in the solo and chorus " Jesus Christ is risen to- day "—in the chorus of which she was worthily sustained by the choir—and in the solo "far blest Redeemer." In the second part, the solo "The son of God goes forth to war" by Mr. Barton, was received with marked apprecia- tion; and the "Rock of Ages" seemed to be exactly suited to tring out Miss Parry's admirable powers, and was indeed a splendid performance en her part. In response to a well deserved encore, Miss Parry repeated a portion of the hymn with equal 'effect. Other solos were sung by Miss Pickavance, Mr. Brearlev, and Councillor Belsher, all of which were well received. The qaartett, "Jesus died for us" was sung by MNI Pickayance, Miss Hewitt, Mr. .Elliott and Mr. Brearlev, after which the entertainment was brought to a close by the chorale "Lo, round the throne of God." The vocalists, almost all of whom belonged to St. Helens, were, after hav- ing been entertained to supper at Whiston, conveyed to Prescot in carriages, whence they reached St. Helens by special train. Cuaseitai FAltm.En3 IND THE Huerr.—At the Broxton Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, a farmer, named Samuel Rowe, of Hatton Heath, was charged with allowing his horses to stray on the highway. In the course of the case the defen- d int complain id of the. way in which his fences were trampled down from time to time by the members of the Cheshire Hunt. The chairmen, Mr. Leche, addressing the defendant, said he surely would not like to do away with fox-hunting, as they were doing in Ireland. Mr. J. R. Dalton, president, occupied the chair; and there was a large attendance. The members of the club were generally agreed in supporting the resolution, which provided that compensation should he made to outgoing tenants for improvements effeeted by them on their land during the term of their tenancy; but an objection was made by Mr. Poimore, of Seeland, a to the cleeee of the resolution which provided that sun compensation should be measured by the increased agricultural value of the hold- ing, Mr. Podmore pointing out that in case a farm had been taken at an excessive rent some years ago, and relinquished during bad times when rents were low the tenant might be called upon to make up the, difference in the rent. Mr. Rigby, of the Cheshire Cumber of Agriculegre, pointed out, in reply, that the latter purl ofeethe__ reenTettee ewe tiled further tb.t eeespeneeafon was to depend upon the actual money outlay made by the tenant Or the general cleanliness of a farm due to the tenant's expenditure and skill. This no doubt would be taken into ceitsideretion in any case of arbitration which might arise. Mr. Podinore then withdrew fihe amendment he had proposed, and the resolution was carried unanimously in pieference to a resolution on the same subject which was formerly carried by thebclub, and which was simply in general terms. 'file club wis uneni- mouely in favour of the second resolution, which was to the effect that notice to quit in agricultural holdings be extended te 12 months. With reference to the next resolu- tion, which was to give power to a county court judge to settle disputes betweeu landlords ant tenants, with the assistance of competent assessors, there was scene little difforeace of opinion, but, ultimately, this clause was ales carried unanintiu-ey.
