The club we/ de- clined blenders() the resolution of the Chamber of Agricul- ture advocating its entire abolition, and carried a resolution in favout of the power of 'distraint being restricted to one year's rent instead of six, as at presene Adiscussion ensued as to whether a "deputation should, be sent to the Premier to enforce these points ee arron e 1 at the last MetiLlP.:, and, ultimately, it was decided not to appoint a deputation at present.

THE EGYPTIAN WAR, THANKSGIVING SERVICE AT WIDNES AND RUNCORN. As in most churches of the Establiihment on Sunday last, a special thanksgiving service for the British Victory,' in Egypt, was held in Runcorn Parish Church on Sunday morning. Hymns and psal.ms suitable for the occasion were sung, and a special prayer was offered. The Rev. I'. M. Arinson preached. The National Anthem was played on the organ as the congregation left the church. In the evening a similar service wasiconducted by the Rev. J. J. Bryant, who preached.

- , At St. Paul's WeSleyan Chapel, Runcorn, on Sunday morning, the Rev. George Hack conducted a special thanks- givingservice for the victory of th British Arms in Egypt. In the course of his remarks, the rev. gentleman said there wee times when peace Was worse than war, and when the sufferings and death engendered by war were Jess than would have been if war had not been waged. War, therefore, under such circumstances became a righteous thing. They believed this had been the case in Egypt. They waged war. not for the purpos6 of nationsl annexation or agrandisement, but for • the protection of British life and property, to deliver Egypt from the curse of a military adventurer and despotism, and that she migift not be hindered in the development of her civilisation. They had much to be thankful for. However much they might admire the bravery of their army and nivy, and the military genius of their general, their first acknowledgments must be to God. Without him, and all arrangements en tke laittlefield, and all diplomatic action would have resulted in disaster. They might have been troubled by the unutterable Turk, hampered by the jealousy of European nations,- while a great uprising of Mahantmedan fanaticism might have seriously endangered their action and prolonged the cam- paign. Instead of this the campaign had been admirably conceived, and a remarkable victory had been achieved with very little loss of life. The God of battles, the God of Gideon, of Daniel, of Hezekiale, the God who was with Plagland on the field of Waterloo, had again been with them. They boned that as great SUCC,SS would attend them in dipiornaeie matters as in the war, and that out of the strife might come to pass peace and prosperity to the Egyptian people. During the service a special hymn was sung by ; the choir, and a prayer of thanksgiving offered by the minister.

The Rev. J. Wright-Williams, vkar, fireadhed i anion on the war at Widnes Parish Church on Stinday eVening. He said to all men the events of the last few m'ntlid had been full of interest, but particularly to Bible readersi and still more particularly to Christians. The lands through which they had travelled in the Bible class had again become prominent before them, and those fields which had been reidenecl by the Pharaohs, the Ptolemies, the Mussehnen,and Napoleon had been invaded by our own army. Leaving out of question the po itical side, for which the pulpit was no place, we ,Inust all feel t. deep!y interested in these events. Looking npon the human side they had to be thankf,Al God, whom it had pleased to prosper the action of our army. Success bad attended our arms—though there had been the usual failure in the commissariat department, for, thank 1 G‘od, we were yet a peace-loving people, and not so accus- tomed to the ways of war. They had to be thankful to God that the war they had entered upon had been, so far, short, sharp, and decisive. The council of our generals had ap- parently been crowned with complete success; perhaps the failure of the joint control had delivered England from one of the statesmen's difficulties. It must now be their prayer that tl,e negotiations of statesmen might be as successful as the army had proved victorious, and that peace, true and substantial, might 'be restored to that unhappy country— Egypt.

The F and G Companies of the 2nd C.R.V., under the 1 command of Captain Hazlehurst, attended divine service at Holy Trinity Church, Runcorn, on Sunday morning. The Rev. William Preston, M.A.„ who occupied the pulpit, preached from the text "Thy servant will go and fight with this Philistine." After defending the profession of arms, for which, he said, he was originally intended, the rev, gentleman said to the Lord of Hosts, we must look for success, and to Him are we indebted—and well might they give Him their thanks as they had done- that day—for the signal success which had attended our campaign in Egypt, one of the shortest and most glorious on record, add- ing another triumph to the brilliant roll of British victorie!. In 25 days our army had disembarked, traversed the desert, stormed a most heavily entrenched position at the point of the bayonet, captured 60 guns, and occupied the fortified capital of Egypt with a loss, though sad, yet numerically very small. Small compared with the 40,000 brave fellows England lost in the Crimea, and well mi4ht our gallant General exclaim in the language of Caessr, " Veni, vkli, vici," (I came, I saw, I conquered.)

At the Ellisbnry Petty Sessions. on Monday, Miss Mar- garet Harrison, of Frodsham, applied for a new license to sell wines at a new refreshment house near the Frodsharn station. The formalities having been complied with the application was granted. NEw-rox HALL ESTATE.—This valuable freehold estate was offered by public auction at the Town Hall, Froisham, on Tuesday, by Mr. J. J. Steward, on behalf of the executors of the late Major Hitchen. The estate was first put up in one lot, but no bid was made, and on the estate being eff,-;red in six lots the reserve was not reached in any case. and they were consequently withdrawn. ACCIDENT AT MR. HADFIELD'S Wouirs.—An accident occurred at Mr. Hadfield's Charcoal Works, Weston, on Sunday, a youtil man named Thomas Mullock, beintz severely burnt owing to the explosion of an accumulation of gas. The patient is under medical care, and progressing towards recovery. CO3UNG LECTURE BY TUE REV. PETER MACKEN'Z[E.— We have pleasure in referring our readers to the announce- ment of the visit of the R2V. div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

INDEPENDENT METHODIST CHATEIL.—The anniversary services in connection with the Independent Methodist Chapel were preached on Sunday afternoon and evening last by Mr. William Wright, of Warrington. There was a good attendance at each service, and the collections were in aid of the trust fund, the sum of £2. Ils. 101 being realised.

TUB BLUR RIBBON MOTEMENT.—An unusual commotion has been occasioned at Go!borne in connection with the Blue Ribbon Army and Gospel Temperance Movement. which was inaugurated in Golborno last Monday weak, and the Congregational schoolroom, in which a meeting was held each evening during the week, was crowded on each occa- sion to its utmost limits. On Saturday afternoon last a public tea party and concert were held in the same building, about 250 persons partaking .of an excelle t tea. At the suLsequent proceedings the att,mdance was over 400, and the chair was occupied by Mr. R. Yates, of Gal- borne, who was supported by Messrs. T. Rosbottom (the originator of the movement in this district), Clayton (of Ince), and Meadows (of Pemberton)._ In addition to appro- priate and interesting addresses by the gentlemen named, an excellent programme of songs, recitations, &c., was gone through, the meeting being a most pleasant an enjoyable one. The Edge Green Brass Band gave several selections, which were very much appreciated. Owing to the success attending the first week's mission, the meetings have been continued during the present week, and there has again been the same crowded attendanges. Up to the present over 600 pledge cards have been purchased, and certainly it would seem as if some good was being done.

EIUYTON. Tux Po-r OFFICE) ROBBRIZY AT Ilurrox.—ln regard to the assault on the postmaster of Iluyton about mid-day on the 21st inst., and the robbery from the post-office of a con- siderable sum of money, la9r Majesty's Postmaster-General has offered a reward of £5O to whoever will give such inform Ition as will lead to the apprehension and conviction of the offender. The reward is payable on a conviction being obtained.

Greifying presents have been made to Miss Rvcroft and Miss Florence .1. Ryeroft, daughters of Canon Rycroft, of Christ Church, Kensington, on the occasion of the marriage of the former to Mr. W. Ff. HAYDOCK. Tim LATE WAR IN EGYPT.—Special thanksglving ger- vices for the speedy and successful termination of the late war in Egypt were held in St. James's Church, liaydock, on Sunday last, The preacher in the morning was the Rev. El. Mason, curate, and in the afternoon, the Rev. IL Sher- lock, M.A., vicar. The latter :ev. gentleman preached an eloquent and interesting sermon with reference to the con- flict, and it was listened to with the greatest of attention throughout. The psalms and prayers were specially selected and the services altogether were fully of a thanksgiving character.

RWIISION OF TFITI VOTEIRS LISTS.-011 Tuesday Mr.-W. L. Foulkes revised the list of voters for Middlewich and the surrounding townships.—Mr. A. E. Paterson, of Altrincham, and Mr. J. H. Cooke, Middlewich, appeared on behalf of the Liberals; and Mr. Lance Bentley, of Knutsford, represented the Conservatives. The Liberals objected to the new claim of Samuel Tippin, of Byley, which the overseers of that parish had inserted in the £l2 list after it had been duly published. The overseer explained that the claim had been made in proper time, but admitted that he misunderstood the instructions on the list, and did .not include it with the others until August. Mr. Foulkes said the claim was valid for another year, but struck the name of the claimant off the list.—Henry Crutchley, overseer of Minshull Vernon, did not put in an appearance, and Mr. Foulkes entered a fine of 30s against him.—The party claims and objections sustained were about equal in number.

div.head: NORTHIVICII.
div.p: NORTHIVICII.

Complaint has keen made to the Northwich Rural Sanitary Authority respecting the large quantities of smoke and the obnoxious vapours that are allowed to proceed from the various works in the neighbourhood. As the manufacturers are known to possess the best smoke consuming appliances, enquiries are being in udt. as to the quantity of coal consumed, the smoke in some instanc's indicating the consumption of unnecessarily large quantities.

div.p: NANT WIC EL

DAULGING TELEGIINPII WIRE. On Tuesday, at the Nantwich Sessions, James Corry, William Wrench, and Ed- ward Corry, boys, were charged with da,waging telegraph wires along the canal bank at Acton. A constable stated that as he was watching the wires on Sunday, the 3rd inst., he saw the defendants and some other boys throw a num. ber of stones at theirs. More than twenty stones were thrown, seven of which hit the wires with great force. Mr. J. F. Stevens, from the engineering department of the Post-office Telegraph, said that a.great deal of damage bad been done in the neighbourhood of Nantwich in consequence of men and boys throwing at the telegraph wites. o.xasionally c im- munication had been stopped in conseqwence. The bench imposed a fine of 5s and costs (in alll2s fid) upon each of the defendants.

OVER. • ONION' Farrt.—This annual fair as been as largely attended as any Over fair for many years back. The amount of stock in sheep and cattle contrasts favourably with its predecessors, while for pigs and onions there was an abun- dance. The former sold at very fair Prices, and the latter at lower rates than usual. The attractions of such gatherings were in great force; swing-beats, riding horses worked by steam, sailing boats without any water, and shooting. gal- leries, Aunt Sally, and every facility for gaining a disordered stomach abounded on every side. But amid all the traffick- ing, noise', shouting and music, a new kind was heard this year, the like of which would have greatly astonished the previous generation; it was no other than Salvation hymns by the Army, with banners flying. RIFLE Cops.—The distribution of the prizes won by this corps in the previous week at the Winsford range, of which a full report appeared in a previous impression, took place in the Drill Shed, on Thursday night. In the absence of Captain Turner, the prizes were given away by Quarter- master-Sergeant Daggett, who, More becoming a regimental staff officer, was the lieutenant of this company. The baits of the men appeared in their regimentals, but through it not being well made known, vine had to appear in plainclothes. After the prize distribution, a vote of thanks was propused hy Corporal Oakes, and carried with acclamation. Mr. Da,gatt acknowledged the same, and proposed that the best thanks of the company be presented to the donors of the various prizes.

BAVR:•.THEAD PARISIT CHURCH HARVEST THANKSGIVING. —On Sunday and Monday last harvest thanksgiving services were held in the Ravenhead Parish Church. On Sunday mornizg the services were preached by the Rev. W. Chap- lin, and in the evening by the Rev. B. A. W. Not:rie, Huyton. On Monday evening the sermon was preached by the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, vicar of Huyton. On all occasions there were crowded attendances, and the collections, which were large, were in aid of the new school at Thatto Heath. The church was elaborately and tastefully decorated with nunwrous greenhouse plants, be- sides corn, grasses, and other autumn produce.

Mr. W. L. Foulkes attended the Town Hall, Sandbach, on Thursday, to revise the list of voters for Arend, Bradwall, Sandbach, and other places in the district. Mr. L. Bentley, of Knuteford, represented the Conservatives, and Mr. Pater- son, of Altrincnam, the Liberals. A number of new claims were allowed. With regard to Sandbach, the overseer had omitted to put on the list a number of new claims, and, when asked the reason, he replied that it was because he objected to them. The Barrister told him he ought to have put them upon the list and objected to them afterwards. The overseer for 'Tustinll Vernon was disallowed hia e-x- -enses for not having attended the Micldlewich court. SHOCKING ACCIDENT.—A shocking fatality occurred on Wednesday to James Ilarrup, aged 30, a married nun, of Sandbach. He had been to Crewe, and, as he was returning home, a young man named James Bullock, who was in charge of a gingerbeer cart, overtook him and gave him a ride. On the way to Sandbach they stopped at a beer- honee and bad some drink. Soon after they had resumed the journey the young man missed hie companion, and on.l going back he found him lying in the road quite dead, hä neck being broken. WINSFORD. FIRE AT STOKER-LA.:IE FAHM.—Early on Senday morn- ing the fire bell at Wiusford mug out the alarm of tire. It was found to be at Mr. Knowles farm, where a large hay- stack was in flames. After it was, as thought, put out, on Suriday night it re-commenced, and little of the stack re- mains of any value. It was worth several hundred pounds, but it is to be hoped it was insured. div.head: ASSAULT BY A SCHOOLMISTRESS
div.p: ASSAULT BY A SCHOOLMISTRESS
AT ST. HELENS. TOTE OF SYMPATHY WITH MISS WEST.

[The appended report should have appeared in last Satur- day's Examiner, but it was unfortunately delayed in transit from St. Helens to Warrington.] On Thursday evening week, a special general meeting of the St. Helens and District Teachers' Association was held in the Holy Trinity School, Peasley Cross, for the purpose of considering the instructions recently issued to inspectors for the working of the MandePa code ; and also for con- sidering the recent "charge of assault against a school- mistress," and expressing sympathy with Miss West. Mr. Brown, master of the Wesleyan schools, St. Helens, presided, and there was a large attendance of teachers of both sexes. The Rev. Mr. Flaherty was also present.—The CHAIRMAN, referring to the instructions to inspectors, said the document containing them had been received with far greater favour and less severe criticism that perhaps any other former docu- ments ever issued from the Education Department. (Hear, hear.) Very great relief would be given to the minds of teachers tofind that so much was to be done to make inspectors pursue their duties on a definite plan throughout every district in the land, so that one district should not have any undue advantage over another district, and thus providing that teachers throughout the length and breadth of the land should be equally dealt with. —Several other teachers also discussed the merits of the code, after which eorne diecuteeien tole place with respect; to the attendance at schools. Figures Were quoted to show that the number of attendance officers engaged at St. Helens was, in proportion to the population, greatly beneath the number engaged at other places, Brighton, Norwich, Ply- mouth, Liverpool, and other places being quoted. Ulti- mately the followinet'- motion wag moved by Mr. Mirror? (Cowley Hill Schools), viz :--e" That this meeting. having considered the remarks of school attendance made by W. Scott Coward, Esq., her Majesty's Inspector for this district, instructs the committee to memorialise the various bodies entrasted with enforcing attendance in this neighbourhood to adopt measures for securing an improved attend trice of children, and to suggest that in the ease ef St. Helens this cannot be done in St. Helens without employing a larger staff of school attendance officers." This motion was seconded by Mr. WALDEN (Haydock), supported by Mr. WARD (St. Thomas's Schools), and other teachers, and unaleimously carried.—The CHAIR/4E4N then said they had now come to the main reason for their being assembled there that night, namely, the recent charge of assault against Miss West. He might say that several individuals, who had happened to hear that they were going to hold that meeting, had asked him sundry and various questions as to whether they were going to "sit on the Bench," but he should like to say at the very outset that they had no desire to do anything of the kind. (Hear, hear.) He should like to say that in their schools they taught their children to honour &nd obey the Queen and all who were put in authority under her, and he felt very sure that no teacher there would say anything offensive of any of the gentlemen who sat on the Bench in connection with the recent charge of assault. He was quite sure that those gentlemen were men of uprightness, integrity, and honour, and men who would not do wrong if they could help it. If it was thought that they had made a blunder it was because they did not happen to know everything that the elementary teachers of St. Helens knew. He might say that he was sorry that the association had not had more timely notice of the trial, but for that they could not blame the holy, but rather the magistrates' clerk who made the summons returnable so soon after its issue. It was only issued on the Friday morning and was not delivered till six o'clock in the evening, and yet was made returnable on the Monday morning. He thought that in a case of this kind, in which the honour and character of a mistress were concerned more time ought to have been given to provide for a defence, so as to success- fully rebut the charges brought against her. This was the first opportunity which had arisen for the elementary teachers of St. Helens to stand shoulder to shoulder. They had too frequently been looked upon as so many separate units that could be easily crushed and, therefore, they had determined to do all they possibly could to help a colleague. In that particular matter they had determined to have a solicitor to watch the ease on behalf of the elementary teachers of the horough of St. Helens, and he believed that had already done gOoa, Their solicitor, after lieten- ing to the whole case, was of opinion that the magistrates were not of opinion that exceeeiva a—a-L.—ea heel t,en nki- iiiikosiereo; he was of opinion that the case had not been decided on the question before the court, but was decided on a side issue, that it was simply decided on un- supported testimony. .(Hear, hear.) Had the magistrates been of opinion that there had been a very severe flogging they would surely have imposed a larger flue than 2s fid, besides not allowing the costs of the other side. It appeared that the whole question depended on one point. One of the magistrates asked the boy if he was struck on the head with the cane before or after the struggle had taken place, and lie (the chairmanl_ believed, and Mr. Fla- herty would I, ar him out in saying that the boy in the first instance said "after," but as the Bench did not hear the answer the question was repeated, and the boy then said " before." (Mr. Flaherty ; That is right). That last answer was taken down, and he believed it was upon that that the whole case depended—had it not been for that the whole case would probably have been dismissed. He cer- tainly, himself, thought that the justice of the case would have been met by a dismissal with a caution. He con- sidered that a boy who had his "funny bouts," and was often run after by the attendance officer, and although only tapped on the head by his mother yet was flogged by his fa, her with a clothes line, was a very ditlicilt boy to deal with. It was perhaps fortunate for theboy that he only had a mistress to do with, or he would perhaps have been treated to some sterner diecipline. In connection with that blew on the head, it was rather strange that although the Rev. Mr. Flaherty was in the lad's house on the morning after the alleged assault, not a word was said about the lump on his head. Most likely the lump had been caused by the lad hims?lf while playing in the streets, and it had theii been placed to the credit of the mistress. The Chairman then referred to the numerous expressions of sympathy with Miss West which had been expressed on all sides, and read sympathetic notices of the case which had neared in The Examiner and another local paper.—The Mr. FLAHERTY then gave a short history of the case He sain'.th echairman had made a slight mistake as to where boy. He had not seen him in his own house at Ice saw the " all, but had 'en him at the schoolroom on the Tuesday On shearing that the case was coming eveninee naturally had a very great into court, he ,4- made public at all antipathy to its 4: gin whose hands it was, and and had gone to the solicitor, e it settled, and he, af,er desired him by all means to ha: oa We consulting his client, had a Miss st , paying one guinea as a solicitor's fee ne guinea, and . ' in- • eluding doctor's expenses, to the parents. Ori this to Miss West, however, she would not erm,sent to pay "hush money," as that would not only be an injrn: to her own school, ut to the schools generally in St. HefmN,', mini consequently the case had gone into the court. With rek-uu to the decision in the case it would not, he said, b-corne to say one•single word. In conclusion, he thanked them on behalf of Miss West for the generous support they had given her in bearing the exprise: of the trial.—The CHAIRMAN read a letter from Mr. N. Lacey expressing sympathy with the' object of the meeting, and encloeiag a subscription towards the defrayment of Mies West's expenses. lii his opinion the case ought to have been summarily dismissed, with a few words of caution from the Bench.—Mr. WARD then moved a resolution " That that meeting having care- fully considered the case against Miss West, in the light of evidence not adduced at the trial, begs to assure her of its unabated confidence in her as an elementary teacher, and also its deep sympathy with her in the recent prosecution.". —This resolution was seconded by Mr. GkREZIGILL, sop- ported by Mr. ASHTON, and carried unanimously.—Mr TAYLOR (Haydock) moved That that meeting sympa- thised with Miss West, and asked her to accept the whole of her costs in that case.—Mr. KENWRIGHT seconded this proposal, which wa9 cordially carried. The Rev. Mr. FLAHERTY returned thanks on behalf of Miss West, after which the meeting closed with the usual votes of thanks.

ROBBERY FROM A FORSDITION STONE.—An extraer• dinary robbery was committed at Oswaldtwistic, near Acciton, early on Tharglay morning. It was found that the corner-stone of St. Paul's new Church, Oswaldrwistle, which was laid last week., had been prlz•id off with a crow- bar, and the bottle containing money and newspapers taken from the cavity beneath. The stone, which weighed a ton, had been carefully replaced, but it was "chippf,d " where the crowbar .had been iced. No arrsts have been made, hut a reward has been Offered. The affair bad caused con- sideralt•le excitement in the neighbourhood. s

Gradually the neck connecting the extremities br comes thinner and thinner until the two ends become ocparate or- ga.nis,ns, and each commetaces on its own account the pro- cess already described. There is nothing in this process of evolution resembling the separation of a young animal or an egg from its parent, nor is there any similarity to the shed- ding of seed by a plant. The two new forms are precisely alike, are of the same age, and endowed. with precisely the same qualities, and their joint predecessor lives in them What infinitesmal portion each maybe of the original pro- tozoon human mathematics cannot calculate. LOTION AGAINST THE RUNCORN GLYCERINE WORKS,

IMPORTANT PROCEEDINGS. A Case which excited much interest in the town was beard at Rulearn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before the Se,. E. A. P. Campbell, (chairman), and Mr. W. Benkes. Mae court-n rn ways crowded. M. Victor Clolus was sum- moned by thr Beard of Commissioners to answer a charge that he did on the 20th July, and after the passing of the Public Health Act 1375, unlawfully establish within the district of the Runcorn Urban Sanitary Authority, certain noxious or offensive trade, that is to say, the trade of a glycerine manufacturer, without. the consent in writing of Bach 11iban Auteority." There was a second summons charging M. Clolus " that he did on the 20ch Jefly, and on divers other days, after the passing of the Public Health Act 1875, unlawfully carry on a certain noxious or offensive trade, that is to sees, the trade of a glycerine manufacturer, which said business had been and was established without the consent in writing of the. Runcorn Urban Sanitary Authority, and that he carried on such business as aforesaid for forty days."—Mr. W. H. Linaker, law clerk to the Corn- miesioners appeared to prosecute, and the defendant was represented by Mr. Fretcher, of Northwich. Mr. Linaker, in his opening statement, said in the summer of last year the defendant acquired the site of the present works on the Sprinch, and procesded to erect what were termed the " Gryceriee Works," which were works for the _refining and purifying of glycerine. Operations were com- menced about the michlle of October, and between that time and the end of the year, complaints were frequently made by the inhabitants of the neighbourhood, and in fact the town generally, of the offensive and noxious stenches which Caine from the works. Owners of property from time to time also wrote to the Commissioners that their tenants suffered from the vapours emanating from the works. At the beginning of the present year, after some representations had been made to the defendant, the latter made a formal and regular application to the Board for consent in writing to establish and carry on the works ler the purposes for which he had erected them. The Corn- miseioners having before them the complaints waich had been made, did not consent to the carryiug on of the trade by tla r defendant as he requested, but suggested that evidence should be forthcoming that the -works were properly con- structed, and that the processes could be carried on without Axis u• ee to the neighbourhood. Mr. Abbot, of St. Helen', was e 'lied in to report on behalf of the defendant. On the 3,4t11 January Mr. Abbot reported to t.he Board that the works were erected on the best known principles, and that the appliances were of the best and most approved class. The Highway and Sanitary Committee deferred the consideration of the report in consequence of the complaints referred to. On the Ist July the Medical Officer complained of the vapours which came from the defendant's works ; and on the 10th of the same month, the Commissioners communi- cated with the defendant and informed him of She complaints, and gave him notice to prevent the smells. On the 19th August, the Commissioners again communicated with the defendant, saying they had received a memorial, dated the 16th August, from the inhabitants of the neigh- bourhood, oomplaining of the noxious and unbearable smells proceeding from the works; and afterwards a resolution was pissed by the Commissioners that notice should be given the defendant that proceedings would be taken against him at the expiration of a month, if the nuisance was not abated. On the 14th September it was resolved that proceedings be taken against the. defendant for contravention of the 112 section of the Public Health Act. When the works were first established the Cornmiesioners thought they would be carried on without being a nuisance to the neighbourhood, and it was only when they Were satisfied upon the report of their medical officer and upon evidence which had been submitted to them that the works were a nuisance—evidence in fact, would be given by people who had been:compelled to give up their houses and leave the neighbourhood, because they could not live amid the stench from the works—that the proceedings were taken. -e—Mr. Fletcher at this point objected to the first summons charging the defendant with establishing the works con- trary to the provisions of section 112 of the Act, quoting the 252nd section to show that this could not be done after the expiration of six months.—Mr. Linaker : I anticipated this objection on the part of the defence, and I took out a Summons for continuing the trade at the same time.—Mr. Fletcher: I ought to have costs.—Mr. Linaker : You can have, if von can show costs.—Mr. Ashton (the magistrates' clerk) : there is no doubt that the 252nd section so reads . as to permit of Mr. Fletcher's ebjection beieg taken.—The Chairman: We have two summonses for establishing the works.—Mr. Linaker : We took one out - for continuing the works.—The Chairman: Then you withdraw one ?—Mr. Fletcher: I doe't think my friend withlraws it. I would rather take that you dismiss it. The summons for establishiag eves dismissed, and the summons for continuing the works was then gone into, and Dr. Monritz, the medical officer of health, was called. He stated he had held that office for 14 years, and had been in practice in the town 18. He remembered the works being erected in the latter part of October last year. For the pest three months there had been mired from them a nuisance highly prejudicial to the health of the inhabitants of the town. He had traced the emissione to the defen- dant's works in his own person. In July he was called to attend a men named Dobson, living in Bold-street, which was about 500 or 600 yards distant from the works. The men was •suffering from gastric catarrh, and he attributed hie illness to the emanations frem the glycerine works,' Hit symptoms were nausea, inability to take food, and intense thirst. IL: did not recover his health for three months. On one occasion he (the doctor) was driving put the works, when be became sick, arid had to pull up his drag. He was nauseated for three days follow- ing. He attributed his sicknese to the gas from the de- fendant's works. For the prst teree or four months be had , smelt the exhalations almost daily, and their effect tied been to increase the mortality of the town very much. The Smell was unpleasant, disagreeable, always.—Cross-examined by Mr. Fletcher: The death rate for the year was about 20 per annum, which was not a high rate. It was very favourable in comparison to the neihbeuring towns. The mortality for July was 32, or a death rate of 25 per 1,000 per annum ; corresponding month in 1881 18 deaths, or a rate of 14 per 1,000 per annum. In August there. were 31 deaths, being at the rate of 21 per 1,000 per annum, while in the cer- responding month in 1381 the deaths were 14, or 11 per 1,000 , per annum. The month he had quoted for 1851 the death ' rate was below the average; this year the average had been considerably exceeded.—Mr. Fletcher hinted that the three months named had been taken because they beat suited the prosecution.—Dr. Mouritz, answering Mr. Fletcher, said Mr. Dobson was suffering from irritation of the mucous rnem- brane of the stomach chlorine gas would not Lave that effect, but irritate the trachea. There was always a good deal of chlorine about Runcorn. —Mr. Fletcher : Would sulphur be calculated to induce the sickness which you complain of? Sulph a- retted hydrogen would.—Mr. Fletcher :There is a great deal of that ia Runcorn? We get it occssionelly.—Were you in Runcorn last Saturday night? Yes.—Did you pass along the main street? Yes.—Detect anything? A strong effluvia.—Did you ascertain what that was ? No.—You did not think it right to trace that horrid stink there was in the in tin street ? I could not trace it in the main street. There would be great difficulty in doing so.—Mr. Fletcher: The fact is there are so many smells in the main street you cann ,t• follow one up. (Laughter.)—Dr. Mouritz said he had visited the glycerine works to m Ike a report. He was shown the place where the liquor wes distilled. He cauld not detect much smell there' but he could on iVfill Brow. It went up the chimney, and he did not put his head up there. (Laughter.)—Mr. Fletcher: Then you believe the observations that you made at Mill Brow in preference to those which you made at the works? Yee.—Can you give me the cause of those deaths which you have recorded? Twelve deaths occurred from diarrhcea and six from maris- lavas or wasting dieeese.—By Mr. Linaker : lie had never had six cases of rriarismus before in Runcorn. He had not the slightest doubt as to where the smell came from.—The Chawmain : These de Iths from marismus were chiefly in- fants? Yes.—Pcoduced by nausea and inability to take food ? Yes. Mr. Henry White, !milder, Runcorn, said prior to M. Chains commencing his manufactory, he occupied a portion of the site. He owned property near the works. Until recently he lived in one of the houses, but he had temporarily removed in consequence of the abominable sae% which emanated from the defendant's works. The house was about 70 or a 100 yards distant from theaworke. His wife and -child, in consequence of the vapour, were attacked with diarrheen general sickness, and inability to take their food. On the night of the let September the stench was so bed that they left the house and went to sleep at his mother-in-law's house in Greenway-roed, where they had since lived. When the smell was bad the child would go turnaling about the house same as if she was drunk. He had no doubt at all but that the stench came from the glycerine works. He had received complaints from his tenants about it.—Cross-exemined by Mr. Fletcher, witness admitted that negotiations had taken place between him and the defendant With regard to leasing his property. He first complained of the nuisance in December. Dr. Robinson, who was the next witness, said he had practicscl in Runcorn for 22 years. He had signed a memorial with regard to the stench. He attended Mrs. White and her daughter on the 28th December lest. The house at that time wee filled with a very offensive smell proceeding from the defendant's manufactory. Ho had seen them on other occasions.—Mr. Linaker : Have you noticed the emissions from the works during the past three months ? No, net perticelerly. I have noticed a very offensive smell from witinw latterly, particularly in the nieht. The smell from the defendant's w)rks would undoubtedly be injurious to a delicate person residing in the neighbourhoed. With regard to the mortality during the past three months he might say there had been an epidemic of scarlatina, and also an epidemic of measles in the town. Diarthea had else been prevalent, but in his emperience of 24 years, the disease used formerly to be more prevalent in n July and August. Some of the cases of masmus might have been the result of diarrlicea, choleric diarrhoea in chil- dren often left a condition of wasting.—Mr. Fletcher You don't mean to say that we have mannfactured measles and scarlatine at these works, do Ton? Certrinly not.—And there has been an epidemic of scarlatina? Almost uni- versal.—Quite sufficient to account for the increased mortality? I should think so. Witness added that he was led to believe that the works had nothing to do with the polluting of the fountain water, and even if they had, he should consider it a benefit than otherwise, especially if it were made so noxious that it could not be used for drinking purposes. He should say that the health of the town had been affected by the nuisance caused by the works. His sympathies were in favour of the works, because they afforded employment to a great number of people, who
could not otherwise obtain work. When he signed the me- morial he wished some steps to be taken for abating the nuisance. He did not intend that the works should b 3

div.head: stopped altogether, Mr. Barker, surveyor to the Commissioners, gave evidence _ _ _ .
div.p: stopped altogether, Mr. Barker, surveyor to the Commissioners, gave evidence _ _ _ .
as to the obnexioas'smell emitted from the —manufactory,

stating that he had received many complaints. He had several times visited the works, and the manager had in- formed him they were going to remedy the matter or made some excuee.—Coss-examined by Mr. Fletcher: He had detected the smell three-quarters of a mile from the works. The report in which be said the smell had not been so bad as heretofore was written on the Thursday; on the Friday the smell was as bad as ever. He visited the works before he made the report. He ex tmined one room and the taps were turned on, and he said the vapoars smelled like ketchup. —Mr. Fletcher: Da you like ketchup? Yes (Laughter).— Then it was an agreeable smell ? It might be agreeable to me but not to other people. But that was nothing to what I smelt outside. If the odour was no worse outside than in I should have nothing to say about it. Mr. John Dobson, carpenter, 10, Bold-street, stated the effect of the gas upon him ; and Mr. Alfred Back, chemist, Bridge-street, deposed to signing the memorial to the Corn- miesioners, wishing that the nuisance should be abated. He had no wish for the Commissioners to take action to stop the works. Mr. Fletcher, in addressing the Bench for the defence, said M. Clolus had grave cause of complaint ageiaet the Runcorn Com:nissioners for the fast and loose manner in which he had been treated by them. Their worships would see that under the Public Health Act the written consent of the Commissioners was necessary prior to the establishraent of what was called an offensive or obnoxious trade within the district. Assuming that the defendant's was one of those trades thus specified, how had the Commissioners treated M. Clolus? Lie had erected the works at a cost of £14,000 in reliance upon- the Commissioners acting towards him in a bona fide, honest and upright manner. In Janu try he applied to the Commissioners for the consent in writing required, and his Liend admitted in his opening statement that the application was made in proper form. He contended that the Commissioners had given that consent ; pntl in sapport of that oontention he would draw attention to the resolution passed by the Commissioners in January of the present year, on the motion of Mr. Wm. Handley, secended by Dr. MacDougall, who would state that that resolution gave permission without qualification.—Mr. Fletcher then read the newspaper account of the proceedings, which stated that Mr. Handley moved that the "required per- mission" be given. In the face of these pro- ceedings, which could be unmistakably established that day by the mover and seconder, and the shorthand writer, who were present, M. Clolus was called upon to answer such a summons—a most arbitrary pro- ceeding. A foreigner was entitled not to more consideration at the hands of the Bench than an Englishman would be entitled to, but he thought he would have grave reason to complain if, after having been misled and trifled with by these town commissioners, he was to be held liable to the. Bench on that summons. The resolution of the Board was in writing, and therefore the consent was in writing. [The resolution, after stating that R. B. Abbot be re- quested to inspect the works, said :—" In the meantime M. Clolus be allowed to carry on the said trade or business."] There was consent recorded in the Commissioners' own book. Mr. Handley was clear that the report of Mr. Abbot WAS to have reference to the 114th section and not the 112:h. The report was simply to guide them in any proceedings against M. Clolus which might be necessary. The 114th section was one which gave the Commissioners ample power to deal with the question if M. Clolus was not doing all in. his power to render the works free from nuisance, and he (Ur. Fletcher) could understand proceedings being taken under that section. He contended that the resolution hes had read was consent in writing within the meaning of the let. There had not been the leestintimation from the town com- missioners that M. Cletus was infringing the 112th section. He challenged Mr. Linaker to show by any of the notices served by them upon M. Clolus that there had been any reference whatever to the 112th section. All the notices had had reference simply to nuisances under the 114th section, and in se doing they had recognised that the works were established by their acquiescence. He touched upon the fact that several witnesses for the prosecution had stated they did not wish the works should be stopped ; and that the petition which was addressed to ,he Commissioners asked them to enforce the 114th section.

He remarked that M. Clolus had works where the same pro- cesses were carried on, erected at Paris, Marseilles, and Glasaow, where the same state of things was going on as was at Runcorn, and he had yet to learn that Paris was a more undesirable place to live in than Runcorn, and that the town authorities of Glasgow and Marseilles were not alive to the interests of their ratepayers. He was ahnoat iiclined to say, although he did not like to say strong things, that it seemed to him that M. Clolus, coming to Runcorn without any friends, the Irish system had been adopted, for inasmuch as he had got no father or mother, no sister or brother, they had determined to give hien a good beating. The Commissioners came very badly out in the affair. Had the Commissioners used their powers under the 114th section instead of acting in this arbitrary way, the defendant would have been prepared to meet them. The course they had taken could not commend itself to their worships under the circumstances of the case. Mr. William Handley said he was a Commissioner in January last. He remembered the 3rd of that month, when the subject of granting a license to M. Clolus Came up for discussion on the application of the law clerk. He moved the resolution that permission to establish the works be given. The resolution was not qualified in any way. He wee well acquainted with the Public Health Act, and his I re3olution was moved so that the Board could have control over the works under the 114th section.—Croes-ex imined by Mr. Linaker : He was not present at the meeting the following month, when the minutes %ere read.—By Mr. Fletcher: He had a good idea of the feeling of the Runcorn people, and he had not heard that they wished the works to be stopped. The name of Dr. MacDaugall was now called,- but there was no answer. Mr. Fletcher said he had summoned Dr. MacDougall, who had had half-a-severeign conduct money, and he did think it was due to the dignity of the court that he should have sent some explanation. What explanation he had to offer he did not know. If the processes of the court were to be set at nought in this m inner, the Bench would have a diffi- culty in dealing with the business of the court. He (Mr. Fletcher) might have put some awkward questions to Dr. MacDougall, but he had no right, therefore, to stay away. lie left the matter for the Bench to deal with, and called Mr. Char!es Nickson, reporter, who deposed that he reported the meeting of the Board of Commissioners on the 3rd January, and prepared the account for the newspaper. The report was correct. There was no qualification to the resolution proposed by Mr. Handley. M. Joseph Ernest De La Rue, the representative of M. Clolus in this conntry, corroborated Mr. Fletcher's statement with regard to the other manufactories. Ho said he was experimentalising with the object of reducing the nuisance, and be hoped he should succeed eventually. The machinery was new. The extraction of glycerine from the soap waste was a new trade and first discovered by M Clolus.—P.S. Whalley, who had been sent in search of Dr. MacDougall, now returned, and said the doctor was not at home. He went away on Saturday night and had not returued.—The Chairman (to Mr. Fletcher) : Do you demand the appearance of Dr. MacDougall ? I am bound to demand it.—The Chairman: You know our only alternative if voudemand it? I cannot forego any evidence. It is for the court to protect its own dignity. I require him just tosay ditto to Mr. Handley. He cannot say any mare, and he cannot say say less—After some further conversation, P.S. Whalley said on Friday he left the summons to appear and half a sovereign at Dr. MacDougall's residence. The doctor was present, but refused to take it. The Chairman : Dr. MacDougall having eeeclined, in de- fiance of the court to attend to a summons, we have no alternative but to issue a warrant for his appearance next Monday, to which day the case will be a earned. The case was then adjourned.

div.head: St HELENS COUNTY COURT,
div.p: St HELENS COUNTY COURT,
TIMP-3DA.Y.—Before J. F. Collier, Esq., Judge,, ard Mr. Tyrer, registrar.

A JUDGE'S VIEW OF CIZEDIT.—William Callan was sued by Patrick Mooney, of Widnes, for 17s 6.1, the balance of a debt for clothing supplied.—The defendant, an elderly man, pleaded inability to pay, and said he was maintained by his wife and son.—Plaintiff, however, stated that defendant had a good clogger's shop and was quite able to pay the amount. He wanted a commitment order.—His Honour said he did not see his way to put the county, to the expense of keeping a man in prison simply because the plaintiff had chose to trust him. He was not obliged to give trust, and it was his own blame.—An order for 4s per month was made. CLAIM BY A. S. HELENS TOBACCONIST.—In this case John Pearce, tobacconist, St. Helens, sued George Pounton, grocer, for £4 33. 4d., the price of a roll of thick twist tobacco.—Mr. Massey appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Husband (Widnes) for the defendant. —Mr. Maesey stated that the tobacco had been supplied on the 12th May, 1881. The order was given on the 27th April, and the delivery took place on the 12th May, and there was no dispute as to either the order or the delivery, nor as to the price of the goods. All the3e things were admitted, and the defence ' would be that these goods were returned to the plaintiff, and upon that the issue would depend. It had been ens- tomary with the plaintiff, as with many other shopkeepers, ' in St. Helens to deliver an invoice with the goods, and get payment for the amount at the next delivery. Rut this ac- count had not been paid, and when the plaintiff asked for payment the excuse bad always been that the bill had been lost, and on that account it had been allowed to stand over. —Mr. Husband, in defence, said what his client said was that the accounts had all been paid from time to time. On one occasion when the plaintiff brought the tobacco in question there had been a balance of 73. 41. standing, to , which plaintiff added the price of the tobacco, but on the tobacco being returned that sum was struck off and a receipt for the residue given. The whole question, he thought, was as to the receipt.—The receipt wa4 then handed to his Honour, who said that some of tbe figures, SA 33.4 d., seemed to have been weitten by a hand different to that of the plaintiff, and ultimately gave a verdict in favour of the plaintiff for the full amount, stating that of course it was impossible for him to say in whose handwriting the inter- polated were.

RUNCORN SCIENCE SCHOOL.

MEETING LAST NIGHT. Last evening the preliminary meeting of the Runcorn School of Science (No. 449) was held in Bethesda School- room, under the presidency of Mr. J. R. Frith. There was a good attendance. The subjects for the session are build- ing construction, machine construction, inorganic chemistry, and alkali manufacture, the teachers being Mr. Thomas Simkin and Mr. Frank H. Tate. - The CHAIRMAN, in opening the proceedings, said it afforded him great pleasure to be present with them that evening. He always took a delight in being present any- where and everywhere, where old and young were desirous of aceiniring knowledge. When he looked back upon his early days he remembered that the advantages which were now offered were not then to be obtained by the young of that generation. The many many associations which were now in existence for the acquirement of science and art did not then exist, and those who wished to improve themselves 'had to struggle hard. He was pleased to see the number of persons present that evening. He should have been glad to have seeia more present, but still they must not despise the day of small things, but proceed in the hope that by and bye the facilities afforded by the classes would be more extensively used. The advantages which were offered by these classes were very great. Every acquirement might be obtained at a very trifling cost. Formerly the advantages which could be derived from these classes were not to be obtained except by those who had an almost unlimited supply of cash. Now, in whatever sphere of life a young man might be placed, e could obtain the advantages, which would be useful to hlm ; or if not useful, it would afford him pleasure, for the acquirement of all knowledge gave pleasure at one time or another. It was astonishing what pleasure know- ledge gave at certain times. When they were viewing manu- facture or treating of an art or a science, if the process of that manufacture, or the art and science was understood, their pleasure was greatly increased. If the manufactures of the country were to be conducted en more scientific prin- ciples, the knowledge must be generally diffused, and he trusted that every effort would be made by the management of those chases to give that instruction. The teachers were men of solid acquirements, and far ahead of the mem- bers of their classes, and the steady attention which they had paid to the subjects upon which they treated, he well knew, would enable them to impart a very great amount of instruction to the students. The success of the past session was very great, and lie was very highly pleased with it. He trusted that the success in the past would only stimulate those who were present and those who might attend the classes, to exert themselves in every possible way; to determine not to be medium scholars, but thoroughly efficient masters of the subject upon which they were engaged. He was very much pleased at seeidg in the paper the other day a lecture by Mr. A. Norman Tait, and he said that on looking over the latest report of the science and art department, with which their classes were connected, he found that in the session 1880-81 the large number of 38,837 students were examined, and 30,518 were successful ; and that of these 17,246 had not been success- ful in a previous year. Altogether 72,300 papers were worked, and 48 598 were successful. In addition, 1,521 students in training colleges succeeded in science examina- tions. The total amount paid on success was—to science schools and training colleges, £47,230 163. id.; and the students in science schools and classes paid fees to the amount of £12,120 179. 61 It was very pleasing that so large a number in our country were attending these classes, which would elevate the rising generation and enable them to compete with the scientific men of the Continent. Englishmen were somewhat behind their Con- tinental friends in scientific knowledge ; he thought they? could hold their own in almost everything else He hoped we should be. at the head of the scientists of the world by- and-bye. tie was very glad to have met them that night, and it was his wish that their labours during the session would prove not only interesting, but of great profit to each student. (Applause.) Mr. POPE, the secretary, gave a short statement as to the success of last year's classes. The total number of students under instruction in science and technicology was 81, v ize— , Building construction 30, mathematics 36, inorganic chemistry 20, alkali manufacture 5; as compared with 23 students in one subject in the previous session. Of the 81 students 42 sat for examination as follows :—Building construction 16, passed 14, percentage of passes $75; mathematics tl2, 4 passed, .percentage of classes 33 3; chemistry 11, 9 passed, , percentage of passes 81'80 ; alkali manufacture, 3 sit and 3 passed. In these examinations 4 outside students sat two in chemistry (an old student, W. Millington, taking Ist advanced), and two in technicoiogy, one of whom, James Frith, obtained sth prize, a bronze medal. There were 170 drawings sent to South Kensington for examination. The Government grant for last session was £32 155., compared with £7 the previous session. Mr. PATE explained how the classes for the study of chenfistry and alkali in nufacture would be conducted, and announced the prizes for which the students could Compete. Mr. 'l'. SIMICIN made a similar statement with regard to the classes for building and machine construction. Time business of enrolling students was then proceeded with.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held at the Board-room, Victoria-road, on Thursday. Mr. Bradshaw presided, and there were also present the Revs. Father Clarke, Father _Finegan, Dr. O'Keeffe, Hartland, R. Shaw, and Denby (clerk.)

div.head: DISTRICT EDUCATION COMAIITEEE.
div.p: DISTRICT EDUCATION COMAIITEEE.

The District Education Committee reported that during I the month of August (five weeks) the numbers of cases summoned before the Committee were applications for pay- ment of fees, 80; for contravention of Education Act, 348; total 428. Fees were recommended to be paid in 67 cases; 13 applications were reused. 29 persons were brought before the magistrates, and convicted, and three children were. sent to industrial schools.
The minutes were passed on the notion of the Rev. Father Clarke.
SCHOOL SIA.NAGEMEHT COMMITTEE.

The committee recommended that the resignation of Miss B. A. Hughes, assistant mistress, Junior Girls' Department, be accepted from the 30th September, 1882; that the follow- ing teachers be appointed to conduct the various classes for the instruction of female pupil teachers, the engagement to date from October 2nd, 1852, and to be determinable on either side by one month's notice, to expire on the last day of any cilendar month:—Geography, Mr. Snaddy ; arith- metic, Mr. Showan ; grammar, Mr. Hunter; school man- agement, Mr. Crawford; music, Mr. Glower; drawing, Miss Clayden ; reading and repetition, Miss Hay; history, Mrs. Morgan; domestic economy, Miss Strickland; sewing, Miss Strong. The committee also reported that they had had before them the letter from the, head master, dated August 14th, 1882, referred to them at the last meeting of the Board, and begged to recommend that the classes f,)l' the central teaching of male ,pupil teachers be commenced on Monday, October 2nd, 1852, and that the three head masters be paid a sum not exceeding twenty pounds per annum for conducting the same.—The minutes were passed with the exception of that referring to the payment of head masters, which was referred back to the committee on the motion of Dr. O'Keeffe. FINANCE COMMITTEE.

The Finance Committee reported that the following ac- counts have been examined by their various _committees, and they recommend the same for payment in due course, viz.:—District Education Committee, £22 4s 6d ; sites and Building Committee, £8 18s Od; School Management Com- mittee, £206 16s 4d; Finance Committee, £35 163 8d ; £273 15s 6d. The Committee stated that since their last report £637 14s 9d bad been paid into Bank.—The minutes were passed, and the Board rose.

div.head: RUNCORN SCOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCOOL BOARD.

-- The ordinary meeting of this Board was held at the offices, Bridgewater-street, yesterday morning. The Rev. Canon Barclay, the chairman, presided. There were also present Rev. Father Fennelly, Messrs. John Simpson, Jas. Pritchard, Thomas Norman, and F. Rigby (clerk).

div.head: AN APPOINTMENT:
div.p: AN APPOINTMENT:
MIS 3 - Gunning was appointed a monitor at the Board school in the place of Rhoda Lowe until the eximination of pupil teachers ; afterwards on the same terms as pupil teachers.

div.head: PRECEPT.
div.p: THE PRECEPT.

On the motion of Mr. PRITCHARD, seconded by Mr. T. NORMAN, it was decided to serve a precept for £2OO upon the overseers.—The asnic: explained that this was the same amount as last year.—The Board had £7O in the bank.

div.head: TENDERS.
div.p: TENDERS.
A number of tenders for the supply of officer ° clothing were considered. That of Mr. James Yates was accepted.
OFFICER'S REPORT.

Mr. BOWYER read his report as follows :—The returns for the past quarter I have not been able to tabulate in the usual way, as I have not yet received the increased accom- modation at the various schools. The total number on the rolls for the month ending September 22nd, was 2,910; and the average attendance 2,005.3 ;:the average attendance for the corresponding period of last year was 2,048 1, show- ing a decrease in the average attendance as compared with last year of 42 8. Number in attendance at private adventure schools under ninepence per week 63. With respect to the adventure schools, I have to report that the one in Arthur-street, kept by Miss Roberts, has been closed ; also one has been re•opened in Suffolk-street by Mrs. Ains- worth, who formerly kept one in Surrey-street. In the returns for the past four weeks, you will notice that there is a decrease in the average attendance, especially in the in- fant schools. This is principally owing to there having been so much sickness in the town during the past month Measles have been exceedingly prevalent, and many chil- dren have been obliged to be absent feom school through so much sickness being in their homes. Since the last meet- ing of the Board I have served 31 final notices upon parents for the irregular and non-attendance of their chil- dren at school. These cases I lay before you, showing the total number of times present and absent since the notices have been served. I also lay before you a list of incorrigi- bles which have been previously dealt with, and have again become irregular, through neglect and carelessness on the parents part. Several of these cases, you will notice, belong to canal boat people, who regularly take them on board their boats. Mr. Bowima said the attendance at the infant schools was very bad. The CHAIRMAN: A school with an average attendance of over a handred, began school one morning with five scholars.—Mr. BOWYER said measles was very prevalent.— Mr. NORMAN remarked that there were still a great many young rascals about the town yet—especially about the station.—Mr. BOWYER said these children were over 13 years of age, and consequently out of his power. He, how- ever, kept a sharp look out upon them, and whenever he found any who ought to be at school he brought them up. —The Board authorised Mr. Bowyer to prosecute 28 parents Ifor neglecting to send their children to school.—The Board then rose.

div.head: McM INN lES, M. P., AT D IRWEN.
div.p: McM INN lES, M. P., AT D IRWEN.

A DEFENCE OF BAZAARS. On Wednesday morning, Mr. J. G. McMinnies, M.P. for Warrington, opened a bazaar at Over Darwen in aid of the Hollins Grove Congregational Church, which was erected 12 months ago at a cost of £3,300, and is still £1,300 in debt. There was a thousand pounds' worth of goods in the baz tar. The Rev. M. Braithwaite, pastor, and a large number of local ministers and influential gentlemen were present. Mr. J. G. MCMINNIES, M.P., on being called upon, said that notwithstanding that a great deal 'had been said and written in public prints lately against bazaars, he confessed he belieyEd in bazaars. He believed in them as a means of great public usefulness in raising money for charitable and religious purposes. (Hear, hear.) For the most part he found that the obj-ctions raised against bazaars were entirely imaginary, and when • any particular in- stances were given of anybody being worse for supporting a bazaar, be found that those instances were entirely illusory and inappropriate. ;Probably a great deal of the abjectian to baz tars arose from the memory of certain abuses that he dared say formerly existed. He had no doubt that in former days extortionate prices were asked for the things they had to sell, and he dared say that young ladies were very unfortunate—and a very proper thing for young ladies to he. (Laughter.) And there were objections to a very gentle kind of what censorius people called gambling, but what they called raffling. Asking high prices was a practice that would cure -itself, -for they would find articles left on their hands until the last day, when they would probably have to be cleared out at half their worth. His own experience of bazaars extended over thirty years, and he did not think anybody was ever worse in any way for supporting bazaars. He remembered not long ago a pre- late in the north of England finding great fault with bazaars. He said that they led to gambling, and ,that he believed it was owing to bazaars that certain noble families had been ruined on the racecourse. He (the speaker) thought that this was very absurd. The prelate, he believed, alluded to the late Mercer's of Hastings, and knowing as be did, something about the young nobleman by reputation, he (the speaker) would be bound to say that he never attended Ia b aaar for religious purposes in his- life, so that the habit of gambling which undoubtedly ruined him was not acquired by attendance at bazaars. Then the bishop sneered very much at what they had to sell at bazaars, and spoke disrespectfully of antimacassars and pincushions. (Laughter.) He (the speaker) thought pincushions were very useful. The bishop said that antimacassars were always sticking to men's buttons' (Laughter.) He (the speaker) thought antimacassars were very useful, and sometimes very ornamental things. At any rate they were quite as useful as the buttons behind a man's coat that they were in the habit of sticking to. (Loud laughter.) It was said that people who took an interest in bazaars did not do so for a single and proper motive, but he did not believe this. He had known young people work fur bazaars with a zeal and enthusiasm that proved they were anxious to promote what they believed to be good philan- thropic and charitable objects. Then it was suggested that young people ,might be better employed than in working for bazaars—in district visiting or Sunday school teaching; but the fact was these means of usefulness were not everybody's avocation. Some people had not the strength, the ability, or the courage for district visiting or Sunday school teach- ing, and it appeared to him that if they had not the avoca- tion for these things that the bishop recommended that they could not be better employed than in supporting institutions of that kind. (Hear, hear.) The hope or expectation that was expressed that Christian people would give money for religious objects, even if there were no bazaars, was an en- tire begging of the question. The question was whether or not working for bazaars was not the best and the most generous way of supporting religious institutions. On the part of . some people they gave their work, their skill, and the taste with which they were endowed, and in this way helped the cause to a much greater extent than they could possibly help it by gifts and of money. (Hear, hear.) It might be preeminently said of bazaars that the end justified the means. He had seen charitable and religious institutions flourish upon, or at any rate kept kept alive, through money supplied in that kind of thing which would never have been kept alive if it had not been fur the pecuniary aupport derived from such means; and then he saw the good done by institutions that had been helped, perhaps founded, by what had been got at bazaars. When he remembered the ignorance that had been enlightened, the comfort that had been given to suffering , people, the religious knowledge that had been imparted by -mch instrumentalities, he mall not help wishing God-speed no institutions like that. (Applause.) He bad seen recently good deal of sneering that young ladies went about on those occasions in handsome dresses. Well, he hail no objection to young ladies in handsome dresses---(much
