div.head: DREADFUL STREiI SCENE AT
div.p: A DREADFUL STREiI SCENE AT
RUNCORN.

Yesterday, at Runcorn Police Court, before Messrs. Wm. Bankes and S. B. Chadwick, a young man named Septimus Massey was brought up on remand from Tuesday, charged with assaulting a young unmarried woman named Sarah Ellen Robinsoe.—The prosecutrix said she lived in Nelson- street, and the prisoner also lived in the same neighbour- hood. On Saturday night, about half-past six, she (witness) was tipsy in the street, where she met a woman named E:lis, who had also had drink. They had some words to- gether. Whilst they were "haggling," Mrs. Massey, the wife of the prisoner, came up, and took a part in the quarrel. She struck witness, who returned the blow, and then a tight commenced between thorn. Witness had Mrs. Massey against the rails, when the latter shouted, "Seph, there are two of them on me." Witness replied there was only one, when the prisoner struck her on the left side of the face with his hand. She escaped from the prisoner and his wife, but they followed her up the street. Prisoner again struck her under the jaw with his fist, making her bite her tongue, and blood flowed freely from her mouth. She was at- tempting to again make her escape when the prisoner kicked her twice on the left side of the body, and whilst she was on the ground knelt upon her. During the time this WAS taking place the prisoner's wife was al so "fighting" her. The prisoner was wearing clogs. Witness became insensible, and had been unable to leave the house until that morning. She had been attended by Dr. Bagnall.— Alice Piers, sister of the last witness, corroborated her statement as to the violence of the prisoner, stating that the latter knocked her sister twice to the ground with his fist.—Mary Wood, Sarah Powell, Mrs. Lind, were called, and deposed to watching the fight, stating the prisoner did not strike the proseentrix. Neither or the witnesses, however, saw the row to its conclusion. When the prose- cutrix beeline insensible they did not render her any aid.—The prisoner alleged that the prosecutrix made en imputatioa against the character of. his wife, and the fight commenced through the former striking the latter. He kicked neither of them. He only took his wife into the house. He called Mrs. Jones, who deposed that the prisoner did not Strike the prosecutrire.—Elizabeth Cresswell said she witnessed the fight for ten minutes, but whilst she was there she did not see the prisoner strike the prosecutrix.—Mrs. Ellen Erinshaw, beerhouse-keeper, Nel- son-street, gave similar evidence. About twenty minutes after the fight she went into the street. All the people had left, but the prosecutrix was lying in the gutter insensible. —Mr. Superintendent Williamson: And you still left her there.—Yes.—Mr. Superintendent Williamson (severely) : It is a Christian neighbourhood you live in. You as a publican's wife ought certainly to have some humanity about you. You see a woman lying on the ground ap- parently lifeless, but you allow her to remain there, and did not take a bit of notice.—Witness: Her mother lived close to.—Mr. Superintendent Williamson (with contempt) : Her mother lived close to I don't know what the magistrates and the public will think of your conduct—l know what I think about it.—Dr. Bagnall stated he saw the prosecutrix about one o'clock on Sunday morning. She was at her own home lying on a couch in a state of unconscieumess. With some difficulty he got her partly conscious. She was badly bruised on one leg, and her jtw appeared as if it had been struck with a fist or kicked. There were no bruises on the body. Her unconsciousness might have been caused by violence. On Monday morning the woman was in a dangerous condition, and appeared as if some injury had been done to her brain—After some minutes consideration with his brother magistrate, Mr. Bankes said : There is no doubt in our minds that Sarah Ellen Rubinson has received gross abuse—violent conduct from someone. Unfortunately from the evidence produced before us this morning, we cannot convict you (the prisoner) with that violence, consequently we shall have to dismiss the case. You must think yourself very fortunate that you are not sent to gaol.

div.head: ADJOURNED LICENSING SESSIONS,
div.p: ADJOURNED LICENSING SESSIONS,
DARESBURY.

The adjourned licensing sessions for the renewal of licenses were held in the' sessions reom, at Daresbury, on Tuesday. The presiding magistrates were Messrs. Peter Stubs (chairman) and James Marson.—The whole of the off licenses were renewed, with the exception of one held by Mr, William Worrell, of Hatton, which Mr. Superintendent Williamson strongly objected to.—Mr. Moore represented Mr. Worrell, and said the application was granted about 12 months ago. On the 30th May last Mr. Worrell was sum- moned for a breach of the Licensing Act, and was fined 20s and costs, but the magistrates did not think it a case of such enormity to endorse his license. Last month he was summoned for a similar offence, and the case was dismissed. Mr. Worrell, who had been born and bred in the neighbour- hood, was a highly respectable man, and there was nothing against him with the exception of the conviction in May last. • Mr.. Moore contended that if his client did commit an offence on that occasion it was done in ignorance of the law. He read a number of testimonials, including one from Mr. Neill, of Whitley, which spoke in eulogistic terms of the personal character of Mr. 'Woman, and Mr. Moore, con- tinuing, said Mr. Worrell, through him, assured the Bench he would never offend again. The nearest public-house to Mr. Worrall's was about half a mile away, and he asked the Bench to give his client another chance. Mr. Moore then called Mr. Johnson Fairhurst, farmer, Hattori, who said Mr. Worrell was a very respectable ruin and he had known him for 40 years. In reply to Mr. upe.rinten- dent Williamson, he said helivel about a mile away from Mr. Worrall's house, and did not know the way in which the applicant conducted his house.—Supt. Williamson objected to the renewal of Mr. Worrall's license on three grounds. In the first place because on the 311 i May, 1832, he was fined in that court 203. and costs for an Offence against his license; secondly, having been so convicted be was not a fit and proper person to hold-a license ; and thirdly, that the license • was not required for the accommodation of the inhabiterOs of the neighbourhood. The applicant was also summoned there last court day for a similar offence, but that case was certainly dismisvd upon a technical point.— Mr. Moore: It was not on a technical point; it was decided on its merits.—Mr. Superintendent Williams:an said with teference to that case he purposed applying to the Bench for •a snmmons against one of the witnesses and also against Mrs. Worrell for committing perjury. He had revived numerous complaints with reference to Mr. WorralPs house from farmers in the neighbourhood. He had continuelly had to send officers for the purpose of watching the illegal traffic in drink, and after the greet trouble the police had had with Mr. Worrell, as a public officer he thought it his bounclen duty to object to the renewal of this license.—Mr. Marsoe : Wleereabouts is this licensed house P—Mr. Superintendent Williamson : It is situated about a mile and a half from the Cat and Lion, on the Tarporley and Warrington-road.—The Chairman : We are both of opinion that the license must be refused.—Mr. Moore : Without any disrespect to the Beech, ' I am instructed to give notice of appeal.

div.head: WIDNES STA_IIR-BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETY.
div.p: WIDNES STA_IIR-BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETY.

The fourth appropriation meeting in connection with this society was held in Waterloo-road schoolroom last evening. There WAS a large attendance, and Mr. J. Brock, j J.P., occupied the chair. Mr. J. Barcroft, of Ramsbottom, was precuL to aeltver a lecture on the principles ef the society.—ln introducing the lecturer to the meeting, Mr. Bnocic said he supposed the objects of the society, in common with those of other building societies, was to enable the members to obtain the ! means wheret)y to build houses. But there was a further object of more than ordinary importance, and that was to give a direct encouragement to thrift. He was sure that if there was one to .en in Lancashire where thrift was needed by the people generally, it was, per- haps, NVidnes. He th*ught that whilst it was well to simply says money, it was better to have a distinct ob- ject in view when. doing so. As a young man, he himself had started with an object in view, vrWch he had succeedel in, accomplis hie, and since that time when he bad a definite object before him, he generally succ,.e,ederl. Mr. BARCROFT then delivered his lecture, and at its conclusion a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to him on the motion ,of the CHAIRMAN, seconded by Mr. TRACY, jun.—On the motion of Mr. REAY, seconded by Mr. LAWRENSON, a similar • compliment Was paid to the Chairman, who departed.—Mr. Fogg was then appointed chairman to conduct the ballot, Mr. Reay and Mr. Lawrenson being the scrtatineers. A boy, named Win. Teesdale drew the numbers. The first drawn was 174, and amid much laughter the holder Was declared disqualified from benefit in consequence of being in arrears with his subscriptions. Singularly enough the owner of the shares represented by the next number drawn, 278, was also in arrears, and had again to be taken. Mr. Samuel Lamb was then declared to ba entitled to £2OO. free of interest for 121,- years, his being the lucky number (52) which was next drawn. The proceedings then terminated.

div.head: LATEST NEWS RIMA.RDING THE EXPLOSION.
div.p: LATEST NEWS RIMA.RDING THE EXPLOSION.

A stop-press edition of the Daily diretri contains the fol- lowing Cairo telegram, dated Thursday evening :—" At seven o'clock the fire .was still raging. The whole of the railway station is in flames, and for the last hour a noise of small ammunition and the explosion of shells exactly resembles the roar of a battle field. No more casualties have been reported. I have just met the secretary of the railway company on the spot, and he informs ma that the ammunition is our own and does not belong to the Egyptians, that it has been kept in sheds and waggons for the last few days, that today it was being removed by the military at the request of the railway authorities, and that the explosion began during the process of removal. The catastrophe is attri- buted to an accidental blow to a percusion ahell. The other railway stock has suffered no damage, having been sOedily removed. Tne troops will probably patrol the streets to- night." Sir G. Wolseley sends the following telegram, dated Cairo, Thursday :—''l regret to say that a large fire broke out at the station this afternoon, whica leas destroyed a large amount of our supplies and stores. Details will be tele- graphed to-morrow." Another account says :—" The explosion at the railway Station continued at short intervals for over three hours, when the rapid recurrence of the reports began to slacken, owing to the energetic efforts of the military,-which had to contend with great difficulties, the pumping material being scanty. The fire was localised and finally got under by nine o'clock. The passenger station was saved, but all the goods sheds, containing provisions for the army for ten days' as well as about a hundred trucks of ammunition, -werede- stroyed. The number of killed and wourrded is smaller than was at first believed, though at present an exact state- ment cannot be made. It is reported on good authority that five men were killed and twenty wounded. Amang the wounded is a surgeon of the 60th Rifles. Many suppositions are current concerning the origin of the fire. The railway officials expressed the belief that it was due to foul play, because they noticed that the trucks on two separate lines of railway burst out into a blaze at the same time, and subsiquently to the first explosion two Arabs were seized in the act of setting fire to some trucks. A third Arab was also detected in an attempt to fire some of the rolling stock, but he escaped. As tke first fragments of shells that were found on the outbreak of the fire belonged to the Egyptian guns, it is surmised that the ignition first occurred among the E,,yption ammunition. The damage, including loss of rolling stock,' is estimated at several thousand pounds. The railway traffic will not stiller any serious interruption. The train service for Alexandria will be re'eumecl some time to- morrow. No private merchandise was burned."

All the s,uspects in Ireland have now been released. Mr. Forster' s Coercion Act expires to-day. The Irish Times of yesterday insists that there is a split in the Parnellite party, and that the conference next month is with the view to settle existing differences. Earl Spencer is-about to make a short vsit to England. He has not left Ireland since the murder of Lord Frederick Cavendish and Mr. Burke.

The Mint Authorities yesterday prosecuted a man named Hugh Kennedy, at Burnley Police Court, for uttering base coin. Three distinct charges were established against the prisoner, who was committed to the Manchester assizes. This is the third case of the kind during the past few days. At Cappah, near Woodford, twelve miles from Loughrea, on Thursday evening, two farmers named Marra and Lakin had a quarrel, in the course of which the former seized a hatchet and struck Larkin a violent blow on the head. The injured man was immediately taken home, but there are no hopes of his recovery. Marra is in custody. Yesterday morning, at the Darwen Police Court, two respectable young men named John Campbell and William Henry Ratcliffe were charged with stealing a coat and a quantity of sheet lead, from off the roof of the new mill be- longing to Messrs. E. Shorrock and Co. Both pleaded guilty, and Campbell was sentenced to three months' hard labour, and Ratcliffe to two months. Yesterday was published a report of the Scotch harvest. Oats are a crop and a third, wheat is rather above an aver- age, and barley fuHy better, especially in quality, than last year. Beans are plentiful and good. The turnip crop is above an average, while the potato crop will yield good re- turns, notwithstanding the extensive ravages of diesa.se. The total value of the chief cereal and root crops is estimated at over eight millions. A meeting of the North Wales Coalowners' Association was held at Wrexham, yesterday, to consider the demand of the men for an advance of 15 per cent. The delegates of the men were invited to meet the masters, and were in-

formed that the association were prepared to make an advance of five per cent. at once, and again consider the question at the end of October. The feeling was in favour of adopting the proposed terms. THE FEVER EPIDEMIC AT ACCRINGTON.

There have been six cases of scarlet fever at Accrington this week, making 15 during the last fortnight. A numbor of new outbreaks have been reported to the local authority within the last few days, but it is stated they are of a mild type. In two houses alone no less than 10 pe'rsons, mostly children, are down with this disease.

div.head: SHOCKING ACCIDENT TO A GIRL.
div.p: SHOCKING ACCIDENT TO A GIRL.

Yesterday morning a shocking accident occurred at Rushton Station, Staffordshire. A girl named Gibson. aged seventeen„whilst hurrying to catch the train, fell across the metals, and the engine passed over her outstretched arms, severing both above the wrists. She also received a severe contusion on the head, from which blood flowed profusely. There is no hope of her recovery. She was removed to Macclesfield Infirmary. SERIOUS CHARGES AGAINST A FARMER.

The Eccleshall (North Staffordshire) magistrates sat till a late hour on Tkursday evening hearing a series of cases against Richard Key, farmer, who was charged by the Lon- don and North-Western Railway Company upon six sum- monses with having given false returns of the milk he sent to Liverpool, with the intent of evading the toll. The charges being proved, defendant, who was liable to penalties amounting to £lOO, was ordered to pay mitigated fines amounting to £l2. CURIOUS LOSS OF MONEY.

In connection with the murder in county Tipperary a curious circumstance has been made known. One of the accused was courting the daughter of a widow whose husband recently died. Some time before his death he hid three £5O notes under the hearthstone from his wife, and on going to look for them some months after found only a few shreds of them left, they being all eaten by crickets. ALLEGED ROBBERY BY A WAITER.

John and Richard Fowles, both of Liverpool, were charged at the Altrincham Police Court, yesterday morning, John with stealing, and Richard with receiving, various ,sums of money belonging to Mr. Doe, the refreshment con- . .

tractor at the Altritich-cim agricultural show. John was engaged as waiter, and during Thursday it was alleged he handed to his brother, the other prisoner, various sums on the pretence of giving him change. Both prisoners were committed for trial.

ALLEGED ROBBERY OF £l2O WORTH OF OPIUM. A man named Bailey and his wife were charged at Liver- nool. yesterday, on suspicion of stealing opium valued at £l2O, found at their lodgings. They were apprehended while endeavouring to dispose of some of the drug, and gave diverse accounts as to how it came into their pos- session. They had come from Dublin recently, and it is believed the drug was stolen from there. The prisoners, were remanded.

div.head: POISONED BY MISTAKE.
div.p: POISONED BY MISTAKE.

An ;vaguest was held at the Clitheroe Workhouse, yester- day, on the body of Sarah Thom, aged 52, a widow, of &laden, who was poisoned by mistake six weeks ago. She was under the treatment of Dr. Howarth, and in mistake for her medicine she took a dose of ammonia from a bottle in her house. The poison caused her throat to swell and her reason to be deranged. In a fortnight she had to be removed to the Workhouse, where she lingered and died. BETTING PROSECUTIONS IN LIVERPOOL.

At the Liverpool Police Court, yesterday, John Crabtree, innkeeper, was summoned for p •rmitting his house to be used for betting, and John Scholfield or Conrod Thornton, alias "The Colonel," was summoned for making bets in the house. Scholfield preferred his case to go before a jury. Crabtree's case only was proceeded with. Information was laid on two dates. Crabtree was fined £25 And costs. Notice of appeal was given.
JUVk.NILE BURGLARS.

The Newcastle-under-Lyne police have in custody two boys named Murray and Cotton, for burglariously breaking int 4 the house of a gentleman named Thomas Cohen and stealing £l5. An entrance to the premises had been effected by wrenching away a grid in the backyard. The toys, being suspectea or trie crime, were arrested, when one of them confessed and pointed out where B of the money bad been hidden in a field at Cliff Vale. MISTAKES IN COMMITMENT WARRANTS.

The presiding magistrate at Nottingham yesterday morn- ing said that mistakes in commitment warrants were of daily occurrence, and the Governor of the Gaol v,,as instructed to lay the matter bP'ore the Home Secretary. A woman com-. plained of her husband being kept in gaol for a month, when only corn nitted for fourteen days. The magistrates said the Gove,,tor would have to keep him; they could not order the Governor to let him go. The friends of thc man could take what action they liked. rRINCE BISMARCK AND THE EGYPTIAN SETTLEMENT.

The Press Association learns that Count Munster, the German Ambassador, who is expected in London this even- ing, bears with him Prince Bismarck's opinion regardinc, the Buyptian settlement, and will have an interview with Earl Granville immediately upon his arrival.

div.head: TH iNKSGIITINGS FOR THE VICTORIES
div.p: TH iNKSGIITINGS FOR THE VICTORIES
IN EGYPT.

In accordance with the suggestion issued to the clergy by the Archbishop of York, thanksgiving • services for the victories of our arms in Egypt were held in the Episcopal churches of Warrington on Sunday last. At the Parish Church the special form of thanksgiving was used, spacial Psalms were sung, and the NAtiollal Anthem was played before the commencement of each service. A lame congregation attended the evening service, but the Rector having on the previous Sunday referred to the victories in Egypt, little reference was made in the morning, afternoon, and evening sertnogs by the clergy to the subject. The form of thanksgiving appointed by the Archbishop of York, was used at St. Paul's church. At the morning service reference was made by the lricar, Rev. S.Wilkinson, to our recent victories, and in the evening an appropriate sermon was preached on the subject by the Rev. H. G. Smith, curate. On each occasion the National Anthem was played as the congregation left the church. At St. Anne's church, the day was set apart for thanks- giving, and the National Anthem was sung before the bene- diction in the evening. But slight reference was made to the victory in the sermon. The Rev. F. Slater preached at St. James's church. Latch- ford, in the morning from Ps. xxx. 2, " Give the Lord the honour due to His name." He said that there were many who would scoff at the thanksgiving services held that day, and say, with a modern statesman, that God was on their side who had the biggest battalions; in other words, that we owed our success in Egypt to our science, to the superior discipline of our troops, to the vigour of our national character. The ancient faith of Eugland, however, still remained, and the thanksgiving offered to God in thousands of churches throughout the length and breadth of the land for the success of our army in Egypt, was a proof that the descendants of those who knelt in prayer before they rushed to the encounter at Bannockburn, of those at ho, after the great victoryof Cressy, made the camp resound with hymns of thanksgiving, still put their trust in the Lord of Hosts, still thanked Him for victory. It was right that England should recognise that victory came from God; but that was not enough. Every blessing brought its re- sponsibility, and it was necessary that England should rise to a sense of her responsibilities. If she were rich and powerful, if she had a mighty empire, and enjoyed the ad- vantages of civilisation, the blessings of Christianity, she was bound to use that which had been given her by God for the.benefit of the people under her sway. She was bound to civilize, to give good governmentepeace, prosperity, above all the Gospel, wherever her power extended. If, however, they demanded this of the national conscience, they must remember that the national conscience was but the aggregate of individual consciences, and that each one was bound to show by his life that he felt this double obligation ; first, to accept all blessings as coming directly from God : and in the second place, to feel that each bleesing brought with it a responsibility, a duty, which would meet him again at the great day of account. Reference to the success of our arms in E?ypt was also made, both morning and evening at St. Thomas's Church, Stockton Heath. Preachin; in the evening, the Vicar (the Rev. T. Sisclair Tofts), said they had beets asked that day to join in praise and thanksgiving to Almighty God for the late victory which He had granted to our army and for res- toring peace in Egypt. In what way had th-ev discharged that duty ? Had their hearts joined with their voices in praising Hint for His goodness and mercy so lately vouch- safed to them? When they considered what a are and Increasing territory He had given to be governed by their beloved Queen, what commotions, what strife and bloodshed He bad suffered to take place in other countries, keeping them at the same time free from sacli outrages, surely they ought as a nation so highly favoured and distinguiahed to "give glory to the Lord youa God." s The Incumbent of St. John's, Walton, the Rey. Arthur Jones, took for his tezt the words, "He led them through

- the depths, as through the wildernese Psalm cvi. and part of the 9th verse. In the course of his sermon the rev. gene pour out tleman said they were called upon that day to their hearts in thankfulness to God for 11i9 great goodness to them of late in bringing to such a speedy termination a war :that many thought would not have ceased in such a short period, and that very much more human life Would have had to be sacrificed before such a happy result as had been brought about in the last few days could be proclaimed throughout the length and breadth of the world. War, at any tines, was a terrible disaster, be it ever so necess3r9; the grief, the desolation, the blanks it caused in hundreds and thousands of once happy homes • the tears of widows and orphans—all these were things sufficient to make them hate tbe very word of war. They might, indeed, grieve because 0t those who were so bereft, but rejoice and raise their heavenly Father that He had seen fit so soon to bring abe,tl N:ctory for them and peace for their enemies. They Title': Indeed, praise Him for having so lovingly led our armlets . through the depths, through what seemed to be very Mae' against them, through distress, and through want. They: should thank Him who led and gave them health alae strength to bear up under scorching suns, to march courage.: ensly against foes who were hardened and acclimatised They might praise Him who "led them through the dePtb6 as through the wilderness, and for having saved them fre.ta the hand of him that hated them." They might praise 110, for having spared our own country so long from the band .set, tke enemy, and we, in whose land so much sin and WickM ness were committed daily should now pray that mercies slight be the means of turning us to littil• ,; vial' could they better show their thankfulness, their grab tude to God, who was in the midst of the battle, than I forsaking sin. Jackson) in the course of his sermon, which at • eoeni; tamed a recapitulation of the events that have transpired in Egypt, referred to the anxiety which ten d.e?! ago was manifested for intelligence from the seat ofof and the feeling with which the news of the subjugati" Arabi and his rebel army, the re-opening of the highvif arYtre Witt, and the measures that were being undertaken that restoration of order and the better government of country, were received. Their thanks were due to Ith.e_ commander for the skill with which he bad plannedro;lo, campaign, and to the army for the vigorous roani 'Jebel which they had carried out his instrections. Whi.e t t did not forget this, their gratitude and praise were v One above them, whom they should not fail to ae:;:- vce. ledge in all their ways for His protecting care and gu'''

TO CONSUMERS OF GAS.—The Warrington Corpora- tion Gas Committee, being desirous of further en- couraging amongst their consumers the use of GAS FOR COOKING and other purposes, are now prepared to Sell, Let out on Hire, or Parchase, Lease, GAS COOKING STOVES at a small half-yearly rent charge. All the stoves will be selected from the best m_kers for ecmomy in consumptionsof gas, perfection in cooking, and constructed on the best scien- tific principles. The Gas Committee, in order to make cook- ing by gas a success, wil lay all extra services and connect the stoves, whether supplied by the Corporation or anyone else, ready for use free of all expense to the consumer.—By order, JAMES PATERSON, M .nager. Gas Works, Warrington, 26th June, 1882. -

WIDNES SCIENCE AND ART CLASSES. Tbe Certificates and Prizes will be distrihuted to the Successful Students at a METING to be held in the VOLUNTEER HALL, on WEDNESDAY NEXT, OCTOBER 4th. E K. Musrratt, Eq., F. H. Gossage, E-q ,B. Carey, E.,q , and J. Br.)ck, Esq., will address the meeting. J. D. MiTsPRATT, ESQ ,will preside. Admission free by Ticket, which may be had from any member of the committee. The Cla3ses will commence Monday, October 9th, 1882. SYLLABUS :—Mondays: Practical Chemistry, 6-30 p.m. to 8-0 p.m.; Alkali Manufacture, 8-0 p.m. to 9 0 p.m. Tuesdays: Art-Drawing, 7-0 p.m. to 8-0 p.m.; Machine Construction and Drawing, 1-0 p.m. to 9-0 p.m. Wednesdays: Art-Drawing, 7-0 p m. to 8-0 p.m.; Building Construction and Drawing, 8-0 p.m. to 9-0 p.m. Thursda4s Inorgan'c Chemistry (Elemen- tary Stage) 7-0 p.m. to 8 0 p.m.: Inorganic Chemistry (Ad- vanced Stage), 8-0 p m, to 9-0 p.m. Fee, 3s. per Class for all Classes, except Practical Chemistry. Fee for Practical Chemistry Bs., ar,d a deposit of 53. for the use of apparatus. This deposit will be returned at the end of the Session if breakages, rte., are made good. The Laboratory Is now being fitted up in the most complete manner. Each Student will have a separate bench with lock- up cupboard allotted to him, and he will have futl control and charge of the apparatus and re-agents. At the end of each lesson eachstudent must put away the apparatus and re-agents in the lock up cupboard. Should a Student], as his key he will be charged Is. for a new one. As the number of benches is limited, it is desirable that intending students should make application at °Lee. If there are more applicants than benches, the Committee reserve to themselves the right of deciding which students are to have the preference. The Library will be open on Sundays from 6 until 9 p.m. J. MORRISON, Hon. BE'.
